evidence.text:

Air France-KLM's second-quarter revenue increased 9.9 percent to EUR 9.3 billion. According to IBA on September 22, 2026, unit revenue rose 8.7 percent, supported by premium demand and cargo.

The earnings mix was less favorable. Adjusted operating profit declined EUR 251 million to EUR 484 million, leaving a 5.2 percent margin, while fuel and emissions costs created an EUR 804 million headwind, according to Morningstar on September 16, 2026.

Management has reduced expected 2026 capacity growth to 2-3 percent and expects a fuel bill of USD 8.9 billion after hedging. The figures show why revenue growth alone is not yet translating into higher operating profit.

evidence.title: Air France-KLM stock falls 1.8 percent on fuel pressure
evidence.text:
Air France-KLM stock (ISIN FR001400J770) was trading at EUR 11.44 on Euronext Paris at 11:16 a.m. CEST on September 24, 2026, down 1.80 percent during the session. The move comes as fuel costs and capacity discipline shape the airline group's operating outlook.

First-half 2026 revenue reached EUR 16.756 billion, up 7.4 percent from the comparable period, according to Ideal Investisseur on September 22, 2026. The same report cited an EBITDA margin of 31.1 percent, net income of negative EUR 133 million and free cash flow of EUR 928 million.

The figures show a sharper split between operating demand and bottom-line profitability. Revenue growth of 7.4 percent provides scale, while the negative net income figure highlights the impact of financing, fuel and other cost items on shareholder earnings.

Air France-KLM improved second-quarter unit revenue by EUR 672 million, but fuel and emissions costs created an EUR 804 million headwind, according to GP Aviation Intelligence on September 14, 2026. That comparison makes cost control the key operating variable. The group had hedged 67 percent of its 2026 fuel consumption and 40 percent of its 2027 consumption, leaving ticket pricing and network utilization central to the margin outlook.

evidence.title: Air France KLM Martina Cargo implements lifting aid
evidence.text:
Air France KLM Martina Cargo implements lifting aid

Working in an air cargo warehouse is a highly physical job that can strain the body, as breaking down pallets involves a lot of lifting and repetitive movements. Air France KLM Martinair Cargo has put a great deal of thought into alleviating the stress, and has collaborated with Swedish supplier, LiftsAll to try out its vacuum lifting aid during build-up and break-down operations. KLM involved its cargo staff closely during two trial phases, letting them work the equipment, assess how practical it was, and suggest improvements. The aim was to make sure the technology worked not just on paper but in the everyday reality of the operation. The test phases were carried out at the KLM Cargo Hub at Amsterdam Airport Schiphol, and since they proved successful, the device has now become a permanent assistant and is in daily use at the hub since 13JUL26.

The vacuum lift takes over much of the effort of moving individual cargo boxes during pallet-breakdown. Motion-capture measurements using Movella Xsens sensors indicate that the device eliminates the lifting strain normally involved in this with task, and the vacuum lifting aid can cope with around 80% of individual boxes. There are a few exceptions such as wet boxes, however, which still have to be moved by hand.

Implementing the lift is one milestone in KLM’s Autonomous Operations program, aimed at improving the efficiency and safety of ground operations, cargo and maintenance, on a daily basis, through enhancing the skills of its staff through the opportunities that new technology offers. Charlotte Elpers, VP Worldwide Operations, KLM Cargo, commented: “ At KLM Cargo, we continuously invest in innovation to drive improvements for both our customers and our people. The vacuum lift is a great example of how technology can make daily operations less physically demanding. By testing solutions together with our employees, we ensure they deliver real value in the workplace. This is exactly the kind of practical innovation we want to accelerate within KLM Cargo .”

evidence.title: Air France KLM Martinair Cargo introduces innovative vacuum lift to make cargo handling less physically demanding
evidence.text:
Air France KLM Martinair Cargo is taking another step towards a more innovative and future-ready cargo operation by introducing a vacuum lifting aid from Swedish company LiftsAll in its Build-up & Break-down operation at the KLM Cargo Hub at Amsterdam Airport Schiphol. Following two successful test phases, the technology has been in daily use since 13 July.

Cargo handling involves many repetitive physical movements, particularly during the breakdown of pallets. The vacuum lift supports employees in handling individual cargo boxes when breaking down pallets, significantly reducing the physical effort involved in lifting and moving cargo.

“At KLM Cargo, we continuously invest in innovation to drive improvements for both our customers and our people. The vacuum lift is a great example of how technology can make daily operations less physically demanding. By testing solutions together with our employees, we ensure they deliver real value in the workplace. This is exactly the kind of practical innovation we want to accelerate within KLM Cargo.” Charlotte Elpers, VP Worldwide Operations, KLM Cargo

The first results are encouraging. Sensor measurements using Movella Xsens motion capture technology show that the vacuum lift removes the lifting effort associated with handling boxes during pallet breakdown.

The technology can be used for approximately 80% of individual boxes. Some cargo, such as wet boxes, cannot be handled with the vacuum system and continues to require conventional handling methods.

Introducing new technology into a live cargo operation requires close collaboration with the people who use it. During two test phases, KLM Cargo employees worked with the vacuum lift in practice, testing its usability and sharing feedback to further improve the lifting aid. This approach ensures that innovation is not only technically viable but also responds to the needs of employees and the realities of the daily operation.

The vacuum lift is part of KLM’s broader Autonomous Operations programme, which aims to make work across ground operations, cargo and maintenance safer, smarter and more sustainable by combining human expertise with new technologies.

For KLM Cargo, it is a practical example of how this approach can make a tangible difference to the people working in the operation every day.

evidence.title: easyJet Announces Massive 18 New UK Routes In 1 Day: See Full List Now
evidence.text:
Yesterday, easyJet announced a raft of new routes from its bases across the UK. All in all, next summer will see it launch flights on 18 corridors, with a third of these departing from airports in Scotland. Spain is an unsurprisingly common theme among the new additions, given its popularity among British tourists , and, next summer, easyJet will grow its Spanish network by flying to Girona for the first time.

Another interesting aspect of the new additions to the easyJet network is the fact that there are relatively few from London. This shows the carrier's commitment to serving all regions of the country as opposed to just the capital city. According to aviation analyst @SeanM1997 on X , almost all of the new routes will operate twice a week. However, any whose frequencies differ will be duly noted.

As detailed in the interactive map that is embedded below, a third of the 18 new routes originate in Scotland. This coverage is spread across two airports, with Aberdeen Dyce Airport (ABZ) being the subject of two of the additions. From March 31, Aberdonians will be able to fly to Barcelona with easyJet, with a second new route to Palma de Mallorca (PMI) in the Balearic Islands commencing on May 3.

Elsewhere in Scotland, next summer will also see easyJet launch four routes from Edinburgh (EDI). The first two will begin serving Tivat (TIV) in Montenegro (once a week) and Hamburg (HAM) in Germany on March 29, with Bilbao (BIO) in Spain and Rome Fiumicino (FCO) in Italy following a day later. Kevin Doyle, who currently serves as easyJet's Country Manager for the United Kingdom, said yesterday that :

"Whether customers are planning a summer beach holiday, a city break, or a chance to explore somewhere new, there's never been a better time to book a flight or package holiday with easyJet."

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

South of the border, England accounts for the remaining 12 additions, with eight of these being from airports that don't serve London. Manchester (MAN) and Newcastle (NCL) will each see one addition, with weekly flights from the latter to Larnaca (LCA) in Cyprus starting on March 31. Just over three months later, on July 3, easyJet will commence operations on its new route from Manchester to Bastia (BIA).

Just down the road from Manchester, John Lennon Airport (LPL) in Liverpool will see two new additions next summer, with both of these corridors serving destinations in Spain. Flights to Girona (GRO) will start first, on March 28, followed by Murcia (RMU) on May 3. In the Midlands, Birmingham Airport (BHX) will get new easyJet flights to Milan Malpensa Airport (MXP) in Italy on March 29 and Tivat on May 3.

Further southwest, this just leaves Bristol Airport (BRS) when it comes to easyJet's non-London English additions next summer. From here, guests will be able to fly to Burgas Airport (BOJ) in Bulgaria as of May 28 next year, with flights to Montpellier Méditerranée Airport (MPL) in the south of France starting on July 1. But what does the picture look like in terms of additions at easyJet's London bases?

EasyJet has a substantial presence at both Paris Charles de Gaulle and Amsterdam Schiphol, giving Air France and KLM access to a much broader pool of European feed without having to add aircraft, frequencies, or scarce slots themselves.

As seen in the table below, easyJet currently operates flights out of four different bases that serve London. Of these, three will see new routes added next summer, with London Gatwick Airport (LGW) being another base from which flights to Girona are being launched. While these will initially operate twice a week from June 3, this frequency will jump to three flights a week on June 29 for the summer peak.

easyJet's London Presence, September 2026

Elsewhere, the earliest London addition will start on April 27, when easyJet launches flights from Southend Airport (SEN) to Rhodes (RHO) in Greece. Shortly afterward, May 1 will see another Greek addition, as the carrier begins flying from London Luton Airport (LTN) down to Thessaloniki (SKG). Gatwick is the only London airport to get two new routes, with its second, to Ajaccio (AJA), set to start on June 30, 2027.

evidence.title: EasyJet Adds 18 Routes For Summer 2027
evidence.text:
EasyJet will add 18 routes from 10 UK airports during summer 2027, continuing to broaden its leisure network ahead of the expected completion of Apollo’s £5.7 billion ($7.6 billion) acquisition of the airline.

The additions will provide 35X-weekly outbound frequencies at their peak, connecting UK airports with 16 destinations across Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Montenegro and Spain.

Spain accounts for six of the additions, including the LCC’s first UK services to Girona. Liverpool-Girona flights will start March 28 and operate 2X-weekly, followed by a 3X-weekly London Gatwick-Girona service from June 3. The carrier will also add 2X-weekly flights from Aberdeen to Barcelona and Palma de Mallorca, Liverpool to Murcia and Edinburgh to Bilbao.

Scotland receives the largest concentration of new routes. Alongside the two additions from Aberdeen, EasyJet will connect Edinburgh with Bilbao, Hamburg, Rome Fiumicino and Tivat. All six routes will operate 2X-weekly.

Other additions include London Gatwick-Ajaccio, Bristol-Montpellier, Manchester-Bastia, Birmingham-Milan Malpensa, Birmingham-Tivat and Bristol-Burgas, each operating twice per week. Newcastle-Larnaca and London Luton-Thessaloniki will operate weekly, while London Southend-Rhodes will be offered 2X-weekly.

The Southend route forms part of a wider expansion at the airport, where EasyJet will base a fourth Airbus A320neo from summer 2027. The additional aircraft is expected to support about 400 direct and indirect jobs, while Southend forecasts passenger traffic will exceed 1 million in 2027.

Overall, 15 of the 18 routes will operate twice per week, while only London Gatwick-Girona will receive 3X-weekly frequencies. The remaining two will operate weekly.

OAG Schedules Analyser data shows EasyJet offered approximately 23.45 million departure seats from UK airports during summer 2026, up 5.2% from 22.29 million a year earlier. Frequencies increased by 3.9% to about 130,400, while the number of airport pairs served rose from 539 to 599, an increase of 11.1%. The carrier added 74 routes and removed 14 between the two seasons, producing a net increase of 60.

Spain remained EasyJet's largest international market from the UK during summer 2026, with approximately 4.55 million departure seats, up 7.3% year over year. The number of UK-Spain routes increased by 15 to 123.

Italy was another area of expansion, with capacity increasing 11.1% to 1.62 million seats and the number of routes rising from 45 to 55.

The network announcement comes ahead of Apollo’s proposed acquisition of EasyJet , which is expected to close during the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Apollo’s ownership will be capped at 49.9% to comply with European airline ownership requirements.

evidence.title: easyJet announces six new UK-Spain flights for 2027, with fares from £35
evidence.text:
easyJet announces six new UK-Spain flights for 2027, with fares from £35

By Harry Dennis • Published: 24 Sep 2026 • 19:50 • 4 minutes read

easyJet is expanding its Spain network with six new routes for summer 2027. Credit: Mick Harper / Shutterstock

Liverpool and Aberdeen have never had a direct flight to Girona, Murcia or Barcelona, but that’s about to change. easyJet has just confirmed six new Spain routes for summer 2027, four of them genuinely new to any airline, with fares starting from just £35 (€40.70).

Liverpool becomes the only UK city flying direct to Girona and Murcia

Liverpool passengers have never had a nonstop option to either Girona or Murcia, and reaching Costa Brava (Spain’s rugged north-eastern coastline) or the sunny south-east has meant connecting through Barcelona or Madrid instead. That changes from March 28 2027, when easyJet’s new Liverpool to Girona service takes off twice a week, on Wednesdays and Sundays, with fares starting from £43.48 (€50.55).

The Murcia route follows a day later, on March 29, flying Mondays and Fridays from £42.98 (€49.97). No other airline currently flies either city pair, so both give passengers across the north-west of England something genuinely new rather than just another option alongside existing services. The Liverpool to Girona route alone is expected to carry around 9,000 seats in its first season.

The UK is already the country with the most connections to Girona airport, and the president of Girona’s provincial council welcomed the expansion as a chance to “diversify, not to depend exclusively on one or two companies, but to have a range of them”, while also spreading visitor numbers beyond the peak summer months.

Paul Winfield, Liverpool John Lennon Airport’s director of aviation development, said easyJet was “continuing to expand the choice available for passengers from Liverpool”, adding that both new services “will give passengers from across the north-west and north Wales even more opportunities to reach popular destinations in Spain direct from Liverpool.”

The Murcia route lands in a region already leaning heavily on British visitors. In the first seven months of 2026 alone, the UK sent 229,578 tourists to the Región de Murcia , up 7.3 per cent on the same period in 2025 and worth €290.6 million in spending, or nearly 30 per cent of all the region’s international tourist income. Regional tourism minister Carmen Conesa called the new route “a new advance to expand connectivity” for a market that already accounts for close to a third of the region’s foreign tourist spending.

Aberdeen gets its first-ever direct flight to Barcelona

Aberdeen’s new routes are arguably the boldest move in the whole announcement. From March 31 2027, easyJet will fly twice weekly, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, to Barcelona, with fares from £38.49 (€44.75), marking what Jonathan Ford, portfolio manager at AGS Airports (which runs Aberdeen Airport), called “the first time the city has been served directly from Aberdeen.”

Ford described the move as “particularly exciting”, and it’s easy to see why. Cataluña’s capital, home to the Sagrada Família and FC Barcelona, is one of the most visited cities in Spain, yet north-east Scotland has had to reach it via Edinburgh, Glasgow or London until now. Aberdeen’s only existing direct links to Spain are Ryanair’s routes to Alicante and Málaga, so easyJet’s arrival is also the airline’s first Spanish service from the airport.

A second new Aberdeen route lands in Mallorca

Aberdeen isn’t stopping at Barcelona. A twice-weekly service to Mallorca begins on May 3 2027, flying Thursdays and Sundays, with fares from just £35.48 (€41.25), the cheapest of all six new routes. Like Barcelona, no airline currently flies this route direct, so it doubles Aberdeen’s number of Spanish destinations from two to four in one announcement.

Kevin Doyle, easyJet’s UK country manager, said the airline’s “Spanish network is greatly expanding with six new routes from the UK, including Girona for the first time”, and Jonathan Ford called Barcelona and Mallorca “proven favourites with UK holidaymakers” now within easy reach of the north-east of Scotland.

Edinburgh’s new Bilbao service brings a low-cost rival to an existing route

Edinburgh’s addition is a little different. Vueling already flies passengers between Edinburgh and Bilbao , the industrial and cultural capital of the Basque Country and home to the Guggenheim museum, so this isn’t a brand new city pair. What it does bring, from March 30 2027, is easyJet’s first presence on the route, flying twice weekly on Tuesdays and Saturdays with fares from £45.48 (€52.88).

That still matters for passengers, though. Doyle called Scotland “always… an important market for easyJet”, and a second airline on any route usually means more seats and more competitive fares rather than one operator setting the price alone.

Gatwick’s Girona flight adds a budget rival to Jet2

The same pattern holds at Gatwick. Jet2 has flown Gatwick to Girona twice weekly since opening its Gatwick base in November 2025, so easyJet’s new service, starting June 3 2027 with three flights a week on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays from £49.48 (€57.53), is a second option rather than a new link as well.

Even so, it’s a meaningful one. The Gatwick service is expected to carry around 8,000 seats in its first year, and having a genuine low-cost alternative to Jet2 should help keep fares honest for anyone heading to Costa Brava’s beaches and medieval old town without wanting to land in Barcelona first and travel on by road or rail.

It’s worth asking, with any route announcement, whether ‘new’ really means new or just another airline joining an existing route. Here, it splits down the middle. Four of the six routes, Liverpool to Girona, Liverpool to Murcia, Aberdeen to Barcelona and Aberdeen to Mallorca, have no existing direct competitor at all and are genuinely new routes. The other two, Edinburgh to Bilbao and Gatwick to Girona, add easyJet as a second, lower-cost option on routes Vueling and Jet2 already fly.

Either way, the airline isn’t a small player testing the water. easyJet now carries more than 100 million passengers a year, flying more than 350 aircraft across more than 1,200 routes in 35 countries, and all 18 of its new routes for summer 2027 are already on sale , with package holidays available for those who want flights and accommodation bundled together.

Given how far ahead the launch dates sit, booking early is likely to be the best way to catch the lowest of these opening fares before they rise closer to departure.

evidence.title: EasyJet announces six new routes from Aberdeen and Edinburgh
evidence.text:
EasyJet announces six new routes from Aberdeen and Edinburgh

Budget airline easyJet has announced six new international routes and package holidays from Scottish airports.

From next summer, new flights will take off from Aberdeen and Edinburgh , offering greater connectivity between Scotland and European cities.

The airline will launch two new summer routes from Aberdeen International Airport to Barcelona, providing the first and only direct connection, and to Mallorca, linking the north east of Scotland with two of Spain’s most popular destinations.

Flights from Aberdeen to Barcelona will launch on 31 March 2027, operating twice weekly on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

Flights to Mallorca will begin on 3 May 2027, operating twice weekly on Thursdays and Sundays.

The two new routes mark further growth for easyJet at Aberdeen, following the addition of services to Paris Charles de Gaulle and Belfast International, giving customers more opportunities to travel directly from their local airport.

Aberdeen International airport will see more easyjet flights (Image: Supplied)

EasyJet is also continuing its growth in the Scottish capital at Edinburgh Airport, with four new routes to Tivat in Montenegro, Hamburg, Bilbao and Rome Fiumicino launching next summer.

The new Edinburgh to Tivat route will become the first and only direct connection between Scotland and the popular coastal destination, opening up a direct link to the Adriatic coast for customers across Scotland.

2 new routes from Aberdeen! ✈️☀️ easyJet is adding Barcelona and Palma de Mallorca to its Aberdeen network in 2027. ✈️ Fly to Barcelona on Wednesdays & Saturdays from 31st March. ✈️ Take off to Palma de Mallorca on Thursdays & Sundays from 3rd May. pic.twitter.com/vlDzsHfP91

— Aberdeen Airport ✈️ (@ABZ_Airport) September 24, 2026

Flights will launch on 29 March 2027 and operate twice weekly on Mondays and Thursdays.

The airline will also launch new flights from Edinburgh to Hamburg on 29 March 2027, operating twice weekly on Mondays and Fridays.

New flights between Edinburgh and Rome Fiumicino, and Bilbao, will follow on 30 March 2027, operating twice weekly on Tuesdays and Saturdays, further expanding the range of European destinations available to customers from Edinburgh.

Package holidays are available to book with easyJet Holidays, inclusive of flights, a handpicked hotel, 23kg luggage, and transfers for the beach destinations of Mallorca and Tivat.

An EasyJet Airbus jet (stock pic) (Image: Nicholas.T.Ansell)

Kevin Doyle, easyJet’s UK Country Manager, said: "Scotland has always been an important market for easyJet and, by providing even more new routes, we’re making it easier for customers across Scotland to connect to more of Europe, and easier for international visitors to explore even more of what Scotland has to offer.

"Affordable, direct flights from local airports with low-cost carriers like easyJet make the benefits of air travel possible for many people, and so it is important that Scotland remains a competitive and affordable place for airlines to invest in connectivity to support tourism and economic growth across Scotland, both for its people and its businesses."

Jonathan Ford, Portfolio Manager at AGS Airports, said: "We're delighted to see easyJet continue to expand its network from Aberdeen with the introduction of routes to Barcelona and Mallorca.

"The launch of a direct service to Barcelona is particularly exciting, marking the first time the city has been served directly from Aberdeen and opening up a fantastic new destination for travellers across the north east of Scotland.

"Both Barcelona and Mallorca are proven favourites with UK holidaymakers, and we have no doubt these routes will prove hugely popular with passengers looking for more choice and convenient access to some of Europe's most sought-after destinations.

"The continued growth of easyJet's offering at Aberdeen is a strong vote of confidence in the market and further strengthens the range of international connectivity available from our airport."

Stephanie Wear, Chief Commercial Officer at Edinburgh Airport, said: "The introduction of Scotland’s first direct route to Tivat is particularly exciting as it opens up Montenegro to passengers for the first time.

"As one of Europe’s increasingly popular destinations, it's great to give passengers easier access to everything Montenegro has to offer.

"Alongside new services to Bilbao, Hamburg and Rome Fiumicino, all well known for their rich history and culture, these routes add even more variety to our European network and further expand the choice on offer at Scotland’s busiest airport."

evidence.title: Here's Why Wizz Air Holdings (LON:WIZZ) Has Caught The Eye Of Investors
evidence.text:
Here's Why Wizz Air Holdings (LON:WIZZ) Has Caught The Eye Of Investors

For beginners, it can seem like a good idea (and an exciting prospect) to buy a company that tells a good story to investors, even if it currently lacks a track record of revenue and profit. Sometimes these stories can cloud the minds of investors, leading them to invest with their emotions rather than on the merit of good company fundamentals. While a well funded company may sustain losses for years, it will need to generate a profit eventually, or else investors will move on and the company will wither away.

Did you know there are some financial metrics that can provide clues of a potential multi-bagger? One common approach is to try and find a company with returns on capital employed (ROCE) that are increasing, in conjunction with a growing amount of capital employed. Put simply, these types of businesses are compounding machines, meaning they are continually reinvesting their earnings at ever-higher rates of return. Having said that, from a first glance at Wizz Air Holdings ( LON:WIZZ ) we aren't jumping out of our chairs at how returns are trending, but let's have a deeper look.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Understanding Return On Capital Employed (ROCE)

For those who don't know, ROCE is a measure of a company's yearly pre-tax profit (its return), relative to the capital employed in the business. To calculate this metric for Wizz Air Holdings, this is the formula:

Return on Capital Employed = Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) ÷ (Total Assets - Current Liabilities)

0.024 = €142m ÷ (€9.6b - €3.8b) (Based on the trailing twelve months to June 2025) .

Therefore, Wizz Air Holdings has an ROCE of 2.4%. Ultimately, that's a low return and it under-performs the Airlines industry average of 13%.

On the surface, the trend of ROCE at Wizz Air Holdings doesn't inspire confidence. To be more specific, ROCE has fallen from 6.1% over the last five years. Meanwhile, the business is utilizing more capital but this hasn't moved the needle much in terms of sales in the past 12 months, so this could reflect longer term investments. It may take some time before the company starts to see any change in earnings from these investments.

Bringing it all together, while we're somewhat encouraged by Wizz Air Holdings' reinvestment in its own business, we're aware that returns are shrinking. evidence.text:
Turkish Airlines Finalizes 100-Jet 737-8 Order With 50 Options

ISTANBUL — Turkish Airlines (TK) has finalized a firm order for 100 Boeing 737-8 aircraft and taken options for 50 more 737 MAX jets, completing an agreement that remained contingent on engine negotiations when the carrier outlined it in 2025.

The airline told Türkiye's Public Disclosure Platform that deliveries are scheduled between 2033 and 2037. Its board made the purchase decision on September 18, five days before the public announcement.

Boeing and Turkish Airlines marked the agreement in New York in the presence of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. The manufacturer described the transaction as the carrier's largest Boeing single-aisle order .

The agreement also gives Turkish Airlines substitution rights for the 737-10, the largest member of the MAX family. Neither Boeing's release nor the airline's market filing divides the 50 options between the 737-8 and 737-10, and neither source discloses a price.

CFM condition cleared for the firm order

Turkish Airlines announced the outline of the MAX transaction in September 2025 , alongside an order for up to 75 Boeing 787 Dreamliners. Although negotiations with Boeing were complete, the airline said the MAX order would be placed only after successful talks with engine manufacturer CFM International.

Reuters reported that a disagreement over long-term engine-maintenance terms delayed the deal and that Turkish Airlines had threatened to withdraw. The airline and Boeing did not disclose the final engine or maintenance terms in their September 23 announcements.

That chronology changes the status of the narrowbody plan Airways reported a year ago . The 100 737-8s are now a firm purchase; the other 50 aircraft remain options.

The 100-aircraft firm order exceeds a 70-aircraft firm order Turkish Airlines signed with Boeing in 2013 . That earlier purchase covered 40 737-8s, ten 737-9s, and 20 Next-Generation 737-800s, with options for another 25 737-8s. Boeing called it the airline's largest order from the manufacturer at the time.

The new 737-8s are due after the first aircraft in Turkish Airlines' 2025 Dreamliner agreement. That package covers 50 firm 787-9 and 787-10 aircraft and 25 options, with deliveries planned from 2029 to 2034.

Turkish Airlines and AJet together operate more than 200 Boeing aircraft across the 737 MAX, 737 Next-Generation, 777, 777 Freighter, and 787 families, according to Boeing.

"This agreement marks another significant step in the continued expansion of our fleet," said Murat Şeker, Turkish Airlines chairman of the board and executive committee. "The new Boeing 737 MAX aircraft will bring greater efficiency and flexibility to our operations, supporting the extensive network we serve from our hub in Istanbul."

The reviewed airline filing and Boeing release do not say how quickly Turkish Airlines expects to take the 100 firm aircraft within the five-year delivery window.

evidence.title: Aena stock gains as DORA III plan and Bank of America target support upside
evidence.text:
Aena stock (ISIN ES0105046009) traded at EUR 25.58 on the Madrid Stock Exchange on September 21, 2026, up 0.79% on the day and within the current IBEX 35 rally environment. According to Bolsamania on September 16, 2026, Bank of America reiterated its buy recommendation on Aena and increased its price target from EUR 30.50 to EUR 30.70, signaling confidence in the regulated investment plan and traffic growth.

DORA III plan drives investment and returns

As TradingView reported on September 21, 2026, Spain has approved the third Airport Regulation Document, known as DORA III, covering the period 2027-2031 and allowing regulated investments of EUR 9.99 billion in Aena's airport network.

According to a presentation to investors cited by La Vanguardia on September 21, 2026, Aena expects to obtain a return of 8.32% on these DORA III investments of EUR 9,991 million up to 2031, highlighting the regulated framework as a key driver of profitability over the next decade.

The same presentation indicates that passenger traffic across Aena's network is projected to reach 363 million passengers by 2031 under the DORA III assumptions, which would represent a significant increase versus current levels and support growth in aeronautical and commercial revenues, as summarized by TradingView .

Bank of America target implies double-digit upside

Bank of America sees the current regulatory clarity and traffic outlook as reasons to maintain a positive stance on Aena. According to Bolsamania , the bank raised its price target from EUR 30.50 to EUR 30.70 and reiterated a buy recommendation, estimating potential upside of 22.8% based on its valuation work.

Measured against the September 21, 2026 closing price of EUR 25.58, the new Bank of America target of EUR 30.70 implies a gain of roughly 20% from that level, underlining that the shares trade at a discount to the value the analyst house assigns under the DORA III framework and expected growth in commercial income.

The analyst note cited by Bolsamania highlights three main drivers behind the 22.8% potential upside: improved visibility on regulated returns after the DORA III approval, ongoing growth in passenger traffic, and expansion of the commercial business across the airport network.

Regulatory and inflation risks remain in focus

Alongside the upside case, Aena faces execution and macro risks around the large investment program. As Expansión reported on September 21, 2026, Aena has indicated that it would delay certain expansion projects if inflation significantly increases construction costs, in order to avoid breaching the EUR 9,991 million regulated investment cap set in DORA III.

This means that while the DORA III framework secures regulated returns of around 8.32% on the planned investments, higher inflation or cost overruns could force a rephasing of projects and potentially slow the pace at which capacity and commercial areas are expanded, as highlighted by Expansión .

The Council of Ministers approval of DORA III for Aena, mentioned in a market brief by SquawkNews on September 21, 2026, provides regulatory certainty, but also ties returns to compliance with efficiency and sustainability targets, adding another layer of operational execution risk over the 2027-2031 period.

Stock holds support after recent pullback

Technically, the share price has recently found support after a correction from record highs. A chart analysis by Expansión on September 21, 2026 notes that the roughly 12% decline from all-time highs at the end of August to the lows of the prior week has been arrested at the base of the upward channel in which the price has moved since late 2022.

The same analysis points to a technical upside target around the zone of prior annual and historical highs, between EUR 27.65 and EUR 27.80, suggesting that if the support at the channel base holds, Aena stock could attempt to retest those levels in the coming months according to Expansión .

Within the IBEX 35 on September 21, 2026, Aena's 0.79% daily gain to EUR 25.58 left it participating in the broader index advance of 0.72% to 19,696.70 points, as shown in data from Territorio Madrid, with an intraday range for the stock between EUR 25.42 and EUR 25.60 and modest positive momentum in line with other transport and infrastructure names.

evidence.title: Aena exceeds €1 billion in net profit during first half of 2026
evidence.text:
Aena closed the first half of 2026 with a net profit of €1.002 billion, surpassing the €893.8 million recorded in the same period last year. The operator projects 3% passenger traffic growth for the full year, driven by temporary diversions to Spain resulting from the Strait of Hormuz crisis and by constraints on rail transport following the accident in Adamuz, the company detailed in a statement. Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) reached €1.7989 billion, representing 6.3% growth year-on-year. Total consolidated revenue stood at €3.2996 billion, with the aeronautical segment contributing €1.7021 billion and the commercial division adding €991 million. Net cash generated from operating activities amounted to €1.5985 billion. The group's airports handled 189,964,768 passengers between January and June, an increase of 3.9%. In Spain, the network recorded 156,246,234 travelers. Despite the growth, the operator cautioned about a lack of visibility for the second half of the year, due to the expiration of fuel hedges and uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict. The company reported weakness in load factors, translating into actual traffic falling short of available seats and affecting the evolution of capacity scheduled by airlines. On the investment front, the company spent €916.3 million during the semester, focusing on facility improvements and operational safety. This amount includes €340 million allocated to the acquisition of a 51% stake in the company that owns Leeds Bradford Airport and a 49% stake in Newcastle Airport , a transaction completed on May 7 . Furthermore, on March 30 , subsidiary Aena Desarrollo Internacional won the concession for Rio de Janeiro Galeão International Airport for 2.9 billion reais (€490.7 million), a contract that will run until May 2039. Operating expenses (OPEX) amounted to €1.4988 billion, driven by an 11.8% increase in personnel costs and a 15.3% rise in other items. Consolidated net financial debt reached €6.724 billion, compared to €5.509 billion at the end of the previous year, raising the debt-to-EBITDA ratio to 1.73 times.

evidence.text:
Aena implemented an artificial intelligence video analytics system designed to monitor ground handling operations on its airport aprons. According to information provided by the operator, the technology is already operational at Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas , Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat , and Palma de Mallorca airports. The system, developed by Indra in collaboration with Synaptic Aviation , monitors in real time the tasks performed from the moment an aircraft parks until it is ready for its next flight. The tool detects actions such as the placement of chocks, baggage loading and unloading, refueling, and catering services, allowing for better use of infrastructure and strengthening safety for airlines and ramp services.

"This project is a tangible example of how Aena's innovation strategy is put at the service of its operational processes and excellence in customer experience," said Luis Cañon , Aena's Director of Innovation and Customer Experience. "The application of Artificial Intelligence in such critical processes as aircraft rotation allows not only to optimize operational efficiency but also to consolidate Aena's leadership in building a smarter, more resilient airport ecosystem committed to airlines and passengers," he added.

It monitors ground handling tasks in real time from aircraft parking until readiness for the next flight, including chocks placement, baggage loading/unloading, refuelling, and catering services.

evidence.title: Aena revoluciona la gestión de sus pistas con inteligencia artificial para acelerar la escala de los aviones
evidence.text:
Aena revoluciona la gestión de sus pistas con inteligencia artificial para acelerar la escala de los aviones

Aena ha dado un salto cualitativo en la modernización de sus infraestructuras con la puesta en marcha de un sistema pionero de analítica de vídeo basado en Inteligencia Artificial . Este proyecto, diseñado para optimizar los procesos de asistencia en tierra o handling, permite monitorizar en tiempo real cada actividad que rodea al avión desde su aterrizaje hasta su próximo despegue.

Implantada inicialmente en los aeropuertos de Madrid-Barajas , Barcelona-El Prat y Palma de Mallorca , esta tecnología busca reducir los tiempos de escala , mejorar la puntualidad y elevar la seguridad en las operaciones de plataforma.

La gestión de las operaciones en plataforma ha entrado en una nueva era digital gracias a la alianza estratégica entre Aena, Indra y Synaptic Aviation . El nuevo sistema de analítica de vídeo utiliza algoritmos avanzados para supervisar de forma automatizada el conjunto de tareas críticas que se realizan durante la escala de una aeronave. Desde la colocación de los calzos y el suministro de servicios de catering hasta el repostaje de combustible y la carga de equipaje, cada movimiento es registrado y analizado para garantizar una coordinación milimétrica entre todos los agentes implicados en la operativa aeroportuaria.

Esta herramienta tecnológica permite a los gestores aeroportuarios obtener una visión sin precedentes sobre la eficiencia de los procesos de rotación . Al detectar posibles cuellos de botella en tiempo real, el sistema facilita una toma de decisiones mucho más ágil y precisa, lo que se traduce en un aprovechamiento óptimo de las infraestructuras existentes.

La implementación no ha requerido modificaciones estructurales en los aeropuertos, ya que aprovecha la red de cámaras actual para convertir las imágenes en datos valiosos que alimentan la estrategia de innovación del gestor aeroportuario.

Mejora directa en la experiencia del pasajero y la puntualidad

El impacto de esta tecnología llega directamente al viajero a través de una mejora en la puntualidad y en la fiabilidad de los vuelos. Al optimizar los servicios de asistencia en tierra, se reducen las probabilidades de retrasos operativos vinculados a la logística de plataforma.

Según los responsables de innovación de Aena, el uso de Inteligencia Artificial en procesos tan críticos no solo consolida el liderazgo de la compañía en la construcción de aeropuertos más resilientes, sino que también refuerza el compromiso con las aerolíneas al ofrecerles un entorno de trabajo más previsible y eficiente.

Desde el Aeropuerto de Palma de Mallorca, uno de los tres centros donde ya opera el sistema, destacan que esta tecnología actúa como un elemento diferenciador y de alto valor estratégico. La disponibilidad de información fiable en entornos complejos facilita la labor de los equipos humanos, quienes ahora cuentan con un apoyo digital para gestionar situaciones de alta densidad de tráfico con mayor seguridad operativa . Este despliegue marca un hito en la digitalización a gran escala, alineando la operativa de tierra con los estándares de los aeropuertos más inteligentes del mundo.

Un ecosistema aeroportuario más sostenible y digital

Más allá de la eficiencia operativa, el proyecto contribuye significativamente a la reducción del impacto medioambiental . Una rotación de aeronaves más rápida y coordinada disminuye los tiempos de espera con motores encendidos y optimiza los desplazamientos de los vehículos de servicio en plataforma, reduciendo así las emisiones de CO2 asociadas a la actividad en tierra. Esta iniciativa forma parte integral de la hoja de ruta de Aena para incorporar tecnologías disruptivas que aporten valor real al negocio y refuercen la seguridad en todo el ecosistema aéreo.

Tras el éxito de esta primera fase en los tres principales aeropuertos de la red española, Aena evaluará la expansión de la analítica de vídeo a otros centros operativos según las prioridades de tráfico y necesidades técnicas.

Con este movimiento, España se sitúa a la vanguardia de la transformación digital en el sector aeroportuario , demostrando cómo la Inteligencia Artificial puede ser la clave para gestionar infraestructuras críticas de manera más transparente, segura y orientada a la excelencia en el servicio al cliente.

evidence.text:
Aena commercial revenue soars 10.8% to €1,466m

By DFNI Staff Writer in Airports , Europe , Financial News , Latest News October 29, 2025 Comments Off on Aena commercial revenue soars 10.8% to €1,466m

Retail and business income drive record performance as total revenue tops €4,785.2m; passenger traffic and profits continue to rise

Aena ‘s commercial revenue climbed 10.8% to €1,466.1m (US$1.56bn) in the first nine months of 2025 , compared to the same period in 2024.

The growth was underpinned by higher sales across retail, food and beverage, and duty free activities, as well as an increase in total business revenue, including both fixed and variable rent invoiced and Minimum Annual Guaranteed Rents, which jumped 13% year on year.

Overall, total sales from Aena’s commercial activities rose 8.7%, highlighting the strength of non-aeronautical income in the group’s diversified business model.

Total consolidated revenue for January–September 2025 reached €4,785.2m (US$5.10bn), an 8.8% increase on the previous year. Aeronautical revenue accounted for €2,556.2m (US$2.73bn), up 5.5%, while the continuing rebound in travel and spending at airports supported both segments.

The company also recorded a net profit of €1,579.4m (US$1.68bn), compared with €1,449.8m (US$1.54bn) in the same period of 2024. Its EBITDA rose 8.2% to €2,882.7m (US$3.07bn), with a margin of 60.2%, reflecting robust operational performance and efficiency gains.

Passenger traffic across the Aena Group , including its airports in Spain, London-Luton, and Aena Brasil (notably Congonhas Airport in São Paulo), grew 4.1% year on year to 294.1m passengers. In Spain alone, the figure reached 247.1m passengers, up 3.9%.

Aena’s net financial debt stood at €5,127m (US$5.46bn), down from €5,498m (US$5.85bn) a year earlier, bringing the group’s net financial debt-to-EBITDA ratio to 1.37 times.

Cash generation remained strong, with net cash from operating activities at €2,525.6m (US$2.69bn), compared to €2,352.8m (US$2.51bn) in 2024. Excluding energy costs, other operating expenses in the Spanish airport network rose €38.4m (US$40.8m), or 4.5%, year on year.

evidence.title: Fraport: computer vision and Artificial Intelligence optimise airport operations
evidence.text:
Fraport: computer vision and Artificial Intelligence optimise airport operations

Special transport units are needed to move cargo and baggage at airports. The solution developed by Axulus Reply for Fraport, one of the leading international companies in the airport business, has contributed to reducing the search and set-up times of the drivers and minimising empty runs.

#Artificial Intelligence #Computer Vision #Axulus Reply

Special transport units are needed to move cargo and baggage at airports. At Germany's largest airport, Frankfurt Airport, an average of 1,400 aircraft movements take place per day. Depending on the type of aircraft and number of loaded cargo or baggage units on the aircraft, a different number of transport units might be required. For this purpose, around 10,000 of these transport units are distributed across the entire apron in various parking areas.

Innovative technology for transport processes

One of Fraport's challenges is that many empty runs occur during transport to and from the aircraft. The drivers have to search for the transport units in the parking areas and transport them to the aircraft. Fraport AG has therefore tested various technologies – equipping the transport units with sensors and camera technology. So far, no technology or solution has been found that is eligible for airport operations. Due to the technological progress in the field of computer vision and AI, this new technology was tested together with Axulus Reply in order to solve the current problem.

The transport units are located in fixed parking areas when they are not being used to load or unload an aircraft. Axulus Reply has installed cameras mounted on a pole in the parking areas, sending a livestream to the cloud to analyse it with an AI pipeline. The analysis determines the type of transport unit, the loading status, and the parking status of each detected wagon. This information is displayed in a web app that shows free and occupied spaces in order to optimise the work of ground handling teams based on this information.

When using new camera technology, it is important that the camera is able to optimally capture parking areas of different sizes, and that larger distances between the camera locations and the parking areas can be bridged. In addition to having the high recognition rate, the new solution needed to be embedded in processes at Fraport and designed to be user-friendly. Dispatchers were to receive capacity data on peak coverage in a simple way.

The Digital Factory – driver for innovation and digital transformation at Fraport AG – announced a worldwide challenge and presented this problem. Here, Axulus Reply prevailed as one of 18 applicants

The solution more than met the high requirements and has proven itself in daily use. It helps to reduce the search and set-up times of the drivers and to minimise empty runs. It thus makes a valuable contribution to cost reduction, makes transport processes more efficient, and has a positive impact on CO2 reduction.

Fraport AG is one of the leading international companies in the airport business and is active at 31 airports across four continents. The airport operator provides all operational and administrative services for airport and terminal operations. The figures, data and facts from 2019 around Frankfurt Airport are impressive: Within 24 hours, more than 1,400 aircraft took off and landed here, and more than 6,000 tonnes of cargo were handled.

Axulus Reply is the Reply Group company focused on providing innovative technology-based solutions based on Industrie 4.0 and IIOT to quickly generate sustainable added value for customers across complex supply and value chains. Axulus Reply specialises in the entire value chain of Engineering Manufacturing/IoT and Supply Chain Execution (SCE). The company focuses on scalable, modular Industrie 4.0 solutions and helps its customers achieve maximum efficiency through comprehensive consulting and technologies.

evidence.title: How Frankfurt Airport uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to transform ground handling efficiency and predict aircraft turnaround times
evidence.text:

How Frankfurt Airport uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to transform ground handling efficiency and predict aircraft turnaround times

International Airport Review 2026-03-30T08:59:00+01:00

At International Airport Summit operators shared practical lessons on visibility, predictability and trust from one of Europe’s most advanced airside digitalisation programmes.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer a future ambition for airport ground operations. At Frankfurt Airport, it is already shaping how aircraft turnarounds are monitored, predicted and optimised in real time.

During the International Airport Summit Berlin panel, AI-driven ground operations , leaders from Fraport, zeroG Lufthansa Group and FRAAlliance shared a refreshingly practical view of what it takes to deploy AI at scale in one of Europe’s busiest and most complex operational environments. The discussion moved beyond theory, focusing instead on data transparency, human trust, collaboration and what really makes AI usable on the apron.

From blind spots to real-time transparency

For many years, turnaround operations relied heavily on assumptions and best guesses. As Christian Ritter, Head of Product & Principal Data Scientist at zeroG Lufthansa Group, put it, operators were effectively “steering highly complex processes like the turnaround without holding the full information into what is happening. This leads to sub-optimal decision-making, which in turn leads to delays and cancellations.”

Computer vision has changed that. At Frankfurt, AI systems now monitor more than 30 turnaround events, generating precise timestamps across the entire process, from on-block and unloading through to boarding, pushback and departure.

Lena Luftschitz, Project Lead Digitalisation Airside Operations at Fraport AG, explained how transformative this visibility has been. “Before, we didn’t really know a lot about what was going on during the turnaround process or how far along we were,” she explained. “Now we suddenly have a huge amount of data available to us.”

The challenge, however, is not collecting data but deciding how to use it.

A recurring theme was the need to avoid overwhelming already stretched operations teams. Frederik Jean, Leader Consulting & Strategy at FraAlliance, stressed that AI systems must focus attention where it matters most. “What we want to achieve is picking out what’s not going according to plan,” he said, rather than flooding users with every available data point.

From an airport operator’s perspective, one of the most valuable outcomes is improved predictability. “The main thing we want to know is when the aircraft will be ready to leave the stand again,” Lena noted. Predicting aircraft ready time and off-block time allows airports to make smarter, earlier decisions across stands, gates and resources.

For ground handlers, the benefits are just as tangible. Lena highlighted how AI-generated timestamps now show exactly when ULD unloading begins. “Airports don’t have to direct their employees on a best-guess basis anymore,” she explained. “They can send people when they’re actually needed, without waiting around.” This is a great workforce productivity saving.

c: International Airport Review[/caption]

Designing AI around people, not just processes

While the technology is powerful, the panel was clear that success depends on human-centred design. Christian emphasised that AI solutions were co-developed with operational users from the start. “We visited them in the ops control centres, looked at how they work, what information they have and what they actually want,” he said. “It’s not about the tech, it’s about how you integrate it into their daily work.”

This approach has paid dividends in adoption and trust. Lena shared a telling anecdote: “One of the turnaround managers told us, ‘It was really great seeing what I suggested actually appear in the dashboard I now use.’ That really helps with acceptance.”

Education also plays a critical role. While AI has become more familiar, Christian noted the importance of explaining how systems work, including their limitations.

People are still the decision makers,” he said. “We just want to give them a tool, and they need to understand the tool to make the most out of it.”

Addressing trust, data protection and resistance

Unsurprisingly, introducing cameras and AI into airside environments raises concerns. The panel did not shy away from this. “Naturally people don’t like being filmed while they work,” Christian acknowledged. Engagement with workers’ councils and strict data protection measures were essential. “We made sure we don’t detect individual people,” he explained. “We track the process, not performance.”

Frederick added that resistance to new systems is natural. “If you show transparency from the beginning and make it clear this is a supporting system, not a replacement for humans, you can really gain trust.”

Crucially, trust-building does not end at go-live. “You’re never really done,” Christian said. “We still collect feedback and amend the system, so it stays relevant for users.”

Frankfurt’s progress has been accelerated by close collaboration between the airport, airline and FraAlliance, a joint venture that helps align objectives and data governance.

“In the beginning, everyone optimises their own systems,” Frederick explained. “What you need is a common vision, shared KPIs and shared goals.” Data sharing is often the hardest step, but once trust is established, momentum builds quickly. “After that, you can proceed with the project at the speed you want,” he continued.

Lena echoed this sentiment from the airport side. “At the end of the day, we’re all working towards the same goal: smooth and efficient operations,” she stated. “Airlines, ground handlers and service providers all benefit if everyone has the same information.”

Operating in a safety-critical environment means innovation must be carefully staged. The panel repeatedly returned to the value of proof-of-concept projects, pilots and incremental rollouts.

“We cannot just stop operations for a day,” Christian said. “So, we keep the risk low at the beginning, start with a pilot, then gradually expand.” Importantly, fallback processes remain in place so operators can revert to existing methods if needed.

This phased approach also helps with regulatory hurdles. As Frederick pointed out, GDPR is “not a showstopper, but a hurdle.” Addressing data protection early, in parallel with technical development, makes it manageable.

What this means for the wider airport community

Frankfurt’s experience shows that AI-driven ground operations are not about futuristic automation, but about visibility, collaboration and trust. Even with imperfect data and partial coverage, as Christian noted, “tracking 80% is still much better than tracking nothing.”

For airports watching from the sidelines, the message was clear: be brave enough to start, small enough to learn and collaborative enough to scale.

These are exactly the kinds of real-world insights that make the International Airport Summit such a valuable forum. As AI, data sharing and operational resilience move higher up the airport agenda, next year’s summit promises even deeper discussion on how innovation can be safely and practically embedded into daily operations.

For those shaping the future of airport performance, Frankfurt’s journey is a compelling reason to be part of that conversation.

evidence.title: Fraport sees 8.2% revenue growth in 2025
evidence.text:
Fraport sees 8.2% revenue growth in 2025

By Jill Sayles in Airports , Europe , Financial News , Latest News , Retail News March 18, 2026 Comments Off on Fraport sees 8.2% revenue growth in 2025

Diversified airport portfolio drives revenue and EBITDA growth, while completion of major investments supports cash flow recovery and dividend proposal

Fraport Group has reported a strong set of results for the 2025 fiscal year, with improved performance across key financial metrics and a return to positive free cash flow following the completion of major investment programmes.

Boosted by growth across all four business segments, group revenue increased by 8.2% year-on-year to €4.2bn, while EBITDA rose by 10.4% to €1.44bn. Free cash flow improved significantly, increasing by around €700m to €24.4m, returning to positive territory for the first time since 2018.

Fraport CEO, Stefan Schulte said: “Our broad diversification has paved the way for a very positive business performance in the past fiscal year, as reflected in the growth both in revenue and operating result.

“Free cash flow is positive again, for the first time since 2018. The completion of major investment projects will significantly boost our free cash flow even further. This will provide us with more leeway in the future to reduce debt and facilitate dividend payments to our shareholders.”

The group states its improved performance was supported by rising passenger traffic across its global airport portfolio, alongside pricing effects and increased demand for ground handling services. Net profit declined by 6.7% to €468.1m, reflecting higher depreciation and amortisation, as well as interest costs linked to the Lima terminal expansion, and the absence of a one-off gain recorded in 2024.

Passenger traffic across the group reached 184 million in 2025, slightly exceeding pre-pandemic 2019 levels. Growth was particularly strong at Fraport’s international assets, including airports in Greece, Antalya and Lima, while Frankfurt Airport remained around 10% below 2019 levels despite a 2.6% increase year-on-year.

Schulte added: “We would be significantly better placed in Frankfurt if we did not have the excessive regulatory costs that continue to limit passenger growth in the German market. A major step forward has come with the Government’s announcement to withdraw the latest increase in aviation tax.

“This step now needs to be implemented. If further cost reductions follow, a reversal of the trend is possible. Sweden’s example shows the kind of growth surges that are possible if aviation taxes are completely abolished.”

Looking ahead, a major milestone will be the opening of Frankfurt Airport’s Terminal 3 on 23 April 2026. The €4bn development will add capacity for around 19 million passengers annually and introduce enhanced passenger processing technologies and upgraded retail and lounge facilities.

Fraport also highlighted progress on its sustainability agenda, with renewable energy from a North Sea offshore wind farm set to supply 100% of the airport’s electricity needs from July, marking a key step towards achieving Net Zero operations under Scope 1 and 2 by 2045.

For 2026, the group expects passenger numbers to reach between 188 million and 195 million across its portfolio, with EBITDA forecast to rise to around €1.5bn. However, net profit is projected to decline in the short term due to higher depreciation and financing costs associated with Terminal 3. Fraport has proposed a dividend of €1.00 per share for the 2025 fiscal year.

evidence.title: Fraport’s International Airports Fuel Scalable Growth Amid Debt Transition and Dividend Shift
evidence.text:
Catch pre-market movers with AI signals.

Fraport’s International Airports Fuel Scalable Growth Amid Debt Transition and Dividend Shift

- Fraport's scalable growth strategy relies on its global airport portfolio, with 7.1% January 2026 international passenger traffic growth driven by strong performances in Brazil (+24.9%) and Slovenia (+20%).

- The company aims to reach €1.5B EBITDA by 2026 through international expansion, balancing capital-intensive investments with planned dividend resumption (€1/share) as leverage ratio improves below 5.0x.

- Key risks include Boeing BA -- delivery delays impacting Frankfurt's recovery and operational volatility from strikes/weather, while sustained international growth across multiple regions is critical to offsetting domestic market fluctuations.

The case for Fraport is fundamentally about scale in a vast, fragmented market. The global airport services industry represents a massive and growing Total Addressable Market, and Fraport's international portfolio is its primary lever for capturing more of it. The company operates a diverse network spanning key hubs like Frankfurt, strategic locations in Brazil and Turkey, and growing markets in Slovenia and Southeast Europe. This global footprint is not just a collection of assets; it's a deliberate strategy to diversify revenue streams and ride the recovery wave across different regions.

Evidence of that strategy's early traction is clear. In January 2026, the group's international business developed particularly dynamically, with total passenger traffic across its actively operated airports rising 7.1 percent to approximately 9.6 million passengers . More striking were the standout performances: the Brazilian airports of Fortaleza and Porto Alegre delivered a combined increase of 24.9 percent, while Ljubljana Airport in Slovenia saw growth exceeding 20 percent. This kind of high-single-digit to double-digit growth across multiple continents demonstrates the model's potential to accelerate expansion, especially as recovery in South America and Southeast Europe continues.

The market outlook, as reflected in analyst metrics, aligns with this growth narrative. Fraport's Smart Score of 3.4 is underpinned by a strong Growth factor of 5, indicating a consensus view that the company's expansion trajectory is a key driver of its long-term potential.

This isn't just about returning to pre-pandemic levels at Frankfurt, which still has room to improve. It's about leveraging the international portfolio to drive the next phase of revenue growth, using established hubs as financial engines to fund and support expansion in higher-growth markets. The bottom line is that Fraport's scalability thesis rests on its ability to replicate its operational model across this fragmented global landscape, turning its diverse portfolio into a consistent engine for market capture.

Revenue Growth Engine: Traffic Capacity and International Leverage

Fraport's projected revenue growth is a direct function of its ability to scale passenger capacity across a diversified network. The company's 2026 outlook calls for core earnings, measured as EBITDA, to reach around €1.5 billion , a 4% increase from the previous year. This forecast hinges on the fundamental driver of higher passenger traffic, a metric where the company's international portfolio is proving to be the primary engine of expansion.

The growth story is not uniform, highlighting the model's scalability. While Frankfurt saw a solid 4.9 percent increase in January , its momentum stalled in February due to operational headwinds from strikes and weather, leaving traffic stable. In stark contrast, the international portfolio delivered dynamic growth, with total passenger traffic rising 7.1 percent in January and continuing to climb in February. This divergence is the essence of Fraport's strategy: using its home market as a financial anchor while its global assets provide the high-growth fuel.

The business model's scalability is evidenced by this broad-based expansion. Growth was not confined to a single region but was seen across all continents in February, with standout performances from its Brazilian, Slovenian, and Greek airports. Cargo volumes also rose, with Frankfurt's cargo increasing 4.8 percent year-on-year in February and the group's logistics sector showing gains. This multi-dimensional expansion-across passenger traffic, cargo, and geography-demonstrates a replicable operational model capable of driving higher EBITDA from a wider base.

The path to the €1.5 billion EBITDA target, therefore, depends on the international portfolio's ability to consistently outpace the home market. Its dynamic growth provides a crucial offset to local volatility and is the key lever for achieving the company's projected profit increase. For a growth investor, this setup offers a clear line of sight: as Fraport continues to leverage its global footprint, the scalability of its operations should translate into a more robust and higher-margin revenue stream.

Financial Mechanics: Capital Intensity vs. Future Cash Flow

The path to scaling Fraport's global ambitions is paved with significant capital expenditure. The company is in the midst of a multi-year investment cycle, funding terminal expansions and infrastructure upgrades worldwide. This heavy spending is the necessary fuel for future growth, but it creates a clear tension with the company's near-term financials. Despite strong revenue growth driven by rising passenger traffic, Fraport expects a significant decline in net earnings for 2026 . The primary culprits are an increased depreciation of around 140 million euros and higher interest expenses of approximately 90 million euros. In other words, the cash being poured into assets today is already hitting the bottom line through higher non-cash charges and debt servicing costs.

This sets up a critical inflection point. The company's 2026 outlook hinges on the successful transition from a capital-intensive build-out phase to one of sustainable cash generation. The key signal is the planned dividend. Fraport intends to pay its first planned dividend payment since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, a 1 euro per share payout for the 2025 financial year, to be distributed in 2026. This move is a major shift in capital allocation, signaling management's confidence that the investment cycle is nearing its peak and that free cash flow will turn positive this year.

The dividend policy itself is a direct roadmap to scalability. The company has tied its future returns to its financial health, specifically its leverage ratio. For now, it will maintain a constant dividend of EUR 1.00 per share until its leverage ratio falls below 5.0x net financial debt to EBITDA. Once that target is hit, the payout is expected to rise to a payout ratio of around 60% to 80% of the Group result. This structure is pragmatic: it ensures shareholder returns are contingent on the company successfully deleveraging after years of heavy investment, protecting the balance sheet as it scales.

The bottom line for growth investors is that Fraport's scalability is not just about top-line expansion. It is equally about financial discipline. The current earnings pressure is a known cost of the build-out. The market will be watching closely to see if the promised cash flow turnaround materializes as planned. If it does, the dividend shift confirms the company is moving from a growth-investment phase to a growth-distribution phase, a classic sign of a business maturing and scaling profitably.

For Fraport's growth story to play out, several key catalysts must materialize, while execution risks loom large. The most critical external dependency is the recovery of Boeing deliveries to Lufthansa. As the CEO noted, Frankfurt airport would reach its pre-COVID passenger traffic levels in 2025 or 2026 as its recovery largely depends on Boeing deliveries to Lufthansa . With Lufthansa accounting for more than 60% of Frankfurt's passengers in 2022, any further delays or bottlenecks in aircraft supply would directly stall the home market's return to peak capacity, undermining the financial anchor for the entire international expansion strategy.

On the execution front, the company faces recurring operational headwinds. Labor disputes and weather disruptions have already proven capable of derailing traffic, as seen in February when strike and weather-related flight cancellations affected around 70,000 travelers in Frankfurt. This volatility highlights a persistent risk to the top-line growth projections. Compounding this is the financial pressure from high debt costs. Fraport expects a significant decline in net earnings for 2026 , driven by increased depreciation and higher interest expenses. Managing this cost structure while continuing to fund global investments is a delicate balancing act.

For investors, the path to scaling profitably hinges on two forward-looking metrics. First, the quarterly leverage ratio is the literal trigger for the company's new dividend policy. The plan is to maintain a constant dividend of EUR 1.00 per share until the net debt-to-EBITDA ratio falls below 5.0x. Monitoring this ratio will be essential to gauge progress toward the promised payout increase and, more broadly, the successful deleveraging after the capital-intensive build-out phase.

Second, the scalability of the international portfolio must be tracked relentlessly. Evidence shows its dynamic growth, with total passenger traffic rising 7.1 percent in January and standout performances in Brazil and Slovenia. However, growth must be sustained and broad-based across all regions to consistently offset local volatility in Germany. The bottom line is that Fraport's ability to capture market share depends on navigating a complex mix of external dependencies and internal execution risks. The catalysts are clear, but the risks are operational and financial, demanding close watch.

Approach 1: Amadeus IT Group Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) Analysis

A Discounted Cash Flow, or DCF, model takes projections of a company's future cash flows and discounts them back into today's euros, aiming to estimate what the entire business could be worth right now.

For Amadeus IT Group, the model used is a 2 Stage Free Cash Flow to Equity approach, based on cash flows available to shareholders. The latest twelve month free cash flow is about €1.41b. Simply Wall St uses analyst inputs where available for the coming years, then extends those projections further out, with free cash flow estimates running to 2035, including a projected €1.76b in 2030.

When all those forecast cash flows are discounted back to today, the DCF model points to an estimated intrinsic value of €51.58 per share. Compared with the current share price of €50.18, this suggests the stock is about 2.7% undervalued, which is a small gap and well within a normal margin of error for this type of model.

For a profitable business, the P/E ratio is often the simplest way to connect what you pay for each share with the earnings that back it. It gives you a quick sense of how many euros the market is willing to pay for each euro of current earnings.

What counts as a "normal" or "fair" P/E depends on what investors expect for future growth and how risky those earnings are. Higher expected growth or lower perceived risk can justify a higher P/E, while slower expected growth or higher risk usually points to a lower one.

Amadeus IT Group currently trades on a P/E of 16.19x. That sits below the Hospitality industry average of 19.75x and also below the peer group average of 19.72x. evidence.title: Kuehne+Nagel and CATL Form Strategic Partnership on Battery Logistics, Fleet Electrification and Scope 3 Emissions Reduction
evidence.text:
Kuehne+Nagel and CATL Form Strategic Partnership on Battery Logistics, Fleet Electrification and Scope 3 Emissions Reduction

Kuehne+Nagel and CATL Form Strategic Partnership on Battery Logistics, Fleet Electrification and Scope 3 Emissions Reduction

(IN BRIEF) Kuehne+Nagel and CATL have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to collaborate on battery logistics, transport electrification and Scope 3 emissions reduction across their value chains. Initial projects will include the electrification of CATL transport flows in Europe and a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks in China using Qiji technology, with the pilot scheduled to begin in 2026. The companies will also explore battery recycling, aftersales support, energy storage and charging solutions for logistics facilities. Kuehne+Nagel said battery-electric vehicles are essential to reducing road freight emissions, while CATL highlighted the partnership’s role in supporting both companies’ sustainability objectives and the wider energy transition. The agreement comes amid rapid growth in electric mobility and energy storage, with demand for electric truck batteries having increased by more than 75% in 2024. The partnership is intended to combine CATL’s battery expertise with Kuehne+Nagel’s logistics capabilities to develop practical, scalable solutions for lower-emission transport and battery supply chains.

(PRESS RELEASE) SCHINDELLEGI, 25-Sep-2026 — / EuropaWire / — Kuehne+Nagel and Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to establish a strategic collaboration focused on battery logistics, transport electrification and initiatives designed to reduce emissions across their respective value chains.

The partnership will initially concentrate on practical projects that combine CATL’s battery and new-energy technology capabilities with Kuehne+Nagel’s global logistics expertise.

One of the first areas of cooperation will be the electrification of CATL transport flows in Europe, with the companies exploring how battery-electric transport can be incorporated more extensively into logistics operations.

The partners are also preparing a battery-swapping pilot for heavy-duty trucks in China, using technology provided by Qiji.

The pilot is scheduled to launch during 2026 and will examine the operational potential of battery swapping as a way to support the electrification of long-haul and heavy-duty road transport.

Beyond vehicle electrification, the cooperation will extend into several related areas of the battery lifecycle and energy infrastructure.

Kuehne+Nagel and CATL intend to collaborate on battery recycling and aftersales support, helping address the logistics requirements associated with battery maintenance, recovery and end-of-life handling.

The companies will also explore energy storage and charging solutions for logistics sites, potentially supporting the wider deployment of electrified transport fleets and associated infrastructure.

The initiatives are intended to contribute to the Scope 3 emissions reduction ambitions of both companies by targeting emissions generated across logistics and transportation value chains.

Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business , said CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share an interest in accelerating the energy transition and advancing toward a net-zero emissions future.

He said the expanded partnership is expected to support both companies’ sustainability objectives while contributing to broader efforts to reduce emissions from transport and logistics operations.

Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel , said battery-electric vehicles are an important part of efforts to decarbonise road freight.

He said faster adoption will depend on technologies that are not only high-performing but also practical in day-to-day logistics operations.

By combining CATL’s expertise in batteries with Kuehne+Nagel’s operational logistics capabilities, the companies aim to develop initiatives that can reduce emissions from their own activities as well as those of customers.

The partnership comes amid continued growth in demand for electric vehicles and energy storage systems.

According to the companies, demand for electric truck batteries increased by more than 75% in 2024, while battery manufacturing capacity continues to expand through the development of additional gigafactories worldwide.

This growth is increasing the need for specialised logistics capabilities covering battery transportation, storage, charging, maintenance, recycling and other services throughout the battery lifecycle.

Through the new cooperation, Kuehne+Nagel and CATL intend to address these requirements while also examining how electrified freight transport can be scaled in different regional markets.

The planned work in Europe and Asia reflects a broader effort by both companies to connect battery technology, logistics infrastructure and operational transport expertise in support of lower-emission supply chains.

With approximately 88,000 employees across over 1,300 sites in close to 100 countries, the Kuehne+Nagel Group is one of the world’s leading logistics providers. Headquartered in Switzerland and listed on the Zurich stock exchange, it is the global number one in Air and Sea Logistics and holds strong market positions in Road and Contract Logistics. Supporting around 400,000 customers worldwide, the Group draws on its global network, logistics expertise, and data-driven insights to deliver end-to-end supply chain solutions for global companies and industries.

Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) is a global leader in zero-carbon new energy technology, committed to providing premier solutions and services for new energy applications worldwide. In 2025, CATL’s EV battery consumption volume has ranked No.1 in the world for nine consecutive years, and it has ranked first in the market share of global energy storage battery shipments for five straight years. CATL enjoys wide recognition by global EV and energy storage partners. So far all the 20 battery factories under the Company’s core operations have achieved carbon neutrality, and it aims to achieve carbon neutrality across the battery supply chain by 2035.
