evidence.title: Nordea and Aalto University to explore the future of AI and human-machine interaction
evidence.text:
Nordea and Aalto University to explore the future of AI and human-machine interaction

Nordea and Aalto University are launching a long term research and education partnership to explore how machine agency will shape the future of services, including banking. The relationship with humans and intelligent machines is rapidly evolving as artificial intelligence moves from a supportive resource to an active decision maker.

Our everyday lives were transformed when the web and applications became available on mobile phones. In the near future, a profound revolution is taking place as AI can understand a persons’ life and context in multiple dimensions, and AI technology evolves into agents that act on behalf of humans, e.g., in shopping, healthcare, and banking. The collaboration between Nordea and Aalto University focuses on a question that is becoming increasingly relevant to everyday life: how can customers choose digital assistants they trust and how those assistants can act in their best interest when managing everyday decisions?

‘Trust is fundamental in everything we do at Nordea. As AI becomes part of everyday life, our responsibility is to ensure that new technologies genuinely improve customers’ experiences, protect their interests and make banking simpler, safer and more personal. Working with Aalto University helps us explore these technologies responsibly, combining academic insight with real world customer needs,’ says Heikki Henttu, Head of Group Technology Strategy and AI in Nordea.

Together Nordea and Aalto University will launch the Future Interfaces Lab . The Future Interfaces Lab is an applied research platform that connects students, researchers, and corporate partners to explore and experiment with the latest technologies at the interface between humans and machines.

Nordea is a founding partner in the initiative, contributing expertise, talent and funding. The collaboration includes joint research projects, new courses and hands‑on development. This work will combine academic research with practical application, with a strong focus on real customer use cases and future banking experiences.

‘Nordea as a financial services institution is the perfect founding partner for the Future Interfaces Lab. The collaboration provides Aalto University with an opportunity to combine our research and teaching to solve practical and societal problems around AI, where the topics of agency, trust and maintaining a human touch are central,’ says Jens Schmidt, Head of the Department of Industrial Engineering and Management at Aalto University.

The Nordics needs to strengthen its AI competitiveness

The partnership aims to strengthen the Nordic’s long‑term competitiveness in AI‑enabled services and invites additional partners to complement the Future interfaces Lab.

‘Providing hands on opportunities in developing students’ skills is an important element of the partnership. Finland, the Nordics and the entire Europe needs to strengthen its AI capabilities to ensure we remain competitive internationally. This is where Nordea as a Nordic financial institution wants to play a significant role, and ensure that the best talents are working towards developing banking services that are more intuitive, secure and valuable for our customers’, says Heikki Henttu from Nordea.

This article was first pubished on 21 May by Aalto University.

evidence.title: Nordea to slash 1,500 jobs as AI impact grows
evidence.text:
Nordea expects to shed 1,500 jobs in the next two years with the use of artificial intelligence (AI).

The bank, which has about 30,000 staff, disclosed its plans to change the “workforce composition” to investors, with €190m in planned restructuring costs.

Nordea’s 2030 strategy was announced in November 2025. At the time, the bank said: “Technology, data and AI will be central to this shift. They will enable Nordea to turn local processes into Nordic-wide ones, reduce platforms and applications, modernise legacy systems and increase engineering productivity.”

It added that the changes would make its technology more resilient and secure.

“By transforming local customer processes into Nordic‑wide value chains, and reducing, simplifying and modernising technology systems and infrastructure, Nordea will make more effective use of its Nordic scale to serve customers even better and operate more efficiently,” it told the stock exchange.

The bank said it will continue to invest in skills, but “with Nordic scale, the impact of AI and process optimisation, Nordea expects to have fewer employees in the future than today”.

It said the job cuts, about 5% of its workforce, are subject to union negotiation and consultation processes, and that it will support employees with reskilling, upskilling and other internal opportunities.

Banks are increasing their adoption of AI as returns on investment grow. According to recent Lloyds Banking Group research, 59% of surveyed firms reported AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey.

In its Financial institutions sentiment survey , it found that 21% of respondents believe AI is directly driving business growth, compared with 8% in the survey a year ago. Meanwhile, a third (33%) of respondents said AI is enhancing customer experiences, up from 14%. The same number said they have deeper customer insights through AI, compared with 18% last year.

Figures from Bloomberg Intelligence put the number of jobs set to be replaced by AI at hundreds of thousands, with CIOs questioned by the organisation expecting 3% of their staff on average to be cut. About a quarter of respondents expect the workforce to be reduced by between 5% and 10% as AI takes over roles, with the back and middle offices likely to be the most affected.

In a whitepaper titled The AI-fication of talents , published last year, the centre for finance, technology and entrepreneurship said three groups of professionals will emerge in the finance sector as a result of the widespread adoption of AI.

It reported that there will be: “mass displacement” of roles centred on execution, which will be increasingly automated; “supercharged professionals” will emerge who use AI to expand scope and scale; and “creative disruptors” will be a small group inventing new models, products and systems.

It’s not just the banking sector that faces huge change in the makeup of the workforce. According to research by OpenAI and the University of Pennsylvania, roles that will be affected include accountants, legal assistants, financial analysts, journalists, translators and public relations professionals. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs published figures in March 2023 that spoke of 300 million jobs exposed to AI across all sectors.

To all Nordea shareholders: How to join and vote at the Annual General Meeting

Nordea’s Annual General Meeting will be held as a virtual meeting on Tuesday, 24 March 2026. As a shareholder, you’re encouraged to participate and contribute to the good governance of the company.

evidence.title: Danske Bank expects further job cuts as AI use expands
evidence.text:
(CB-16); the desktop layout below renders the same text as a restyled . --> Danske Bank expects further job cuts as AI use expands

Denmark's largest bank has shed hundreds of roles already this year and says automation will keep reshaping its workforce through 2028

Danske Bank is not done trimming its headcount. The Danish lender confirmed it anticipates further workforce reductions as artificial intelligence embeds itself deeper into daily operations.

Frans Woelders, the bank’s head of technology and services, made clear this isn’t about eliminating one department and calling it a day. The influence of AI, he said, will ripple across the entire organization rather than landing in any single corner of the business.

Danske Bank already cut 420 jobs in February 2026, then followed that with another 262 positions in May, 199 of which were based in Denmark. Those are not rounding errors for a bank with roughly 19,472 employees. That’s more than 680 roles gone in about four months, with the bank citing efficiency gains from digital tools and AI as the primary driver.

Danske Bank has raised its annual technology investment to approximately 4.5 billion DKK, targeting 2 billion DKK in annual productivity gains from AI and related tools by 2028. The overarching plan, called Forward ’28, sets a cost-to-income ratio ceiling of 43% and a return on equity target above 14.5%.

AI pilots and cloud partnerships signal the direction

Danske Bank recently completed Denmark’s first AI-agent payment pilot in collaboration with Mastercard . The bank has also deepened its partnership with Amazon Web Services, expanding AI capabilities through Amazon ’s Bedrock platform.

The broader Danish labor market context adds texture. A September 2026 analysis by Danmarks Nationalbank found that firms adopting AI are hiring fewer new employees, with younger and highly educated workers facing a disproportionate impact. Overall employment levels have remained relatively stable for now, cushioned by labor market flexibility, but the central bank’s findings suggest the hiring slowdown is real and concentrated among the demographic that traditionally lands knowledge-economy roles.

evidence.title: Danske Bank Completes Denmark’s AI Agent Payment with Mastercard
evidence.text:
Danske Bank and Mastercard ( NYSE: MA ) have completed what both companies describe as Denmark’s first payment initiated and finished by an artificial intelligence agent.

The pilot, announced on 21 September 2026, is an early live test of so-called agentic commerce inside a regulated Nordic bank rather than a standalone fintech demonstration.

In the trial, a customer asked an AI assistant to arrange a coffee tasting through Mastercard’s Priceless.com experiences platform.

The agent then selected the session, completed the booking, and settled the charge on its own using a Mastercard issued by Danske Bank.

Mastercard ’s Agent Pay rails handled the payment, while PayOS coordinated the full transaction path from instruction to settlement.

Agent Pay, introduced in April 2025, is Mastercard’s infrastructure for letting verified AI systems pay on a cardholder’s behalf.

Purchases are authenticated with Mastercard Payment Passkeys, and the design is meant to keep the customer in control: the person still grants permission, the transaction remains visible, and the issuer can see that an agent, not the cardholder tapping a website, started the payment .

Erik Gutwasser , Mastercard’s Northern Europe division president, said the aim is to make AI -assisted buying simpler without sacrificing transparency or security.

Mark Wraa-Hansen , Danske Bank’s head of personal banking in Denmark, framed the test as part of a broader look at how customers might interact with financial services.

The bank , he said, is examining the technology with an emphasis on usefulness, trust, and customer control, and the Mastercard partnership is meant to show that new automation can sit inside existing security and transparency requirements.

The Danish transaction follows earlier European Agent Pay pilots.

Mastercard completed what it called Europe ’s first live AI-agent payment with Santander in March 2026, then a French first with Worldline and Crédit Agricole.

The Danske Bank case matters because it ran through an incumbent issuer’s card and systems, not a sandbox wallet.

That raises practical questions banks now have to answer: how much authority an agent receives, how that authority is limited, how to separate a customer’s intent from the agent’s interpretation of it, and who bears the loss if the agent books the wrong thing.

For Danske Bank the payment experiment sits alongside other AI work.

The lender has been expanding cloud and model infrastructure with Amazon Web Services , including Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore, to move agent-style tools from tests into production.

Separately, it has piloted a Model Context Protocol server so corporate clients can connect their own AI assistants to bank data through Premium APIs .

The card payment is a consumer-facing counterpart: an agent that does not only recommend an experience but pays for it.

Agentic commerce compresses a familiar shopping sequence. Instead of searching, opening a site, entering card details, and confirming, the user states a goal and the agent carries the purchase to completion within agreed limits.

Critics note that convenience only works if consent, authentication , merchant acceptance, and dispute rules keep pace.

Mastercard ’s approach tries to treat the agent as a recognized party on the network, using tokens and passkeys so issuers can distinguish agent-led spend from ordinary card use.

The coffee tasting was a modest use case. Its significance is architectural.

A large Danish bank and a global network showed that an AI agent can book and pay inside live issuer infrastructure while leaving a verifiable consent trail. It now remains to be see if that model scales to everyday retail. It will depend on controls, customer willingness, and how quickly merchants accept agent-initiated checkout.

evidence.title: Mastercard Helps Danske Bank With Denmark-First Agentic Transaction
evidence.text:
Mastercard Helps Danske Bank With Denmark-First Agentic Transaction

Mastercard said it has helped Denmark’s Danske Bank reach an agentic payments milestone.

Complete the form to unlock this article and enjoy unlimited free access to all PYMNTS content — no additional logins required.

yes Subscribe to our daily newsletter, PYMNTS Today.

By completing this form, you agree to receive marketing communications from PYMNTS and to the sharing of your information with our sponsor, if applicable, in accordance with our Privacy Policy and Terms and Conditions .

Using Mastercard’s Agent Pay, Danske was able to complete a transaction in which an artificial intelligence (AI) agent made both the purchase and payment on a customers’ behalf, the payments giant announced Monday (Sept. 21).

According to a news release, this marked the first time in Denmark that an AI agent has made such a payment/purchase, booking a coffee tasting through Mastercard’s Priceless.com experience platform.

“AI can help make everyday life simpler, but trust and security must come first,” said Erik Gutwasser , Mastercard Northern Europe’s division president. “ Agent Pay is designed to ensure that AI-powered transactions are transparent, securely authenticated and always under the consumer’s control. At the same time, the solution gives card issuers better insight into transactions initiated by AI agents.”

According to the release, the transaction shows how AI agents can make purchases for customers while making sure payment is made with the customer’s permission and “under a secure and verifiable framework.”

We’d love to be your preferred source for news .

Please add us to your preferred sources list so our news, data and interviews show up in your feed. Thanks!

Danske Bank said it also sees opportunities in AI-powered payments , but stresses the importance of customer value, trust and control.

“AI-powered payments represent a new way for customers to interact with financial services. At Danske Bank, we are exploring the possibilities of the new technology with a strong focus on customer value, trust and control,” said Mark Wraa-Hansen , Danske Bank’s head of personal banking for Denmark. “Our collaboration with Mastercard shows how new technology can be combined with security and transparency to create payment experiences that are simpler, smarter and more secure for customers.”

Mastercard introduced Agentic Pay in 2025 and recently debuted Agent Pay for Machines, a service that lets agents transact with each other .

PYMNTS CEO Karen Webster spoke last week with Mastercard U.S. Co-President Chiro Aikat about the rise of agentic commerce at a time when 132 million Americans are already AI users.

He compared the development with previous changes in payments where consumers had to learn things like whether to swipe or dip a card, behaviors that eventually became routine.

“EMV, pay by phone and others as well,” Aikat said. “Agentic is exactly like that. In many ways, it’s accelerating faster.”

However, faster familiarity with AI doesn’t mean consumers will yield spending authority at the same rate. Webster cited PYMNTS Intelligence research showing thatexact divergence.

“We’ve seen this in our data,” Webster said, pointing out that consumers’ “interest over time in terms of delegating authority has declined, even though usage has increased.”

evidence.title: Swedbank Robur
evidence.text:
Expertens varning: ”Kan vara en dold indexfond”

Aktivitetsgraden är låg i flera av de mest populära fonderna i Sverige, visar Di:s granskning. Det får Aktiespararnas chefsjurist Sverre Linton att reagera. ”Här kan det vara så att förvaltaren lagt sig nära index för att minska risken att underprestera. Det är en klassiker”, säger han.

Kartläggning: Globalfonder – ett minfält av indexkramare

Globalfonden är särskilt populär hos svenska sparare och en central pusselbit i deras portföljer. Men bland de största fonderna som tar extra betalt för aktiv förvaltning verkar vissa vara indexkramare, visar Di:s genomgång.

Kartläggning: Fondfällan – småsparare blir blåsta på förvaltningen

Sparare kanske betalar för aktiv förvaltning, men riskerar i själva verket att placera sina pengar i en dold indexfond. Di granskar aktivitetsgraden i marknadens största Sverigefonder – och den är misstänkt låg i flera jättar.

Swedbank Robur Fonder har minskat sitt innehav i teknikkoncernen Lagercrantz.

Storbanken minskar i Wallenbergs vitvarubolag

Swedbank Robur Fonder har minskat sitt samlade innehav i vitvarubolaget Electrolux Professional till cirka 14,1 miljoner aktier, motsvarande 4,9 procent av kapitalet och 3,9 procent av rösterna i bolaget. Det framgår av ett flaggningsmeddelande.

Swedbank Robur Fonder har minskat sitt innehav i friluftsbolaget Thule till 4,8 procent av kapitalet och rösterna.

Swedbanks klimatpåverkan är betydligt större än tidigare känt, avslöjar bankens hållbarhetsrapport. Klimatnotan mer än tiofaldigas, när fondbolaget Swedbank Robur lyfts in i rapporten, rapporterar Aktuell Hållbarhet.

Rekordintäkter för Icas nätdoktor: ”Vi är ödmjuka”

Den digitala vårdgivaren Min Doktor, som har Ica som storägare, redovisade i fjol sitt första lönsamma helår sedan starten tolv år tidigare. Intäkterna tog också fart och ökade till rekordhöga 400 miljoner kronor. ”Det känns fantastiskt”, säger vd:n Jonas Vig.

Flera storköpare i Scandic efter Eiendomspars försäljning

Fackförbundet Unionen, Sensor Fonder och Swedbank Robur har under november antingen kommit in som nya ägare eller kraftigt ökat sitt innehav i Scandic Hotels.

Swedbank Robur sålde under november hela sitt innehav i detaljhandelsbolaget Rusta.

Swedbank Robur gör som konkurrenten – lanserar ny försvarsfond

Swedbank Robur lanserar en ny försvarsfond, som fått namnet Security and Defence. Det framgår av ett pressmeddelande.

Swedbank Robur Fonder har ökat innehavet i Truecaller till 5,9 procent av kapitalet och 2,7 procent av rösterna.

Tunga ägarprofilen lämnar Swedbank Robur

En av de tyngsta institutionella rösterna på Stockholmsbörsen, Marianne Nilsson som länge varit ägarstyrningsspecialist på Swedbank Robur, kommer att lämna fondjätten senare i år. ”Det är ett beslut som jag har tagit för att frigöra tid för nya saker”, säger hon till Di.

Fonder på toppnivå – då täljer storbanker guld

Med genomsnittliga uppgångar på 14 procent i aktiefonder blev fjolåret lyckat för svenska fondsparare. Än mer nöjd är fondbranschen då vinsterna hos de största bolagen steg med 2,7 miljarder kronor, motsvarande drygt 30 procent.

Fondjätten tar hem vinst i Saab – amerikaner köper

Fondjätten Swedbank Robur har trimmat ned sitt innehav i försvarsbolaget Saab kraftigt, till ett värde av 2,1 miljarder kronor efter aktiens branta uppgång, enligt färsk månadsstatistik från Holdings. Amerikanska fondbolag och ETF:er har i stället köpt aktier.

Swedbank Robur har minskat sitt innehav i bostadsutvecklaren JM och äger nu 4,6 procent av aktierna i bolaget. Det framgår av ett flaggningsmeddelande.

Splittring bland Fortnoxägarna: Swedbank Robur avser tacka ja

AMF och Lannebo planerar att nobba budet på affärssystembolaget Fortnox. Däremot uppger nu Swedbank Robur, som äger nästan 5 procent av aktierna, att de är positiva till erbjudandet. ”Baserat på den information som finns tillgänglig i dag är vår avsikt att tacka ja till budet”, uppger fondbolaget.

EQT:s och Olof Hallrups jättebud på Fortnox åker på ett bakslag, kan Di avslöja. Affärssystembolagets näst största ägare, pensionsförvaltaren AMF, sätter nu ned foten och nobbar erbjudandet. ”Det finns betydande värden kvar”, säger AMF:s aktiechef Anders Oscarsson.

Swedbank Robur flaggar upp över 10 procent i Addnode

Swedbank Robur Fonder har ökat sitt innehav i it-företaget Addnode till strax över 10 procent av kapitalet och 7,9 procent av rösterna.

Spricka bland Nibes storägare: ”Styrelsen behöver vitaliseras”

Missnöjet pyr bland storägare i folkaktien Nibe. Inför årsstämman på torsdag har vd:n Gerteric Lindquist och hans allierade drivit igenom att det inte ska ske några förändringar i styrelsen — andra storägare hade gärna sett en förnyelse. ”Styrelsen behöver vitaliseras”, säger AMF:s aktiechef Anders Oscarsson.

evidence.title: Swedbank muutis hinnakirja
evidence.text:
Swedbankis jõustus 31. augustil uus hinnakiri, mis muudab nii mõnegi teenuse hinda ja tingimusi.

Suurem muudatus puudutas seda, kellele ja millistel tingimustel pank teenuseid pakub. Swedbank täpsustas senisest selgemalt, millist seost Eestiga peetakse piisavaks. Näiteks ei piisa enam ainult sellest, et inimesel on Eestis kinnisvara. Ettevõtete puhul ei loeta piisavaks seoseks üksnes kinnisvarainvesteeringuid või Eesti väärtpaberite omamist.

See tähendab, et pank võib klientidelt küsida rohkem infot ja dokumente, et aru saada, miks neil on Eestis pangakontot vaja või milline on nende tegelik seos Eestiga. Vajadusel tuleb tõendada ka seda, et inimesel on õigus Euroopa Liidus elada.

Tavaklientide jaoks on ilmselt kõige märgatavamad muudatused seotud turvalisusega. Swedbank rõhutab nüüd veel tugevamalt, et internetipanga paroole, PIN-koode ja muid sisselogimisandmeid ei tohi mitte kellelegi jagada. Kui tekib kahtlus, et keegi teine võib andmeid kasutada, tuleb sellest kohe pangale teada anda.

Samuti võib pank mõne makse puhul küsida senisest rohkem lisakinnitusi. Näiteks võidakse kontrollida, kas inimene teeb tehingut päriselt ise. See võib tähendada täiendavaid kinnitusi või muid turvakontrolle. Panga sõnul aitab see pettusi ennetada, kuid mõned maksed võivad seetõttu tavapärasest kauem aega võtta.

Muudatusi tehti ka pangakaartide tingimustes. Swedbank selgitab nüüd täpsemalt, mida tähendab kaardimakse broneering. Lihtsalt öeldes tähendab see seda, et kui raha on juba broneeritud, siis on see sisuliselt kaupmehele edasi liikunud ning pank ei saa makset enam tagasi pöörata.

Muutus ka pakettide kuutasu võtmise aeg. Kui varem võeti tasu kuu keskel ehk 15. kuupäeval, siis nüüd tehakse seda iga kuu 2. kuupäeval. Klientidele lisandus ka üks positiivne muudatus: alates 27. augustist ei võta Swedbank enam miinuses arvelduskontolt 0,2-protsendilist päevaviivist.

Näiteks tõusis 31. augustist teiste riikide residentidele arvelduskonto avamiseks esitatud dokumentide läbivaatamise tasu 200 eurolt 250 euroni. See puudutab inimesi väljastpoolt Eestit ja Euroopa Liitu, sealhulgas näiteks Norra, Islandi, Liechtensteini, Suurbritannia ja Šveitsi residente.

Kallimaks muutusid ka mõned pangakaartidega seotud teenused. Deebetkaart Plussi ja Mastercard Private Banking Cardi avamise tasu tõusis 2,50 eurolt 4 euroni. Samuti kasvasid krediitkaartide lisakaartide kuutasud: Gold krediitkaardi puhul 5 eurolt 7 euroni ning Platinum krediitkaardi lisakaardi puhul 15 eurolt 17 euroni.

Lisaks tuleb nüüd rohkem maksta pensionikonto teise samba väljamakse avalduse eest, mille tasu tõusis 10 eurolt 15 euroni.

Paljude teiste muudatustega saab tutvuda Swedbanki kodulehel .

evidence.title: „Swedbank“ skolina dar 10 mln. eurų „Cyber City“ vystytojai „Spartai“
evidence.text:
„Swedbank“ skolina dar 10 mln. eurų „Cyber City“ vystytojai „Spartai“

Bankas „Swedbank“ skolina dar 10,23 mln. eurų informacinių technologijų miestelio „Cyber City“ vystytojai bendrovei „Sparta“. Bendra paskolos suma projektui siekia 73,3 mln. eurų.

Finansavimas suteiktas užbaigus komplekso Vilniaus Naujamiesčio rajone statybas ir įregistravus 100 proc. objekto baigtumą. Lėšos skirtos kitoms bendrovės paskoloms refinansuoti, pirmadienį pranešė bankas.

„Tai, kad „Cyber City“ šiandien yra užbaigtas ir pasiekė maksimalų užimtumą, rodo, kad modernių, tvarių ir strategiškai patogiose vietose esančių biurų poreikis Vilniuje išlieka aukštas“, – pranešime teigė „Swedbank“ Nekilnojamojo turto ir energetikos klientų skyriaus vadovas Martynas Trimonis.

„Swedbank“ pirmą paskolos dalį – 42,4 mln. eurų – projektui suteikė 2021 metais, 2024 metų vasarą ji buvo pratęsta penkeriems metams suteikiant dar 11,3 mln. eurų. 2025 metų pradžioje ketvirtojo komplekso pastato statyboms užbaigti paskolinta dar 11,6 mln. eurų, o dabar – papildomai 10,23 mln. eurų.

Beveik 2 hektarų buvusios tekstilės gamyklos „Sparta“ teritorijoje išvystytą „Cyber City“ kompleksą sudaro keturi pastatai, kurių bendras plotas siekia apie 40 tūkst. kv. metrų. Juose įrengtos biurų, komercinės ir bendrosios erdvės, poilsio zonos bei konferencijų infrastruktūra.

Didžiąją dalį technologijų miestelio patalpų nuomojasi technologijų ir investicijų grupės „Tesonet“ įmonės bei kitos technologijų įmonės.

Kaip užpernai rašė BNS, „Tesonet“, kurios du naudos gavėjai netiesiogiai valdo dalį „Spartos“ akcijų, į miestelio statybas investavo apie 50 mln. eurų.

evidence.title: „Swedbank“ suteikė papildomą 10,23 mln. eurų finansavimą „Cyber City“ projektui
evidence.text:
„Swedbank“ suteikė papildomą 10,23 mln. eurų finansavimą „Cyber City“ projektui

Vilniaus Naujamiestyje užbaigus informacinių technologijų miestelio „Cyber City“ statybas, „Swedbank“ suteikė papildomą 10,23 mln. eurų finansavimą projekto vystytojai bendrovei „Sparta“. Bendra banko finansavimo suma šio projekto plėtrai pasiekė 73,3 mln. eurų.

Papildomas finansavimas suteiktas užbaigus komplekso statybas ir įregistravus 100 proc. objekto baigtumą. Lėšos bus skirtos kitų bendrovės finansinių įsipareigojimų refinansavimui.

„Tai, kad „Cyber City“ šiandien yra užbaigtas ir pasiekė maksimalų užimtumą, rodo, kad modernių, tvarių ir strategiškai patogiose vietose esančių biurų poreikis Vilniuje išlieka aukštas. Mums buvo svarbu prisidėti prie šios ambicingos pramoninės teritorijos konversijos nuo pat pirmųjų statybų etapų iki galutinio rezultato. Bendrai šiam projektui „Swedbank“ skirtas 73,3 mln. eurų vertės finansavimas rodo mūsų tikėjimą tvaria miesto plėtra ir partneriais, gebančiais kurti pasaulinio lygio erdves technologijų sektoriui“, – sako Martynas Trimonis, „Swedbank“ Nekilnojamojo turto ir energetikos klientų skyriaus vadovas.

„Papildomas „Swedbank“ finansavimas žymi svarbų „Cyber City“ projekto etapą – užbaigus statybas ir pasiekus pilną komplekso užimtumą, galime toliau kryptingai stiprinti jo, kaip technologijų ir inovacijų ekosistemos centro, vaidmenį. Vertiname ilgalaikę partnerystę su banku, kuri leido nuosekliai įgyvendinti šį projektą. Tikime, kad „Cyber City“ ir toliau išliks vieta, kur technologijų įmonės gali sėkmingai auginti aukštos pridėtinės vertės verslus“, – teigia Rūta Chadasevičiūtė, „Sparta“ vadovė.

M. Trimonis taip pat akcentuoja informacinių technologijų , finansų, verslo paslaugų ir kitų žinioms imlių veiklų svarbą ekonomikai.

„Šių paslaugų eksportas sparčiai plečiasi, šalies įmonės vis sėkmingiau konkuruoja tarptautinėse rinkose. Aukštos pridėtinės vertės paslaugų eksportas pernai pasiekė 10 milijardų eurų – daugiau nei dešimtadalį nuo šalies BVP – ir per pastarąjį dešimtmetį išaugo net dešimt kartų. Taigi, augant sektoriui, auga ir darbuotojų poreikis“, – sako ekspertas.

„Swedbank“ finansavimą „Cyber City“ vystymui teikė etapais. Pirmoji paskolos dalis 2021 m. siekė 42,4 mln. eurų. 2024 m. vasarą finansavimas buvo pratęstas penkeriems metams, papildomai suteikiant 11,3 mln. eurų paskolą. 2025 m. pradžioje ketvirtojo komplekso pastato statyboms užbaigti buvo skirta dar 11,6 mln. eurų, o paskutiniuoju etapu suteiktas papildomas 10,23 mln. eurų finansavimas.

Is Swedbank (OM:SWED A) Still Attractively Priced After Its Strong Multi Year Share Price Run

Never miss an important update on your stock portfolio and cut through the noise. Over 7 million investors trust Simply Wall St to stay informed where it matters for FREE.

If you are wondering whether Swedbank's share price still offers value after a strong run, this article will help you weigh what the current price might already be pricing in.

Swedbank's shares last closed at SEK 349.0, with returns of 1.1% over 7 days, 1.9% over 30 days, 7.3% year to date, 49.4% over 1 year and 97.1% over 3 years. This naturally raises questions about how much of the story is already in the price.

Recent news around Swedbank has mainly focused on its position in the Swedish banking sector and how investors are assessing its capital strength and exposure to the broader Nordic economy. These themes help explain why markets are paying close attention to the stock after such strong multi year returns.

On our framework Swedbank currently scores a value rating of 3 out of 6. Next we will look at what different valuation approaches say about the current price and then finish with a way to assess value that goes beyond any single model.

Swedbank delivered 49.4% returns over the last year. See how this stacks up to the rest of the Banks industry.

The Excess Returns model looks at how efficiently a bank uses shareholders' equity and whether its returns exceed the required cost of that equity. In simple terms, it asks how much value Swedbank may add for shareholders above the return they could reasonably demand for the risk they are taking.

For Swedbank, the starting point is a Book Value of SEK200.85 per share, with a Stable Book Value estimate of SEK201.21 per share, based on weighted future book value estimates from 4 analysts. On this equity base, the model uses a Stable EPS of SEK28.74 per share, informed by weighted future return on equity estimates from 5 analysts, and an Average Return on Equity of 14.28%.

The required Cost of Equity is set at SEK12.55 per share, implying an Excess Return of SEK16.19 per share. When these excess returns are projected and capitalised, the model arrives at an intrinsic value of about SEK569.14 per share. Compared with the recent share price of SEK349.0, this approach suggests the stock trades at a 38.7% discount to the model's intrinsic value estimate.

Our Excess Returns analysis suggests Swedbank is undervalued by 38.7%. Track this in your watchlist or portfolio , or discover 227 more high quality undervalued stocks .

Head to the Valuation section of our Company Report for more details on how we arrive at this Fair Value for Swedbank.

For a profitable bank like Swedbank, the P/E ratio is a useful way to think about value because it directly links what you pay per share to the earnings the bank generates for you as a shareholder.

What counts as a "normal" or "fair" P/E depends on how quickly earnings are expected to grow and how risky those earnings are. Higher growth and lower perceived risk usually support a higher P/E, while slower growth or higher risk tend to justify a lower P/E.

Swedbank currently trades on a P/E of 11.96x, which is slightly above the peer average of 11.60x and the Banks industry average of about 11.25x. Simply Wall St's Fair Ratio for Swedbank is 12.02x. This Fair Ratio is a proprietary estimate of the P/E you might expect given factors such as the company's earnings growth profile, profit margins, risk, industry and market cap. Because it pulls these elements together into one figure, it can be more informative than a simple comparison with peers or the wider industry.

Swedbank's actual P/E of 11.96x is very close to the Fair Ratio of 12.02x, which points to the shares being priced at about the level this framework would suggest.

P/E ratios tell one story, but what if the real opportunity lies elsewhere? Start investing in legacies, not executives. Discover our 101 top founder-led companies .

Earlier we mentioned that there is an even better way to understand valuation. Let us introduce you to Narratives, which let you attach a clear story about Swedbank's future to the numbers you see on Simply Wall St. Narratives work by turning your view on its revenue, earnings and margins into a forecast, linking that forecast to a Fair Value, and then comparing that Fair Value to the current price. All of this happens inside an easy tool on the Community page that updates automatically when fresh news or results arrive. This means you can see, for example, how one Swedbank Narrative with a Fair Value of about SEK213.52 sits against another on the same company with a Fair Value of SEK390.0 and decide which story you find more realistic.

For Swedbank however we will make it really easy for you with previews of two leading Swedbank Narratives:

These sit on opposite sides of the debate and give you a clear sense of what needs to happen for the current share price of SEK349.0 to look either attractive or stretched.

Fair Value in this bullish narrative: SEK390.0

Implied discount to this Fair Value: 10.5%

Swedbank is seen as benefiting from the Swedbank 15/27 plan, tighter cost control and more efficient customer interactions, which together support higher activity levels, revenue and earnings in this narrative.

Analysts behind this view factor in steady revenue growth, only a modest reduction in profit margins from 47.6% to 45.1%, and earnings reaching SEK36.0b, or SEK32.03 per share, by about February 2029.

To reach the SEK390.0 Fair Value in this scenario, the bank would need to trade on a P/E of 14.6x on those future earnings, with investors assigning a higher multiple than today while using a 6.24% discount rate to bring those expectations back to today's terms.

Fair Value in this more cautious narrative: SEK213.52

Implied premium to this Fair Value: 63.5%

This narrative focuses on the effect of mortgage rate moves on Swedbank's interest income, with the author expecting a reduction in mortgage rates from about 4.5% to 3% and a sizeable hit to net interest income before it gradually rebuilds.

The author expects customer numbers and average loan size to rise, yet still sees an initial reduction in net interest income and group revenue before other services grow at about 10% per year and offset part of that pressure.

Based on these assumptions, the implied Fair Value of SEK213.52 sits well below today's share price, which reflects both the earnings path the author sets out and a materially lower future P/E multiple of 7.79x combined with a higher discount rate of 8.92%.

Together these Narratives frame a wide range of outcomes, from a case that leans on digital progress, sustainability related demand and disciplined execution, to one that highlights rate sensitivity and pressure on interest income. Your own view on which storyline is closer to reality will likely guide how you interpret Swedbank's current share price against these Fair Values.

evidence.text:

Handelsbanken's 1H Report: Strong Balance Bank Meets a 13% NII Warning

- Handelsbanken released its 1H 2026 report amid a 13% YoY net interest income decline, testing cost discipline resilience in softer rate environments.

- Q1 showed a 3% adjusted operating profit drop despite a SEK 1.1B VAT refund, with cost-to-income ratio falling to 39.5% from 41.5% in Q4 2025.

- The bank maintained strong capital buffers (17.2% CET1 ratio) and stable credit quality (0.01% loss ratio), offsetting inflation through efficiency measures.

- Investors seek confirmation that cost discipline, capital strength, and NII pressure stabilization will sustain business resilience beyond Q1.

Handelsbanken's 1H report tests whether cost discipline can outlast a softer rate backdrop

Handelsbanken has now released its interim report for January–June 2026. The bank's investor-relations page says the report was due on 15 July at 07:00 CET, with a press conference and Q&A at 09:45 CET led by CEO Michael Green.

This is a bank built around "up close and personal" advice and a model aimed at more satisfied customers and lower costs . Even so, investors now have to weigh that setup against 13% year-over-year decline in net interest income . The key question is whether this is a temporary earnings squeeze from falling rates or the start of a longer period of pressure.

Q1 showed a cleaner operating picture beneath the headline numbers

The first step is to separate one-off items from the running business. Q1 included a VAT refund of SEK 1,127m , which improved the reported quarter but says little about the underlying business. Handelsbanken reported operating profit of SEK 8,195m , but adjusted for the VAT refund, operating profit declined 3% . That underlying result is the clearer signal for investors.

My view remains constructive, not upbeat. Handelsbanken's low-cost model still looks credible in a tougher rate environment, but the half-year commentary needs to show that cost strength and balance-sheet quality are holding up as net interest income comes under pressure.

A tax refund can improve a quarter, but it does not make the business run better. The more durable signal is efficiency. In Q1, the cost-to-income ratio was 39.5%, down from 41.5% in Q4 2025, and expenses fell 2% quarter over quarter. The bank also said recent efficiency measures had reduced its running cost base enough to offset inflation and annual salary increases. That suggests cost discipline remains intact rather than weakened.

The balance-sheet buffer is still strong. Handelsbanken's CET1 ratio was 17.2%. It was slightly higher at 17.6% in Q4 2025, so there has been no sudden break, and the position remains robust. Credit quality also looked stable, with a credit loss ratio of 0.01%, the same as in Q4 2025. For now, that cushion still appears sufficient to support lending through a softer period.

What the half-year report needs to confirm

Q1 gave a useful read on resilience, but the interim report needs to confirm whether that resilience held for the first half. Investors should look for three things:

If those points hold, the Q1 softness looks more like temporary compression than a deeper break in business quality.

evidence.title: Infosys expands DNB bank partnership to upgrade financial crime detection systems globally
evidence.text:
Infosys expands DNB bank partnership to upgrade financial crime detection systems globally

BENGALURU: Infosys has expanded its strategic collaboration with DNB Bank ASA, Norway's largest bank, to modernise the lender's financial crime operations using the NICE Actimize X-Sight Enterprise platform.

Under the agreement, Infosys will act as the systems integration partner and help DNB replace fragmented legacy systems with a unified cloud-native platform designed to strengthen financial crime detection, improve risk monitoring and support regulatory compliance across multiple jurisdictions.

The programme will involve enterprise architecture design, platform integration and data migration. Key functions, including customer and payment screening, customer due diligence, transaction monitoring and fraud detection, will be consolidated onto a single software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform with a unified case management system.

Infosys said it will deploy NICE Actimize's X-Sight platform to integrate anti-money laundering and fraud management capabilities. The platform uses artificial intelligence (AI), analytics and automation to improve customer risk visibility and identify complex financial crime patterns.

Elin Sandnes, Chief Operating Officer and Group Executive Vice President Technology & Services at DNB, said: "Protecting customers and the integrity of the financial system requires us to continuously raise the bar on detection and investigation."

She added that the collaboration with Infosys and NICE Actimize would strengthen the bank's ability to "detect, investigate, and prevent complex financial crime more effectively" while supporting its digital transformation and compliance objectives.

Craig Costigan, Chief Executive Officer of NICE Actimize, said financial institutions were increasingly seeking "more intelligent, cloud-native approaches to combat evolving financial crime".

According to Infosys, the modernisation programme is expected to improve detection accuracy, speed up investigations and enhance the bank's response to regulatory requirements through AI-driven automation and analytics.

Dennis Gada, Executive Vice President and Global Head of Banking and Financial Services at Infosys, said the project would help DNB move "from fragmented controls to a unified, intelligence-led operating model".

The expanded collaboration builds on the existing relationship between Infosys and DNB as the bank continues to modernise its technology infrastructure and financial crime management systems.

Personal loans grew by 3.2% year-on-year, with mortgage inquiries doubling after Norway's central bank cut rates—a stark contrast to the stagnation seen in many European markets. Corporate lending also surged, with Norwegian businesses and international clients boosting loans by 1.8% and 3.3%, respectively. The bank's loan book now totals NOK 2,024 billion, a testament to its broad customer reach.

Crucially, credit quality remains exceptional: 99.3% of loans are in low-risk stages 1 and 2, with impairment provisions dropping to NOK 677 million. This resilience reflects DNB's conservative underwriting standards and Norway's strong economic fundamentals—2% unemployment, rising real wages, and steady GDP growth.

The star of DNB's Q2 performance was its 27.1% year-on-year jump in fee and commission income to NOK 4.4 billion, driven entirely by the Carnegie acquisition. Launched in May 2025, DNB DNB -- Carnegie has solidified its position as the Nordic leader in investment banking, completing 119 global capital markets transactions by mid-year. This diversification is vital: fee income now accounts for a larger slice of total revenue, reducing reliance on net interest margins, which face pressure from rate cuts and deposit competition.

The Carnegie integration also signals DNB's ambition to expand beyond Norway. Its Nordic and global clients now benefit from combined expertise in M&A, equity raisings, and wealth management—a critical edge in a fragmented European banking sector.

While DNB's cost-to-income ratio rose to 38.8% in Q2—slightly above its 38% target—this reflects strategic investments in digital innovation and one-off Carnegie integration costs. Operating expenses hit NOK 8.7 billion, driven by higher personnel costs in Norway's tight labor market and investments in AI tools like its top-ranked chatbot and a new Digital Investment Advisor.

The 40% threshold remains a red line, but DNB's CET1 capital ratio of 18.3% provides ample buffer. Management has emphasized that efficiency gains from automation and branch rationalization will curb costs over time.

DNB's path is not without headwinds. The recent 25% risk weight floor on Norwegian mortgages—effective July 2025—will shave 0.7 percentage points off its CET1 ratio, testing capital flexibility. Yet DNB's capital strength and geographic focus—80% of loans in Norway—position it to weather these shifts. The bank's ROE target of >14% and 3-4% annual loan growth remain achievable through disciplined cost management and Carnegie's synergies.

Julius Baer Appoints New Chief Operating Officer Asia

Julius Baer has announced the appointment of Pamela Tseng as Chief Operating Officer Asia, effective 16 November 2026.

Julius Baer has announced the appointment of Pamela Tseng as Chief Operating Officer Asia, effective 16 November 2026.

Based in Singapore, Tseng will be responsible for driving key business improvements in both client and employee experience in Asia. She will report to Jean Nabaa, Chief Operating Officer and Member of the Executive Board, and Jimmy Lee, Region Head Asia and Member of the Global Wealth Management Committee.

She brings extensive leadership experience in operational management and will lead the function across the Asia region, helping the Bank’s business to operate efficiently and securely. Her appointment supports the continued evolution of the whole Julius Baer operating platform, delivering greater efficiency and resilience for all our clients and colleagues.

She joins Julius Baer from Standard Chartered Bank, where most recently she held the role of Global Chief Operating Officer for Private Banking, having previously served as COO for Wealth Solutions and Affluent Banking. With extensive multi-market experience in leading large-scale transformation, as well as driving platform innovation, growth, and operational efficiency, she brings strong leadership and a proven track record of delivering strategic change. Prior to joining Standard Chartered Bank, she held senior leadership roles at Citi in New York and Hong Kong, and earlier with Accenture in Singapore and Beijing.

The Bank also announced that Andreas Zingg, the current Chief Operating Officer Asia, will retire from Julius Baer after 23 years with the Bank. During his tenure with Julius Baer, Zingg played an instrumental role in strengthening the Bank’s operating platform across Asia, leading key transformation initiatives and building a resilient, client-focused operations organisation. Tseng will work closely with Zingg to ensure a smooth transition.

Commenting on the appointment, Nabaa said: “I am delighted to welcome Pamela Tseng to the Bank. Her proven track record in overseeing complex, large-scale operations, driving strategic transformation, and cultivating high-performing teams will be a tremendous asset to the Group. Given her deep understanding of Asian markets, I am confident she will further strengthen our capabilities across the region. I look forward to working closely with her as we continue to advance our business in Asia and globally and deliver exceptional outcomes for our clients. At the same time, I would like to thank Andreas Zingg for his contributions and wish him a fulfilling next chapter.”

Tseng said: “I am honoured to join the Bank at such an exciting time for the Asia business. The region presents significant opportunities, and I look forward to growing the business with colleagues across our markets and functions to further strengthen our operating platform, enhance the client experience and support the Bank’s long-term strategic ambitions. I am excited to be part of an organisation with such a strong heritage, talented people and unwavering commitment to clients.”

Asia is a core market for Julius Baer and a vital engine of growth. The Bank continues to strengthen its investment in talent, infrastructure, and expertise to better serve the dynamic needs of high and ultra-high-net-worth clients throughout the region.

This year celebrates two decades of Julius Baer’s established presence in Singapore and Hong Kong. As two of the Group’s seven global booking centres and host to one-quarter of its worldwide workforce, these hubs have become the second- and third-largest operational bases outside Switzerland. Tseng’s appointment reflects the Bank’s ongoing dedication to delivering exceptional client service and driving sustainable growth in Asia.

evidence.title: Julius Baer’s Rajguru Flags Inflation Risks From Monsoon, Oil
evidence.text:
Julius Baer’s Rajguru Flags Inflation Risks From Monsoon, Oil

Rupen Rajguru of Julius Baer India warns that low monsoon rainfall and rising oil prices could push up inflation. While he remains optimistic about private-sector banks due to strong credit growth, he suggests investors stay cautious on IT services, where significant growth may take one to two years to materialize.

Rupen Rajguru, Head of Equity Investments and Strategy at Julius Baer India, has highlighted concerns regarding India's macroeconomic stability as the southwest monsoon tracks 14% below normal levels. This deficit, combined with persistent global oil prices, poses a risk of an uptick in inflation. If food prices rise due to lower agricultural output and energy costs remain high, it creates a challenging environment for price control.

Despite these pressures, the Reserve Bank of India is expected to keep interest rates unchanged in the near term. The central bank is likely to focus on liquidity management tools—strategies to control the amount of cash circulating in the system—rather than moving the repo rate. With systemic liquidity currently estimated at around Rs 10 trillion, the financial system maintains a buffer that helps protect against immediate volatility.

For investors, the banking sector, particularly private-sector banks, remains a core area of focus. These institutions continue to demonstrate strong credit growth and comfortable funding profiles. Recent inflows from Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR-B) deposits have also provided support, helping to lower short-term money market rates. This reduction in the cost of funds is gradually being passed on, with some major private banks already lowering their Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate (MCLR), which helps sustain demand for loans.

In contrast, the outlook for the IT services sector remains cautious. While the industry is actively integrating artificial intelligence, productivity gains from these technologies have not yet been sufficient to overcome pricing pressures and stiff competition. For investors considering entry points into the IT sector, the timeline for a durable growth recovery is projected to be 12 to 24 months away.

Investors monitoring these trends should look for updates on food inflation data and trends in global crude oil prices, as these factors will influence the central bank's future stance. Furthermore, tracking whether private banks can maintain their lending margins and credit growth in the coming quarters will be essential for assessing the health of the financial sector.

Julius Baer Names Manu Sharma CEO Of Global Enterprise Services

Julius Baer has appointed Manu Sharma as Chief Executive Officer of Julius Baer Global Enterprise Services, its newly established Global Capability Centre (GCC), giving him the mandate to build and scale an organisation that will support the wealth management group’s operations globally.

The appointment brings Sharma, a financial services executive with more than 24 years of experience, into a role spanning organisational development, governance, operating models and global capability building.

Julius Baer Global Enterprise Services has been set up as a GCC to support the group across markets and functions. Sharma will be responsible for developing the capabilities, culture and operating structure required for the centre to serve the wider organisation.

The mandate also places emphasis on creating a scalable and future-ready operation as Julius Baer develops its global support model. Sharma shared the development on LinkedIn, outlining his focus on building the new organisation and working with teams across the group.

Sharma brings experience across retail and corporate banking, wealth management, capital markets and non-banking financial services. His career has included responsibilities involving business growth, digital transformation, governance, risk management and client operations.

He has worked with financial institutions including HDFC Bank, HSBC and Deutsche Bank. His background also includes experience in setting up Global Capability Centre operations, which aligns with his new assignment at Julius Baer.

Before joining Julius Baer Global Enterprise Services, Sharma held senior leadership responsibilities at Deutsche Bank. He served as chairman of a mid-layer non-banking financial company focused on wealth management and structured finance, alongside his role as Chief Operating Officer of the wealth management business.

His responsibilities covered strategy and business development, profit and loss growth, regulatory compliance, governance, risk management, funding and operational management.

He was also part of the country leadership and an Asia-Pacific governance forum, providing oversight on compliance, risk and business matters.

Sharma’s appointment gives Julius Baer an executive with experience across wealth management and large-scale financial services operations as it builds its new GCC. The next phase will centre on how the operation develops its capabilities while integrating with the group’s global functions and governance structure.

Raiffeisen Bank International withdraws from the Belarusian market

The Austrian banking group Raiffeisen Bank International AG (RBI) has signed an agreement with Soven 1 Holding Limited (UAE) on the sale of 87.74% in Priorbank JSC and its subsidiaries. This is reported in the RBI press release.

Thus, RBI has completed negotiations on the sale of Priorbank, announced on February 14, 2024.

The transaction is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2024, subject to regulatory approval.

The transaction will have a negative impact on the consolidated profit of RBI in the amount of 300 million euros due to the difference between the purchase price and the book value of Priorbank JSC.

At the time of closing the transaction, the impact on the CET1 ratio of the RBI group excluding Russia is expected to be about -5 basis points, due to the estimated difference between the purchase price and the book value of capital, as well as the deconsolidation of the RWA of Priorbank JSC.

In addition, at the closing of the transaction, a further negative impact on the consolidated profit of RBI Group in the amount of about 500 million euros is expected. However, this will not have an impact on the regulatory capital and the RBI capital adequacy ratio, as it is associated with the reclassification of historical exchange differences, which are currently recognized in other comprehensive income.

After the completion of the transaction, RBI will finally exit the Belarusian market and simplify its operations in accordance with the strategy to reduce the risks of operations in Eastern Europe.

Priorbank JSC will maintain full independence within the framework of the structure of the new owner of Soven 1 Holding Limited.

Raiffeisen Bank International is one of the largest Austrian banking groups. The headquarters is located in Vienna (Austria).

Priorbank has been operating in Belarus since the end of 1989, and joined the RBI group in 2003.

evidence.title: Raiffeisen Bank International's Multi-Million-Dollar Court Victory and a Defense Against Short Sellers
evidence.text:
Raiffeisen Bank International's Multi-Million-Dollar Court Victory and a Defense Against Short Sellers

The bank announced a legal milestone in Russia: The Vienna Regional Court for Civil Matters awarded RBI and its Russian subsidiary, AO Raiffeisen, approximately 3.15 billion euros in damages, ORF reported. The default judgment against the Russian investment firm Rasperia Trading followed a thorough judicial review, in which the court deemed RBI’s claims admissible and well-founded.

“We have a responsibility to the shareholders of Raiffeisen Bank International to take effective action against the damages incurred in Russia,” emphasized RBI CEO Michael Höllerer regarding the court’s decision. Rasperia now has four weeks to file an appeal.

EU Sanctions as the Trigger for the Cascade

The legal dispute stems from EU sanctions that prevented the construction group STRABAG from paying dividends to Rasperia. Because STRABAG has no assets in Russia, Rasperia instead sued the local RBI subsidiary and secured a Russian judgment in the spring of 2025 for 2.4 billion euros.

RBI countered in July with its own lawsuit in Vienna. As soon as the Vienna ruling becomes final, RBI plans to apply to the Austrian Financial Market Authority (FMA)—the competent sanctions authority—for the release of Rasperia’s currently frozen assets. There is uncertainty regarding Rasperia’s backers; historically, the sanctioned oligarch Oleg Deripaska was considered the owner. RBI remains the largest Western bank in Russia but is under massive pressure from the European Central Bank (ECB) to drastically reduce its local exposure.

Standing Up to Short Sellers: RBI Firmly Rejects Criticism

In parallel with its legal success, the bank is facing accusations on the stock market, as reported by Finanzen.at. A short-seller report published by Grizzly Research temporarily put pressure on Raiffeisen shares. RBI responded promptly in a press release and rejected all allegations “in the strongest possible terms.” The bank is currently considering legal action against the authors.

The bank accused the authors of factual errors and misleading claims. It stated that the companies named in the report were either never clients of RBI or AO Raiffeisenbank, or had already been blacklisted by the bank prior to any official sanctions.

The report ignores the conservative calculation of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR). As of June 30, 2026, the Group’s LCR stands at 136% (135% excluding Russia). In this calculation, over 7 billion euros in high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) held by the Russian subsidiary are strictly excluded. In both the lawsuit against Rasperia and the sale of the Belarusian subsidiary (Priorbank JSC), the bank maintained close coordination with sanctions authorities such as the U.S. OFAC and the Austrian FMA. In the days before and after the lawsuit was filed in Austria, as well as during asset sales, all steps were transparently coordinated with the regulatory authorities.

evidence.title: Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% after a short seller accused the lender of helping Russia evade sanctions. The bank called the report misleading and factually ...
evidence.text:
Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% after a short seller accused the lender of helping Russia evade sanctions. The bank called the report misleading and factually wrong.

Shares in Raiffeisen Bank International fell 9% during trading on September 17 after the short seller Grizzly Research published a report accusing the bank of helping Russia evade sanctions.

Raiffeisen said the report was misleading and contained factual errors. “We remain confident in the strength of our compliance systems, which have been audited repeatedly,” a bank spokesperson said. The spokesperson also said the company has spent years trying to sell its Russian business and leave Russia.

In its report, Grizzly Research called Raiffeisen and its Russian subsidiary “one of the key channels for evading sanctions.” The report’s authors say $1.19 billion in trade with Russia went through the bank, including trade in sanctioned goods used by Russia’s armed forces.

Analysts at Bloomberg Intelligence say Grizzly Research may be exaggerating Raiffeisen’s sanctions risks. In their view, transactions through the bank’s Russian subsidiary are not in themselves evidence of sanctions evasion.

The bigger risk comes from regulators: any close scrutiny from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control or the European Central Bank could further complicate Raiffeisen’s already difficult exit from Russia.

Raiffeisen Bank International’s main asset in Russia is its subsidiary, AO Raiffeisenbank. AO Raiffeisenbank remains the largest Western lender in the country and has not been hit by Western sanctions.

Raiffeisen announced plans to wind down its Russian operations as early as the first weeks of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but it has yet to leave the Russian market.

Russian authorities are blocking the sale of Raiffeisen’s Russian business. Any deal requires their approval, but Moscow wants to keep the bank in Russia as a conduit for settling payments with Western countries, chiefly Europe. At the same time, the United States has pressured Raiffeisen over its dealings with Russia.

The Excess Returns model looks at how much value a bank can create over and above the return that shareholders require. It starts with the equity invested in the business, then asks whether ongoing returns on that equity are high enough to justify a higher share price.

For Erste Group Bank, the model uses a Book Value of €65.90 per share and a Stable EPS of €10.27 per share, based on weighted future Return on Equity estimates from 13 analysts. The implied Average Return on Equity is 15.01%, compared with a Cost of Equity of €4.76 per share. That gap feeds into an Excess Return of €5.51 per share, which is capitalised over time using a Stable Book Value of €68.44 per share sourced from six analysts.

Putting this together, the Excess Returns valuation produces an estimated intrinsic value of about €183.91 per share. Against the recent share price of €109.40, this points to an implied discount of 40.5%, suggesting the shares trade below this model's estimate of value.

For a profitable bank like Erste Group Bank, the P/E ratio is a useful shorthand for what you are paying for each euro of earnings. It captures how the market weighs earnings against perceived growth potential and risk, which is often how bank shares are compared day to day.

In general, higher growth expectations and lower perceived risk can justify a higher P/E, while slower growth or higher risk usually line up with a lower "normal" multiple. Erste Group Bank currently trades on a P/E of 13.94x. evidence.title: Erste Group implements Neterium's transaction screening system
evidence.text:
Erste Group implements Neterium's transaction screening system

The system transition followed a one-year pilot phase with extensive testing and tuning, culminating in full deployment as of September 2024. The partnership between Erste Group, a major financial service provider in Central and Eastern Europe, and Neterium, an API-native and cloud-based regulatory technology provider, was initially launched on 19 September 2023.

Its primary aim has been to enhance Erste Group’s compliance infrastructure with a scalable, efficient transaction screening tool. Over the past year, the screening solution, Jetflow, underwent rigorous testing to ensure it aligns with the operational demands of Erste’s core markets.

Jetflow, Neterium’s main transaction screening solution, offers real-time, API-driven watchlist screening. The tool was designed to provide high throughput, low latency, and robust data analytics, aiming to increase transparency and efficiency for large-scale institutions such as Erste Group.

Officials from Erste Group Bank AG, remarked on the integration and described it as an excellent fit for their current and future needs. Neterium representatives talked about working with Erste Group during this transformation and described it as a significant experience. They also expressed their eagerness to move forward with this productive, long-term partnership.

The completion of the integration marks a key development for both companies as they strengthen their capabilities in financial security and compliance across Central and Eastern Europe.

More information about the two companies

According to the official press release, Erste Group is a financial service provider in Central and Eastern Europe with around 45,000 employees serving millions of customers through approximately 2,000 branches in seven countries, namely Austria, Czechia, Slovakia, Romania, Hungary, Croatia, and Serbia. As of mid-2024, Erste Group reported total assets of EUR 344 billion, a net profit of EUR 1.6 billion, and a Common Equity Tier 1 ratio (pro forma) of 15.5%.

Neterium was founded in 2017 and is an API-native RegTech firm specialising in financial crime prevention. The company provides SaaS solutions that integrate advanced screening capabilities into financial platforms, supported by the latest technologies and expertise in financial crime compliance.

evidence.title: OTP Bank stock holds 47,500 forint resistance
evidence.text:
OTP Bank stock (ISIN HU0000061726) closed at HUF 46,240 on September 21, 2026, up 0.2 percent, while the BUX added 0.1 percent to 152,996 points and trading volume on the Budapest exchange reached HUF 18.8 billion. Vilaggazdasag said at 06:45 on September 21, 2026, that the shares were still trading below HUF 47,500, which had turned into the next resistance zone.

According to Vilaggazdasag on September 21, 2026, OTP had not broken through HUF 47,500, and the same analysis placed support between HUF 45,950 and HUF 46,280. The stock therefore finished the session inside a tight technical band rather than at a fresh breakout level.

At the same time, Privatbankar reported that OTP climbed 0.2 percent to HUF 46,240 and that the broader market closed only 0.1 percent higher. That combination leaves the bank's move modest but still better than the flat-to-mildly positive index backdrop.

The session range in the Budapest market data quoted by Privatbankar ran from HUF 46,010 to HUF 46,940, with OTP changing hands at HUF 46,240 at 17:08:35. The trading tone was firm enough to keep the share near the upper half of that range, but still below the HUF 47,500 ceiling flagged by Vilaggazdasag.

For investors, the number that matters most today is the gap between HUF 46,240 and HUF 47,500. A move through that level would change the short-term picture more than the modest 0.2 percent daily gain.

Today, Luminor announces that its shareholders, a consortium of private equity funds managed by Blackstone, and DNB Bank, have agreed to sell their shares in Luminor Holding to OTP Bank. OTP Bank PLC (OTPBF) Q1 2026 Earnings Call Highlights: Strong Profit Growth Amidst Tax Challenges

This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Profit After Tax Increase: 13% year on year.

Stage 3 Ratio: Slight improvement to 3.4%.

For the complete transcript of the earnings call, please refer to the full earnings call transcript .

OTP Bank PLC ( OTPBF ) reported a 13% year-on-year increase in Profit After Tax, driven by a 17% rise in Net Interest Income.

The bank's Net Interest Margin continued to improve, showing a positive trend compared to the previous year and quarter.

Retail deposit market share in Hungary increased, indicating strong customer relationships and trust.

The bank's liquidity ratios remain strong, with a Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of 77% and a Liquidity Coverage Ratio of 227%.

OTP Bank PLC ( OTPBF ) has restarted its share buyback program, reflecting confidence in its financial position.

The first quarter results were negatively impacted by substantial one-off taxes in Hungary, distorting the financial performance.

Net Fee and Commission income showed only a 1% growth year-on-year, affected by regulatory constraints and lower transactional income in Russia.

The bank faces increased cost pressures, with a 17% FX-adjusted cost growth, raising concerns about cost management.

The political and economic situation in Hungary, including high sector taxes, poses challenges to the bank's profitability.

OTP Bank PLC ( OTPBF ) experienced operational issues in Uzbekistan, affecting loan growth in the region.

Q : How do you expect cost growth to evolve given the 17% FX-adjusted cost growth, and can you reassure that revenue growth will drop to the bottom line despite cost inflation? A : Laszlo Bencsik, Chief Strategic and Financial Officer, explained that the 17% cost growth is high, particularly in Russia due to investments in compliance, regulatory control, and IT. Despite this, NII growth was also 17%. While cost control is monitored, there are no plans for drastic measures. The focus is on Hungary, where measures are being taken to reduce HQ size and improve efficiency.

Q : What is the likelihood of a significant Bank Tax cut in Hungary next year, and how might the contraction in sovereign spreads impact your financials? A : Bencsik noted that a Bank Tax cut this year is unlikely due to the fiscal position. However, there is an expectation for a gradual decrease in the Extra Profit Tax in Hungary over time. The contraction in sovereign spreads does not have an immediate capital impact as most government bonds are in the Hold-to-Maturity portfolio.

Q : Can you comment on your headcount strategy and the margin outlook across key markets? A : Bencsik stated that there is no overall headcount policy for the group, as different entities are at different stages of development. The focus is on Hungary, particularly the HQ, for efficiency improvements. Regarding margins, the outlook is positive, with potential for better performance than last year, especially in Hungary due to strong retail deposit growth.

Q : What is the outlook for fees, particularly in Russia, Hungary, and Bulgaria, given the recent slowdown? A : Bencsik explained that fee income growth was modest due to declines in Russia and delayed fee adjustments in Hungary. In Russia, transactional fees and FX conversion margins declined, which is expected to continue. In Hungary, fee growth should recover in the second half of the year.

Q : Can you provide updates on M&A activities and the level of excess capital available for potential acquisitions? A : Bencsik mentioned that while they continue to explore M&A opportunities, any deal must create value for shareholders. The effective Tier 1 capital ratio is 17.9%, providing room for share buybacks or acquisitions. The focus remains on creating value rather than pursuing deals under pressure.

evidence.title: OTP Bank Joins CLSSettlement in Push to Cut FX Risk
evidence.text:
OTP Bank Joins CLSSettlement in Push to Cut FX Risk

OTP Bank, Hungary’s largest lender, has become the newest direct member of CLSSettlement, as demand rises across Europe’s banking sector for more efficient ways to handle foreign exchange flows.

The move brings CLS’s tally of settlement members to 75, following ABN AMRO’s return in June after more than a decade away.

CLSSettlement processes over $7 trillion in payment instructions daily across 18 currencies. By using a payment-versus-payment (PvP) model, the system sharply reduces the risk that one side of a currency trade fails to deliver — an issue that continues to trouble regulators and market participants alike.

For OTP, the decision is both a technical and strategic shift. “Mitigating FX settlement risk is a key priority for OTP Bank,” said Attila Bánfi, managing director of OTP Global Markets. “Joining CLSSettlement reflects our focus on building a more resilient FX operation and aligning with the best infrastructure the market has to offer.”

CLS’s multilateral netting mechanism — which offsets trades among participants — also helps banks unlock significant liquidity. According to the firm, members can reduce daily funding needs by up to 96%, freeing up capital for lending or trading activities.

Lisa Danino-Lewis, CLS’s chief growth officer, said OTP’s addition fits into a wider trend. “More banks are moving toward direct settlement as regulatory scrutiny grows and institutions look to tighten risk controls while improving efficiency,” she said.

OTP’s membership comes at a time when central European banks are increasingly active in global FX markets, driven by cross-border trade and investor flows. The Budapest-based lender has grown its regional presence over the past decade, with operations in countries including Romania, Serbia, Bulgaria, and Croatia.

Related IBM Adds Swift Ledger Access to Digital Asset Haven via ISO 20022

Meanwhile, ABN AMRO’s re-entry earlier this year marked a return to the infrastructure it helped launch in 2002. The Dutch bank stepped back in 2009, opting for indirect access via third-party providers — a model many institutions are now moving away from as internal risk management becomes more central to strategy.

evidence.title: KBC Group: KBC Bank Ireland (now Exicon DAC) to return its banking licence to the Central Bank of Ireland on 30 April 2024
evidence.text:
KBC Bank Ireland (renamed Exicon DAC on 8 February 2024) can confirm that it will return its banking licence to the Central Bank of Ireland on 30 April 2024, after having received approval from the Central Bank of Ireland and the European Central Bank.

KBC Bank NV Dublin Branch staff will continue to be available to support any queries from customers. Customers retain their legal and regulatory protections. (More information for customers on https://www.kbc.com/en/kbc-ireland.html )

KBC Bank Ireland wishes to sincerely thank its customers and stakeholders for their trust over the past decades and express its deep gratitude to all KBC Bank Ireland employees who have maintained the highest of standards in their work, providing continued support to customers and to each other while preparing the orderly exit.

KBC Bank Ireland was established in 1973 as Irish Intercontinental Bank . In 1978, KBC Bank took a 75% interest in Irish Intercontinental Bank. KBC Bank acquired a full 100% shareholding in 1999. On the 30th anniversary of KBC's majority ownership in 2008, the Bank was renamed KBC Bank Ireland plc.

Given the challenging operational context for European banks and after careful consideration, KBC Bank Ireland entered into a legally binding agreement with Bank of Ireland relating to the sale of substantially all of KBC Bank Ireland’s performing loan assets and its deposit book to Bank of Ireland Group on 22 October 2021. In addition, a small portfolio of non-performing mortgages (NPEs) was also acquired by Bank of Ireland as part of the transaction ( link to press release)

KBC Bank Ireland closed the sale of substantially all of its assets and liabilities to Bank of Ireland on 3 February 2023 ( link to press release) and started preparing the return of its banking licence to the Central Bank of Ireland.

As KBC Bank Ireland would no longer be operating in the Irish market, on 25 May 2023 KBC Bank Ireland and KBC Bank NV, acting through its branch in Ireland, agreed the transfer of any remaining accounts and servicing activity to KBC Bank NV Dublin Branch. On 13 September 2023 the Minister for Finance approved the Transfer. On 1 December 2023 KBC Bank Ireland completed the transfer agreement in respect of substantially all of its remaining assets and current and future liabilities to KBC Bank NV Dublin Branch which includes all unidentified and identified residual customer or regulatory claims or liabilities of the Bank. KBC Bank NV Dublin Branch is licenced by the National Bank of Belgium in Belgium and is regulated by the Central Bank of Ireland for conduct of business rules. On 8 February 2024 KBC Bank Ireland was renamed Exicon DAC.

evidence.title: Belfius names head of trade finance
evidence.text:
Belgian lender Belfius has promoted Laurianne Bouchart to head of trade finance.
