evidence.title: Best Orange Cake Ever
evidence.text:
Orange cake is a moist and tender cake bursting with fresh orange flavor. I’ve tried many orange cakes over the years, but this easy orange cake recipe stands out for its soft crumb, balanced citrus flavor, and simple preparation.

This homemade orange cake is made with fresh orange juice and orange zest, while a combination of butter and oil keeps it moist for days. It doesn’t need syrup, and I actually think the orange flavor gets even better the next day.

I’ve been baking for more than 15 years, and this orange cake recipe with orange juice has become one of my family’s favorites. The batter comes together quickly using simple ingredients, making this a simple orange cake recipe from scratch for both beginner and experienced bakers.

I’m the only baker in my family, and this homemade orange cake has everything I look for in a good cake: a moist and tender crumb, balanced orange flavor, and just the right amount of sweetness.

This orange cake recipe with orange juice doesn’t need syrup to stay moist, and its flavor gets even better the next day.

You can bake it in an 8.5 x 4.5-inch loaf pan, 8-inch Bundt pan, 9-inch round or square pan, or a 12-cupcake pan .

For the best results, measure the ingredients carefully using measuring cups and spoons, and make sure to read my Pro Tips below for the little details that help this orange cake turn out perfectly.

All you need are simple pantry ingredients to make this moist orange cake recipe at home.

Eggs: Give the cake structure, richness, and a tender crumb.

All-purpose flour: Gives the cake structure while keeping the crumb tender. You can use cake flour for a finer, lighter crumb.

Baking powder: Helps the cake rise and gives it a light and fluffy texture.

Milk: Adds moisture and richness to the cake batter.

Fresh orange juice: Gives this cake made with fresh oranges its bright, natural citrus flavor.

Orange zest: Adds a stronger orange aroma and flavor without adding extra liquid.

Oil: Helps keep the orange cake moist and tender for days.

Melted unsalted butter: Adds richness and buttery flavor. Using both butter and oil gives this cake the best of both worlds.

This orange cake recipe comes together quickly, but a few simple techniques will help you get a soft, moist cake every time.

Step 1: Sift the dry ingredients Sift the flour, baking powder, and other dry ingredients together, except the sugar. This helps create a tender crumb and prevents lumps in the cake batter.

Step 2: Mix the wet ingredients In a separate bowl, beat the oil, melted butter, and sugar until well combined. Add the eggs one at a time, then add the milk, fresh orange juice, and orange zest.

Step 3: Combine the wet and dry ingredients Gradually add the flour mixture to the wet ingredients. Mix gently just until combined. Do not overmix , or your orange cake may turn out dense. A few small lumps in the batter are fine.

Step 4: Bake the orange cake Pour the batter into the prepared baking pan and bake on the middle rack of a preheated oven until the cake is golden and cooked through.

Step 5: Cool and serve Allow the cake to cool before slicing. You can enjoy it the same day, but the orange flavor becomes even better the next day .

This homemade orange cake is delicious on its own, but you can also serve it in different ways:

This orange cake recipe is delicious as it is, but you can easily change it up with these simple variations:

I use all-purpose flour for this orange cake recipe because it gives the cake a soft but sturdy crumb. For a lighter, finer texture, you can use cake flour or a homemade cake flour substitute.

For the best orange flavor , I recommend fresh orange juice. Bottled juice can have a different flavor and may contain added ingredients. Fresh juice combined with orange zest gives this cake its bright citrus taste.

Yes. You can make this orange cake with oil instead of using both oil and butter. However, I prefer the combination: the oil helps keep the cake moist, while the butter adds richness and flavor.

Avoid overmixing the batter and overbaking the cake. Using oil, butter, milk, and fresh orange juice also helps produce a moist orange cake that stays tender for days.

Allow the cake to cool completely before storing it.

If you have tried this orange cake recipe and liked it, please give it a 5-star rating and leave a comment below with your experience!

Muna is a food blogger and a food photographer. She is passionate about sharing easy-to-follow and delicious recipes from around the world. Her goal is to help you recreate restaurant-style meals in the comfort of your own home, using readily available ingredients and straightforward instructions.

Do not confuse it with +33 9 69 39 39 00 , which is the international number of Orange's general customer service: that line is answered in French.

If the English line is closed or busy, you can still call the general French helpline on 3900 and ask to be transferred. Operators on the main line will usually try to find an English-speaking colleague, although there is no guarantee.

Orange France replies to public and private messages on its X / Twitter , Facebook , LinkedIn and Instagram accounts. Response times are usually within a few hours during business days, but the social-media team cannot handle billing details or contract changes that require identity verification.

Postal mail is mostly used for formal complaints and for the contract cancellation letter when you terminate by registered post ("lettre recommandée avec accusé de réception"). Orange uses different addresses depending on the topic.

If the mediator's reply is still not satisfactory, you can finally refer the case to the Médiateur des Communications Électroniques , an independent arbitrator for the French telecoms industry.

The fastest way to reach Orange in English in 2026 remains the dedicated helpline 09 69 36 39 00 , ideally called during business hours from Monday to Saturday. A Selectra advisor handles the call for you, in English, and finalises the Orange subscription or change in one go.

Calling 09 69 36 39 00 from any French line is included in unlimited landline-to-landline call allowances, so it is free of charge with any modern French mobile or fixed plan. Calling +33 9 69 36 39 00 from abroad costs the standard international rate from your local operator. The call is free of any per-minute surcharge from Orange itself.

Email is not the recommended channel for cancellation. The safest options are a phone call to the 3900 customer service (or the English helpline), a cancellation request through the Espace Client portal, or a registered letter to the Orange Service Résiliation address in Bordeaux. evidence.title: Orange Belgium Launches Cyber Protection to Secure Small & Medium-Sized Businesses
evidence.text:
Orange Belgium Launches Cyber Protection to Secure Small & Medium-Sized Businesses

From ransomware attacks to online fraud, cyber incidents make the headlines almost every week, and large companies are far from the only targets. The number of cyber-extortion victims worldwide rose by 44.5% in 2025, with small and medium-sized enterprises accounting for two-thirds of affected organisations. To help smaller businesses strengthen their defences, Orange Belgium is launching Cyber Protection, a managed cybersecurity solution for small & medium-sized companies with up to 30 employees. The service protects their computers around the clock by combining AI-powered threat detection with support from Orange Cyberdefense experts.

Around 100 ransomware attacks are reported in Belgium each year, and the consequences can last much longer than the attack itself: IT systems remain offline for an average of 21 days. These attacks are not limited to large corporations. Research by Orange Cyberdefense shows that attacks on small businesses rose by 53% in one year, while medium-sized businesses saw a 52% increase. In response, nearly 44% of companies have increased their cybersecurity budgets. With end-user devices and servers accounting for 54% of affected assets, the computers people rely on every day remain a critical line of defence. For many SMEs, the challenge is not recognising the risk but having access to affordable cybersecurity expertise.

24/7 protection without the need for an in-house security team

Following the launch of Dynamic SOC in April 2025, Orange Belgium is extending its cybersecurity portfolio to smaller organisations. Cyber Protection is a managed Endpoint Detection and Response solution designed for small office/home office businesses and small to medium-sized companies, meaning they benefit from enterprise-grade monitoring without having to manage the security themselves. It protects up to 30 Windows and macOS devices 24/7 and monitors activity in real time. Unlike traditional antivirus software, which mainly detects known threats, Cyber Protection combines AI-driven behavioural analysis with expert monitoring to detect both known and previously unseen attacks.

When the system identifies suspicious activity, it can automatically block or isolate the affected file to help prevent a threat from spreading. Users can follow the status of every protected device, detected threat and quarantined file through a real-time dashboard and receive alerts when an event requires attention. Orange Cyberdefense experts analyse alerts around the clock and can block threats proactively, giving smaller companies access to continuous monitoring without requiring them to build a Security Operations Centre (SOC) of their own.

Cyber Protection works continuously in the background, allowing business owners to focus on running their business rather than monitoring cyber threats.

In addition to protecting against cyber threats, Cyber Protection helps businesses meet key regulatory requirements. The solution supports compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) by enabling rapid detection and response to potential data breaches, and by providing detailed incident logs for investigation and reporting. It also aligns with the new NIS2 Directive, which requires organizations to implement robust cybersecurity measures, including continuous monitoring and timely incident reporting. By integrating Cyber Protection, small businesses can strengthen their security posture while supporting their legal obligations under European regulations.

Cyber Protection makes enterprise-grade cybersecurity accessible to even the smallest businesses. Installation takes only a few minutes through the Orange Cyberdefense portal, making the solution easy to deploy even without dedicated IT resources. Cyber Protection is available from 17 August 2026, with monthly plans ranging from €6 for one computer to €126 for 30 computers, excluding VAT.

Werner De Laet, Chief Enterprise Officer at Orange Belgium

Small businesses often depend on a limited number of devices, but that does not make the consequences of an attack any smaller. One compromised computer can interrupt daily operations, expose sensitive information or cut a company off from the tools it needs to serve its customers. At the same time, many entrepreneurs do not have a cybersecurity specialist on staff. They need protection that works continuously, keeps them informed and brings in expert support when it matters most. With Cyber Protection and the support from Orange Cyberdefense, we want to make that level of security more accessible, so business owners can focus on their work without having to become cybersecurity experts themselves.

Ray Sharma is an Industry Analyst and Editor at The Fast Mode. He has over 15 years of experience in mobile broadband technologies and solutions, conducting research and analysis on various technology segments and producing articles and write-ups on the latest developments within the sector. He is also in charge of social media engagement and industry liaisons.

evidence.title: Orange Business Live 2026 Calls for Stronger Corporate Cybersecurity Governance
evidence.text:
Orange Business Live 2026 Calls for Stronger Corporate Cybersecurity Governance

Orange Côte d’Ivoire warned businesses that cybersecurity has become a strategic governance issue as cyberattacks increase across Africa.

Cyberattacks recorded in Côte d’Ivoire rose from 2 million in the early 2020s to 27 million, making the country the world’s 51st most targeted in 2025, according to Orange.

Experts said companies must integrate cybersecurity into leadership decisions, with governance accounting for 70% of cybersecurity effectiveness compared with 30% for technology.

Orange Côte d’Ivoire called on companies to place cybersecurity at the center of their governance strategies as digital threats continue to expand across Africa. The company hosted the 21st edition of Orange Business Live on July 9, 2026, in a hybrid format under the theme: “Cybersecurity, governance and responsibility: the new risk triangle for companies.”

The event brought together business leaders, cybersecurity experts and partners to discuss the growing impact of cyber threats and the need for organizations to strengthen resilience and regulatory compliance.

Ferdinand Tra, Orange Business & Broadband director and president of Orange Cloud & Cyber Solutions, said cybercriminals do not target specific countries but instead focus on organizations with security weaknesses.

Tra explained that Côte d’Ivoire’s digital transformation, driven by cloud adoption, digital financial services and online platforms, has increased the country’s exposure to cyber risks.

According to Tra, cyberattacks in Côte d’Ivoire increased from 2 million in the early 2020s to 27 million incidents, making the country the 51st most targeted globally in 2025.

“The question is no longer whether a company will be attacked. The real question is how it prepares, how it ensures business continuity and how it protects its customers when an attack occurs,” Tra said.

Carole Lepregnon, director of audits and compliance at Côte d’Ivoire’s National Agency for Information Systems Security, said cyber risk now affects both public institutions and private companies regardless of their size or sector.

Lepregnon identified three major sources of vulnerability. First, she pointed to basic security weaknesses, including weak passwords, outdated systems and poorly configured servers.

Second, she highlighted the gap between the speed of digital transformation and the deployment of cybersecurity measures.

Third, she noted that many organizations still view cybersecurity mainly as a technical issue rather than a strategic responsibility. According to Lepregnon, governance and internal policies account for 70% of cybersecurity effectiveness, while technology represents 30%.

She also recalled that the General Security Framework for Information Systems (RGSSI), adopted by decree in 2021, establishes the national cybersecurity standard that all organizations operating in Côte d’Ivoire must follow.

“Cybersecurity is not a matter for IT specialists. It is a matter of governance, legal responsibility and trust toward customers, partners and the state,” she said.

Through its subsidiary Orange Cloud & Cyber Solutions, Orange provides services covering cloud computing, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and data management. As part of this evolution, Bouygues Telecom is replacing its legacy SNMP based monitoring service assurance platform with the Expresse solution, featuring an architecture focused on AI analysis, telemetry and modern GUI for efficient customer support. This strategic shift will enable significantly deeper, real-time visibility across complex, multi-vendor network environments .

evidence.title: Alberto Manguel in Istanbul: Iliad and Odyssey still speak to shared humanity
evidence.text:
Alberto Manguel in Istanbul: Iliad and Odyssey still speak to shared humanity

W riter, translator, and literary scholar Alberto Manguel met readers in Istanbul, arguing that Homer's Iliad and Odyssey continue to speak to modern experiences of war, displacement, and the search for home while reminding readers of what he described as humanity's shared values.

Manguel was in Istanbul for a signing of his book " Homer's Iliad and Odyssey: A Biography ," a Turkish version published in Türkiye by Yapi Kredi Publications, before taking part in a talk titled "Alberto Manguel Talks About the Iliad and Odyssey" at Yapi Kredi Kultur Sanat Loca. The discussion was moderated by translator and film writer Kutlukhan Kutlu.

Speaking before the event, Manguel recalled having visited Türkiye several times and said his first trip to Istanbul had been with his son when he was around 14 or 15.

He also pointed to a family connection with the country, noting that his nephew had married a Turkish woman and that he had relatives in Ankara.

Classics grow as generations read them differently

Manguel said the idea of writing biographies of books had come out of a publisher's proposal and that he chose the Iliad and the Odyssey when asked to focus on two major works.

He argued that classics become richer as they pass from one generation to another because every new group of readers adds another layer of interpretation, effectively keeping the works alive.

Referring to French writer Raymond Queneau's observation that every book is either an Odyssey or an Iliad, Manguel said the two epics capture fundamental patterns of human experience.

"Books are about human life, and every life consists of a journey and a battle. Therefore, everything we write in literature reflects the great metaphors of the Odyssey, which represents life as a journey, and the Iliad, which represents it as a battle," he said.

Manguel added that readers tend to choose books in which they recognize themselves and that a book capable of deeply affecting a reader can, in a sense, become part of that person's autobiography.

Manguel said the Iliad and the Odyssey had been read differently across history, adding that it is impossible to know exactly how Homer's contemporaries understood or listened to the poems.

In Rome, he noted, the Iliad later became tied to the idea that Romans descended not from the victorious Greeks but from the defeated Trojans, with Aeneas escaping Troy with his father and son and becoming part of Rome's founding story.

He also pointed to echoes of Homeric themes in the Arab world, even though Homer was not translated completely into Arabic, drawing parallels between Sinbad's journeys in One Thousand and One Nights and the obstacles faced by Odysseus, as well as between accounts of warfare and themes found in the Iliad.

Manguel said contemporary audiences are once again turning to the epics for reasons connected with the concerns of the present day, pointing to Christopher Nolan's production based on the Odyssey as an example.

He connected the story of Odysseus with people forced to leave their homes and travel through unfamiliar places, saying refugees can find themselves confronted not with hospitality but with hostility.

Manguel also referred to refugees from Ukraine and Gaza, saying they were being met through the violation, rather than the observance, of traditions of hospitality.

Turning to the Iliad, he said the epic may be told through the language of the victors, but its tragic focus repeatedly falls on victims, including Hecuba, Andromache and the women of Troy.

"Today, in our world surrounded by fake news, greed and political ambition, the Iliad and the Odyssey tell us things about our common humanity that we must not forget," Manguel said.

Manguel also underlined the historical importance of Troy, which lies within modern Türkiye, saying the site holds a place in world history comparable to landmarks such as the Colosseum and the Acropolis.

He said Türkiye should take pride in being home to that heritage.

Manguel added that meeting Turkish readers was particularly meaningful to him, saying that listening to readers' responses gives writers a valuable opportunity to understand what audiences find in their books and to build a dialogue with them.

evidence.title: The Most Famous Artworks Depicting Scenes From Homer’s Iliad
evidence.text:
The Most Famous Artworks Depicting Scenes From Homer’s Iliad

Homer’s The Iliad , which recounts the fabled story of the Trojan War, is perhaps the most famous of ancient Greek literary works. Its subject matter is rousing and electrifying yet also profoundly human. It is a tale of war and conflict but also of love and loss. With themes so central to the universal human experience, it is no wonder that Homer’s epic is still being referenced to this day.

In fact, scenes from Homer’s epics have passed through the gifted hands of many famous artists, whether of sculptors or painters. Below are some of the most famous artworks that skillfully depict scenes from The Iliad .

The Most Famous Artworks Depicting Scenes from Homer’s Iliad

The Euphronios Krater is, as its name suggests, a crater, a type of vase used in antiquity to mix wine with water. This crater was the work of Euphronios, a vase painter and potter who lived in Athens during the 6th to 5th century BC. He is an important artist from antiquity who worked with the red-figure technique in his vases.

In the Euphronios Krater, the artist captures two scenes from Greek mythology . The one at its front comes from the Trojan War. It illustrates the death of Sarpedon, a young son of Zeus who fought valiantly on the side of Troy and met an untimely end. In a moment of sorrow, the gods Hypnos (Sleep) and Thanatos (Death) carry his lifeless body, while Hermes, the messenger of the gods, observes the procession.

This artwork is a powerful example of how ancient Greek artists, even nearly two centuries after the publication of The Iliad , were inspired by Homer’s work in their art. It is a testament to the deep influence of Homer’s epic poem. Today, it can be found in the National Archaeological Museum of Cerveteri in Italy.

Achilles and Briseis (or Briseis taken away from Achilles)

Achilles and Briseis is a fresco which again emphasizes the thorough magnitude of Homer’s work. It was discovered in Pompeii in the House of the Tragic Poet and dates from the first century AD.

This Roman fresco, painted in bold, vibrant colors, portrays that scene at the opening of The Iliad in which the Trojan captive Briseis is ushered away from Achilles by Agamemnon’s men. Briseis had originally been awarded to Achilles as a prize of war. However, after Agamemnon (the Mycenaean king and commander) had to return his own captive, Chryseis, to appease Apollo, he demanded Briseis instead.

One can clearly make out the chiseled figure of Achilles, sitting on a chair holding his spear with an affronted expression on his face. Beside him with his back to the viewer is Patroclus , who is seen handing a shrouded Briseis over to Agamemnon’s men. The significance of this artwork is that it pictures a defining point in The Iliad— the beginning of the wrath of Achilles.

Andromache Mourning Hector, by Jacques-Louis David

Jacques-Louis David was a French neoclassical painter known for his portrayals of scenes from the ancient Greek and Roman periods. From his works inspired by The Iliad and its characters, the most renowned by far is Andromache Mourning Hector , painted in 1783.

As its name suggests, it shows the Trojan princess Andromache grieving for her husband Hector, killed by Achilles. All light falls on the striking expression of grief in Andromache’s face. The painting also shows her son with Hector, Astyanax, attempting to comfort her, but her gaze remains upwards, blinded by her loss.

The muted, subdued hues of David’s painting combined with the strong feelings it provokes on the viewer render it one of the most masterful executions of the scene of Hector’s death in The Iliad .

The Life of Achilles, by Peter Paul Rubens

The Life of Achilles isn’t a single artwork but a series of tapestries crafted by Peter Paul Rubens showcasing eight defining scenes from the course of Achilles’ life. These allow a comprehensive glimpse into the life of the glorious hero.

Rubens begins from Achilles’ childhood, painting the scene during which his mother Thetis dipped him into the river Styx to grant him immortality. As in The Iliad , Thetis holds her son from his right heel, the spot that ultimately became his demise. This series of tapestries continues with Achilles’ education by the centaur Chiron , while Rubens also portrays some key scenes from Homer’s epic, including Briseis Restored to Achilles and The Death of Hector . All are painted in Rubens’ characteristic Renaissance-Baroque style with lively colors and vivid emotion.

The last tapestry in Rubens’ series visualizes perhaps the strongest scene, the death of Achilles. Charged with feeling, it shows Achilles succumbing to his death, while what goes on around him could be described as “gentle chaos.” As such, this tribute to Achilles from an artist such as Rubens, as well as from all other artists across the globe, amplifies the status and impact of The Iliad as a work that knows no boundaries, spatial or temporal.

evidence.title: Homer: Did the Man Behind the Iliad and Odyssey Really Exist?
evidence.text:
Homer: Did the Man Behind the Iliad and Odyssey Really Exist?

Homer was one of the most important figures in ancient Greece . His contribution to ancient Greek culture was immense, due to his two most famous poems – the Iliad and the Odyssey . To the ancient Greeks, the works of Homer were as important as the Bible is today. It’s ironic, then, that many scholars actually question whether or not Homer was real . What does the evidence show?

The main reason some scholars doubt that Homer ever existed is because of a lack of contemporary evidence. Most scholars believe that Homer was supposed to have lived in the eighth or even ninth century BC, whereas the first reference to Homer appears to be from the late seventh century BC. This would be between one and two centuries after his supposed lifetime. This gap is viewed as too large for scholars to be confident that he really existed.

One historian has made a different kind of argument . Adam Nicolson argues that the Iliad and the Odyssey show signs of originating from about 1000 years earlier than when Homer is supposed to have lived. This would mean that Homer cannot have been their author. Since Homer’s only contribution to history is as the supposed author of those poems, that would take away his historical standing.

Another argument is that there is supposedly evidence that the Iliad and the Odyssey did not have the same author. This would mean that ‘Homer’ was just a fiction created to neatly explain the existence of both poems.

A key issue involved in this debate is the matter of when Homer really lived. Herodotus claimed that Homer lived ‘no more than 400 years’ before his own time. That would place Homer in the ninth century BC.

But notice that he said ‘no more’ than that length of time. This means that this was the upper limit. Some scholars think that Herodotus had information that Homer lived 10 generations before his own time, and that he was using an upper limit of 40 years per generation in his calculation. A more realistic estimate would be 25 years per generation, which would place Homer in c. 700 BC.

Some other ancient historians explicitly placed Homer in this era, or even a little later. Strabo referred to certain ancient chroniclers who placed Homer at or just after the time of the Cimmerian invasions of Anatolia. That would place Homer in the seventh century BC. The fourth century BC writer Theopompus and the third century BC writer Euporion also supported that date.

This would mean that the earliest reference to Homer, from the late seventh century BC, is actually a near-contemporary reference. This would mean that we can reasonably trust its reliability.

The issue of when the Iliad and the Odyssey were written

Homer could not have been the person who wrote the Iliad and the Odyssey if those poems actually came from over 1000 years before Homer supposedly lived. But the case made by historians such as Adam Nicolson is very weak. They point out that these poems contain certain similarities to stories found all over Europe, indicating that they originate from thousands of years ago.

But this objection is easily explained. Homer could have been using motifs and tropes that were familiar to him. These motifs could have originated thousands of years before Homer’s supposed lifetime, but that does not mean that the poems themselves did.

Could Homer have been the single author of the Iliad and the Odyssey?

The fact is that there is still a lot of debate over whether or not the Iliad and the Odyssey were composed by a single author. It is not a closed case by any means. Different scholars have different opinions. The key reason why some scholars think that they may have been composed by different people is because of discrepancies between the two poems.

There are differences in the way that the poems present certain matters. For example, the Iliad seems to present a positive view of the Phoenicians, while the Odyssey seems to present a negative view of them. The former also presents Achilles’ attitude about death in a very different way to how the latter poem presents it.

However, these are not irreconcilable differences. Apparent differences in viewpoint can be easily explained as being due to different contexts. In the Iliad , Homer was focusing on the glory of the Phoenician items that were being used by certain characters. Obviously, it would make sense for Homer to glorify the things being used by his heroes. But in the Odyssey , which is a story about voyaging, the rivalry between the Greeks and the Phoenicians at sea would obviously be more relevant.

Importantly, both poems display the same style of language. Also, scholars have shown that the language of both poems comes from the same era. These two facts support the idea that they could have had the same author. In any case, it is a question that scholars still debate.

In conclusion, scholars still do not agree about whether or not Homer was real. However, most of the arguments against Homer being real are not particularly strong. For example, it is claimed that there is no near-contemporary reference to him, but the evidence actually indicates that his supposed lifetime should be placed in the seventh century BC, not the eighth or the ninth.

This would mean that the earliest reference to him comes from just a few decades after he supposedly lived, making it a reliable source by any reasonable standard. The other arguments against Homer being real are also fairly weak. Nonetheless, the issue of whether or not Homer was real is still far from settled.

evidence.title: Iliad is stepping up its expansion in Italia and is aiming for its first annual profit
evidence.text:
Iliad is stepping up its expansion in Italia and is aiming for its first annual profit

Domestically, revenue rose by 10.2 per cent and operating cash flow jumped to 106 million. On the issue of frequencies: ‘A rebalancing is needed’. Consolidation remains a long way off

For feedback, please contact english@ilsole24ore.com

For feedback, please contact english@ilsole24ore.com

For the first time since it entered the Italian market, Iliad is on track to post an annual profit. Following a second quarter that closed with a profit of around 44 million, the French group expects 2026 to mark a definitive turning point. “Over the course of the whole year, the contribution from our operations in Italia will be positive for the Group, and this truly represents a significant change: after five or six years of major investment, we are seeing a positive contribution to EBITDA and, now, to cash flow as well,” it was explained during the call with journalists.

This marks the culmination of a journey that began in 2018, built on a series of offers, network investments and growth in the customer base. But above all, it is a sign that Italia is no longer merely the market in which Iliad burns through capital to gain market share: it is becoming one of the pillars underpinning the group. In the first half of the year, Italian revenues rose by 10.2 per cent to 665 million (well above the group’s 3 per cent increase), whilst EBITDA after lease costs grew by 20.2 per cent to 229 million. The margin rose from 31.6% to 34.5% and operating cash flow jumped by 75.2% to 106 million, partly due to the normalisation of capital expenditure, which fell to 124 million.

Thomas Reynaud, the group’s CEO, described Italia as “probably the main source of satisfaction this half-year”. And the figures explain why. At the end of June, Iliad had 12.8 million mobile users and 568,000 fixed-line users, making a total customer base of 13.3 million. In the residential sector, the brand “has overtaken Telecom Italia”, said the CEO, and has become the third-largest brand in the residential human SIM market. The company also claims to be the leader in net customer acquisitions in both mobile and fixed-line broadband, and reports record levels of customer satisfaction.

The Italian result carries even greater weight because it comes at a time when France, the company’s traditional market, is growing at a much slower pace. In the first half of the year, French revenue rose by 1.5 per cent to 3.32 billion, whilst EBITDA after lease fell by 1.9 per cent to 1.29 billion. Poland, on the other hand, recorded revenues of 1.26 billion, up 3.5 per cent, and EBITDA after lease rose by 5.8 per cent to 575 million. Overall, the group generated revenue of 5.24 billion, with operating margins of 2.09 billion and operating cash flow of 1.29 billion, up by 10.2 per cent. Net profit fell to 502 million, weighed down by the comparison with the one-off items in 2025 relating to the sale of 50 per cent of the subsidiary OpCore (which comprises Iliad’s data centres in France and Poland) to the InfraVia fund.

Italy’s path, however, now intersects with the spectrum issue. The licences expire in 2029, and AGCOM is consulting the market on a possible renewal until 2037 in exchange for investment commitments. iliad considers the current distribution of spectrum to be unbalanced and fears that a renewal without corrective measures will end up freezing the existing balance of power for several more years. “We have launched the spectrum consultations. In Italia, we will contribute to the consultations and firmly believe that a rebalancing is necessary in line with national and European legislation. And this is what we will state during the consultations,” said Reynaud, adding nothing further during the call with journalists.

In its financial statement, however, Iliad Italia itself states that ‘Iliad’s growth trajectory in Italia is taking place within a context that requires a regulatory framework capable of supporting long-term investment. The third consultation launched by AGCOM on the procedures for renewing mobile spectrum licences represents a strategic focus: a comprehensive renewal of usage rights from 2030 onwards, without any adjustments to the current balance, would risk cementing a discriminatory market structure until 2037, without recognising the value of the investments made to date in network development’.

As for consolidation, however, the door in Italia appears to be ajar for the time being. Following unsuccessful attempts with Vodafone Italia, which was subsequently acquired by Swisscom, and with TIM , the prospects for Wind Tre also remain remote. Reynaud reiterated that the baseline scenario continues to be that of ‘a four-operator market’: Iliad, Tim, Fastweb+Vodafone and Wind Tre.

The group’s real industrial challenge is currently being played out in France, where Iliad is participating, alongside Orange and Bouygues Telecom, in the deal involving SFR’s assets, which, if completed, is set to transform the group’s scale and propel it to third place amongst European operators.

Meanwhile, the group headed by Xavier Niel is raising the bar even beyond traditional telecommunications. Scaleway, the cloud and artificial intelligence subsidiary, is growing at a rate of over 50 per cent a year, whilst OpCore, a 50-50 joint venture with InfraVia, aims to exceed 400 megawatts of data centre capacity in Europe. This is the other side of the transformation: using the cash flow generated by the networks to fund cloud services, data centres and computing power.

evidence.title: Iliad’s Scaleway advances ‘giant killer’ plans with European cloud tie-ups
evidence.text:
Iliad’s Scaleway advances ‘giant killer’ plans with European cloud tie-ups

Scaleway acquires assets from French analytics and AI platform Saagie, after agreeing partnerships earlier this month with France’s biggest TV co, state compute and science centres

Scaleway has acquired some assets from Saagie, which is based in Normandy and specialises in data operations designed to design and deploy data workflows.

Saagie was established in 2013 and its platform was designed to improve the collaboration, integration and automation of data flows between data processors and those who consume it, such as data scientists, business analysts and business users. It can be used for for real-time analytics and GenAI but has been in receivership since May 2024.

Scaleway is Iliad Group’s cloudco, which makes much of its European roots and ownership. The amount of the transaction was not disclosed. According to Scaleway’s MD, Damien Lucas (pictured), his company will use Saagie’s acquired assets to expands its platform-as-a-service offer and “provide a state-of-the-art data ecosystem,” for applications like Industry 4.0 and GenAI.

Scaleway will soon make Saagie’s products available in all its European locations – Amsterdam, Milan, Paris, Stockholm and Warsaw, and will open an office in Rouen, which is in Normandy to ensure continuity for local workers.

Earlier in June Scaleway signed two strategic partnerships and provided more information about its European goals at the VivaTech in 2025 event.

The first was with France Télévisions (FT) France’s biggest audiovisual group. Under the agreement, FT will use Scaleaway’s cloud to host and process data related to its content. Also the two will jointly develop the tools and systems needed for streaming services hosted on Scaleway’s cloud platform.

They say their alliance is a big step towards building an alternative European cloud for the audiovisual sector.

Scaleway also announced an agreement at the show with Grand Équipement National de Calcul Intensif (GENSI), which was created by France’s public authorities in 2007, and the National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS ). This is the only French organisation active in all scientific fields, apparently. They plan to further European AI by building “a sovereign public/private continuum unique in Europe”.

This new partnership has three main aims:

Damien Lucas, CEO of Scaleway, and Aude Durand, Deputy CEO of the iliad Group, announced at a press briefing at VivaTech that Scaleway will shortly be launching its business in Italy and Sweden.

The iliad Group already operates in these two countries via its B2C telecom business under the Free brand in Italy since 2018 and it became a major shareholder in Sweden’s Tele2 last year . Tele2 operates in Sweden and the Baltic countries.

Scaleway plans to speed up its European expansion by drawing on the iliad Group’s infrastructure and commercial reach within the continent. As part of this, in April Scaleway teamed up with Play – Iliad’s Polish subsidiary. Under their agreement, customers using Play Business Solutions were given access to Scaleway’s cloud – “one of the most comprehensive portfolios of advanced tools developed in Europe,” as the press release had it.

Damien Lucas, CEO of Scaleway, said at VivaTech, “These announcements mark a turning point for Scaleway. By joining forces with key players such as France Télévisions, GENCI and the CNRS, we’re further demonstrating our determination to build a trusted European cloud that’s capable of rivalling the global giants.

“Our expansion into Italy and Sweden is just one of our milestones, driven by our clear goal of becoming the number one tech champion for digital sovereignty in Europe.”

evidence.title: Rethinking the classics: Homer’s ‘The Iliad’ is a rap battle
evidence.text:
Student leaders, activists detained for Jantar Mantar protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar

Review: Karthik Subbaraj’s ‘Dorothy’ has to be seen to be believed

Podcast: How a Jain merchant family navigated business, from Mughal India to modern Ahmedabad

India rejects Organisation of Islamic Cooperation remarks on J&K as ‘unwarranted’

CJP to start nationwide protest if CEC Gyanesh Kumar does not resign in 48 hours

Why Australia has tightened visa, immigration rules for foreign students

Son of SC judge who heard election commissioner appointment act case is EC lawyer

Assembly polls: BJP spent more in Bengal than Congress did in four states, one UT

Delhi history: How Sanjay Gandhi’s ‘beautification’ drive cost the Congress its goodwill

‘The Vvaan: Force of the Forrest’ review: Lookkiing ffor a miiraclle

Homer’s The Iliad is one of the foundational stories of European civilisation. The Iliad is a long poem – an epic – thought to have first been put down in writing in the eighth century BC, though the story is set several hundred years before, perhaps as early as the 12th or 13th century BC.

It explores a few crucial violent weeks within a much longer war between an alliance of Greek city-states and the city of Troy over Helen, the most beautiful woman in the world. In it, we find ancient Greek gods and humans sharing a common reality. They concurrently star as the central characters of both a mythological and an earthly dramatic encounter, on which the fate of a people rests.

In his work, public philosopher Cornel West argues that there is a “gangster” inside all of us . The challenge, West teaches, is to learn to keep these “gangster elements” in check so that we can still live with decency and integrity in an often violent and unjust world. This struggle, I contend, is at the heart of both Homer’s The Iliad and the art of battle rap.

Battle rap is an art form where two or more MCs confront one another in a freestyle rap that includes boasts, insults, wordplay and disses (related to but not to be confused with rap beefs like the Kendrick Lamar and Drake feud ).

The history of this kind of verbal jousting goes back at least to flyting – poetic duels usually involving rhyming insults, widespread in northern Europe in the late medieval era. (See Assassin’s Creed Valhalla for its recent reimagining.) And it also has African roots . But its latest iteration is thought to have emerged in the hip-hop scene in New York in the 1980s. The 1981 Busy Bee versus Kool Moe Dee battle at the Harlem World club in New York is an important part of hip-hop lore.

It was arguably the 2002 film 8 Mile , however, that starred real battle rap legend, Eminem, that made the art form well known beyond hardcore rap aficionados. Today it is a pop culture streaming event , with millions of followers and official leagues.

The object of a battle rap is to display flow, braggadocio and quick wit. Humour is often a plus, but lyrically dexterous, rhythmic, creative “burns” are the name of the game.

Both art forms encourage us, the listeners, to react, reflect and ultimately select with which speaker to side. We are thrust into the centre of the action without much of a narrator to explain things.

Both The Iliad and rap battles are part of the oral poetic tradition, since we think The Iliad was orally recited for generations before it was put down in writing. They are therefore both addressed to a live audience.

The Iliad is a story of war between Greeks and Trojans, but also of “beefs”. Menelaus versus Paris over the hand of Helen. Achilles versus Agamemnon, the king of the Greeks who wrongs him by expropriating one of his slaves. And Achilles versus Hector, the Trojan prince who kills Patroclus, Achilles’s closest friend.

The high moment of the poem is arguably the encounter between Achilles and Hector. Before they battle to the death, Hector offers Achilles a deal: whoever wins won’t disrespect the other’s body.

In response, Achilles belows: “Curse you, Hector, and don’t talk of oaths to me. Lions and men make no compacts, nor are wolves and lambs in sympathy: they are opposed, to the end. You and I are beyond friendship: nor will there be peace until one or the other dies.”

Achilles is calling out Hector’s attempt at showing nobility of character, because Hector tries to separate the duty to wage conflict from rage and disrespect of his enemy. Achilles flatly rejects the proposal. For him, the only reason to fight is to satiate his grief-induced rage and so no respect can be given even after death.

Ultimately, Achilles kills Hector and desecrates his body, but Hector was clearly the better man. Two worldviews collide. Which one should we side with?

In a battle rap, the question of how we judge which MC to be victorious is always at stake. Do we side with the MC who best “rocks the mic” by pleasing the audience, or the one who more lyrically and intelligently cuts the opponent to the bone?

Here are five more themes shared by The Iliad and battle rap.

Battle rap has made gifted MCs into street rap legends. Long before record deals were the prize, MCs battled for respect and street fame.

This pursuit of legendary status also lies at the very heart of The Iliad , as Achilles is warned by his mother, the goddess Thetis, that he will die if he fights in the Trojan war, but in return his “glory never dies”.

Battle rappers and the warriors in The Iliad act in their own name but they also represent wider groups heralding from different places. They all, in some way, carry responsibility for and aim to bring reflected fame to their respective communities.

Most battle raps take the form of a take down of the opponent, but the real object is to demonstrate verbal prowess . Simply entertaining will not cut it. “You now have to make sense of what you say, in order for us to give you the power,” summarises hip-hop legend KRS-One .

The Iliad opens with a muse telling the audience that the epic will recount the “wrath of Achilles”, but in fact we find skilful interventions in speech that make us wonder whether the reasons for conflict can ever justify the grief it causes.

What is truly worth living and dying for are central themes in The Iliad , as in battle rap. There we find talk of loyalty, honour, respect, courage, friendship and fame.

The overt answers given can be taken as embraces of a certain kind of toxic masculinity where dominance, rage, cunning and violence are celebrated, but maybe these answers subtly point to their ultimate hollowness .

Lurking behind the repeated injunction to “be the best”, battle rap and Homer’s epic invite the question of what is truly worth admiring: skill, dominance, wealth, integrity, courage, beauty, truth, justice, love or glory? They provide no singular answer.

Instead, we are left to sit within what West calls the “funk of life” – the mess of it all. From there, we can see that the stories we tell ourselves have the power to shape and define our actions and our very lives.

So the main question becomes: at a time when simplistic stories of violence and domination are presented to us as easy answers to complex social realities, can we create new and richer stories of our own?

Joshua Forstenzer, Senior Lecturer in Philosophy and Co-Director of the Centre for Engaged Philosophy, University of Sheffield.

This article first appeared on The Conversation .

The most useful way to assess BT Group is to move past short-term price noise and examine whether its operating model is becoming more dependable. Its core exposure to fixed-line, mobile and broadband communications gives the story an identifiable commercial engine, but a credible investment case also requires financial follow-through. The key is not whether management can describe an opportunity; it is whether customer behaviour, operational choices and capital allocation produce results that can be sustained through less supportive conditions.

The investment case starts with operating evidence

BT Group operates through fixed-line, mobile and broadband communications. That description matters because it identifies where revenue quality begins, yet it does not by itself establish an attractive investment. Investors should look for demand that is repeatable, supported by a defensible customer proposition and converted without excessive spending. Reported growth deserves more confidence when it is accompanied by stable retention, sensible pricing and evidence that the company can serve additional customers without allowing complexity to absorb the benefits of scale.

Cash conversion separates momentum from durable progress

Cash provides a useful cross-check because accounting progress and economic progress do not always arrive together. Working-capital movements, exceptional costs and capitalised investment can temporarily flatter or depress conversion, so one reporting period rarely settles the argument. A better approach is to examine the direction across several updates and ask whether management explanations reconcile with the balance sheet. Consistent conversion would give BT Group more flexibility to fund development, manage shocks and avoid relying on expensive external capital.

Capital allocation should then be judged against the companys stage of development. Reinvestment may offer the best return when customer demand is proven and internal projects have credible paybacks. Acquisitions can accelerate capability, although they add integration and valuation risk. Dividends or buybacks may be appropriate when surplus capital is genuinely available. The important point is coherence: each decision should reinforce the strategy while maintaining enough financial headroom for the less predictable elements of fibre investment, competition and pension obligations.

Valuation needs a realistic range of outcomes

The sector backdrop can influence both results and investor patience. Conditions affecting fibre investment, competition and pension obligations may change faster than the company can adjust its cost base or investment programme. That creates operating leverage in both directions. Investors should therefore distinguish a temporary external headwind from deterioration in competitive position. If peers face similar pressure while BT Group protects customers, pricing or delivery standards, the relative evidence may remain constructive even before reported growth fully recovers.

Valuation brings those observations together. A low multiple is not automatically a bargain if earnings are vulnerable, just as a demanding multiple can be justified only by unusually reliable growth and returns. Scenario analysis is more useful than a single precise target. A cautious case can reflect weaker demand and slower margin progress; a central case can assume competent execution; and an optimistic case should require specific proof. This framework makes clear which assumptions carry the greatest weight and where disappointment could cause the sharpest reassessment.

Key milestones can reshape market expectations

The principal challenge is fibre investment, competition and pension obligations. Management cannot remove every external variable, but it can show preparedness through transparent targets, conservative financing and timely operational decisions. Warning signs would include repeated changes to definitions, widening gaps between adjusted profit and cash, or investment that rises without a visible commercial return. More reassuring evidence would include stable unit economics, realistic guidance and an ability to explain setbacks without weakening the long-term logic of the strategy.

evidence.title: Virgin Media O2 extends small cells rollout to Tonbridge, Kent
evidence.text:
Virgin Media O2 extends small cells rollout to Tonbridge, Kent

Five small cells have gone live in Tonbridge

Virgin Media O2 has expanded its small cells rollout in the UK to Tonbridge, Kent.

The latest rollout has been carried out with infrastructure-as-a-service provider Freshwave, which also helped out the telco deploy small cells in Canterbury, Kent, earlier this month.

In total, five small cells have been switched on in Tonbridge to provide additional 4G and 5G capacity in some of Tonbridge's busiest areas.

Small cells are designed to enhance mobile capacity and reduce network congestion in densely populated areas.

They are typically fixed to existing street furniture, such as lamp posts, and are seen as a simpler alternative to bulkier telecom infrastructure, which might look out of place or draw criticism from residents. These small cells are designed to blend in with the existing infrastructure discreetly.

Virgin Media O2's deployment of small cells is part of an effort by O2, Freshwave, Kent County Council and local MP Tom Tugendhat to bolster mobile infrastructure in the town.

Tom Tugendhat MP, member of Parliament for Tonbridge, Edenbridge, and North Downs Villages, said: “We are all too familiar with how frustrating not being able to access phone signal and internet can be, and the impact an inefficient and unreliable signal has in Tonbridge town center. People expect their mobile connection to work wherever they are.

“I’m delighted this is changing, starting with the new small cells now live in Tonbridge. This investment will help improve connectivity across our town center and demonstrates what can be achieved when local partners work together to deliver the infrastructure communities need."

"These new small cells will provide additional capacity in some of Tonbridge's busiest locations, helping residents, businesses and visitors stay connected. We are grateful for the support of Tom Tugendhat MP and our local partners in helping make this deployment possible," added Professor Rob Joyce, director of mobile access engineering, O2.

In total, Freshwave has signed more than 40 open access agreements with local authorities across the UK and has deployed more than 800 small cells on behalf of the MNOs.

The company has partnered with Virgin Media O2 on several occasions, supporting small cell deployments for the telco in Guildford , Cornwall , and in Manchester .

Rachel Swift, Virgin Media O2’s executive director of brand and marketing, is set to leave the business following the introduction of a new leadership structure.

The shake-up comes after the arrival of consumer CEO Lyssa McGowan, who joined the business in July to lead the newly-merged commercial and operations functions.

Since then, the company says she has been “working at pace” to reorganise the leadership team to ensure there is “greater prioritisation, simplification, alignment and focus on the areas that will make the biggest difference” to customers across its three brands – Virgin Media, O2 and Giffgaff.

McGowan will now oversee marketing across the business as part of her role, bringing with her a fresh look at the direction and role of the Virgin Media O2 brands.

As part of these changes, chief operations officer Rob Orr and chief commercial officer Christian Hindennach are also leaving the business.

Swift joined Virgin Media O2 in 2024 after four years at Tesco Mobile. Part of her task was to “reset” the O2 brand , which led to the introduction of the ‘Essential For Living’ platform that repositioned the brand as an enabler of “life’s greatest moments”.

A Virgin Media O2 spokesperson says: “Throughout her time at Virgin Media O2, Rachel has led brand and advertising with heart and ingenuity, delivering stand out campaigns and helping to shape the Virgin Media and O2 brands for their next chapter. We thank her for her contribution and leadership, and wish her every success for the future.”

O2’s marketing boss on returning to its founding ethos to ‘reset’ the brand

McGowan, who reports to CEO Lutz Schüler, spent more than a decade at Sky, culminating in her role as chief consumer officer. Most recently, she was CEO of Pets at Home.

At the time of her appointment, Schüler said it had always been the company’s ambition to bring together the commercial and operations teams.

“This is a highly competitive and rapidly evolving market, so just doing what we’ve always done isn’t the answer – we need to be simpler, faster and focused,” he added.

“These changes will do that with Lyssa being exactly the right person to lead our new consumer unit. Lyssa has a wealth of experience, and I have full confidence that she will bring fresh thinking and healthy challenge to the executive team.”

Having joined Virgin Media O2 six months ago, tasked with overhauling O2’s brand strategy, Rachel Swift says she wants to re-establish its reason for being but won’t “change things for change’s sake”.

The retailer increased digital marketing spend by 56% during the first half, as international growth accelerates.

Virgin Media O2 owners target cost cuts amid debt pressure

Pressure is building on Virgin Media O2 as bond investors scrutinize the UK telecoms group's ability to manage its heavy debt burden in a tougher broadband market. Its shareholders, Telefónica and Liberty Global, are targeting about £600 million in savings through potential job cuts and lower operating and capital spending.

Proposed savings plan and bond market strain

Investor anxiety intensifies after a summer sell-off in Virgin Media O2 bonds, driven by concerns over whether the company can continue servicing its £22 billion debt pile. The pressure is particularly visible in its roughly £1.1 billion of senior unsecured debt, with one $925 million bond falling to 61 cents on the dollar on Thursday from about 78 cents at the start of July.

Some of the group's senior secured bonds, viewed as safer by investors, have also dropped below 80 cents on the dollar in recent months after trading at 92 cents at the beginning of the year. The decline has made Virgin Media O2 a focal point for investors in Europe's junk debt market. Competition weighs on customer base Virgin Media O2 is facing intensifying pressure from a growing number of smaller fibre network operators, known as altnets, that have raised £31 billion to attract customers from Virgin Media O2 and BT-owned Openreach with cheaper fibre broadband offers.

The company sheds 33,500 broadband customers in the first half of 2026, adding to the 138,400 it lost last year. Virgin Media O2 has 5.42 million broadband customers at the end of June, underscoring the commercial strain behind its owners' push for savings.

The Financial Times reported in July that the company's two owners were also weighing options to reduce debt, including a possible cut to its £200 million dividend. Telefónica and Virgin Media O2 decline to comment, while Liberty Global does not respond to requests for comment.

evidence.title: Virgin Media O2 owners consider £600m cost cuts - report
evidence.text:
Virgin Media O2 owners consider £600m cost cuts - report

Could include layoffs at the telco in effort to service debt pile

Virgin Media O2's owners are looking to drive cost cuts of £600 million ($810m) at the UK telco.

As reported by the Financial Times , the company's main shareholders, Liberty Global and Telefónica, are pushing to make the cuts in an effort to ease investor concerns about the company's debt pile.

The FT, which cites sources familiar with the matter, reports that the cost cuts could come through a mixture of job cuts and reductions in operating and capital expenditure.

It comes after Virgin Media O2 was hit by a sell-off in its bonds over the summer, with the sell-off putting pressure on the company's £1.1 billion ($1.49bn) of senior unsecured debt, pushing the price of a $925 million bond down to 61 cents on the dollar on Thursday. At the start of July, it was trading at about 78 cents.

Investors in the telco have become concerned about Virgin Media O2's ability to service its £22bn ($29.7bn) debt.

A previous FT report over the summer noted that Virgin Media O2's owners have mulled other options to reduce the debt, which has included plans to cut its £200m ($270m).

The company has been busy building out its mobile and full fiber networks in recent years, with the latter market being particularly competitive against Openreach and a host of alternative network providers (altnets).

The telco has previously shed jobs in the years after its merger was completed, with around 2,000 jobs cut in 2023 , while earlier this year it was reported that up to 300 jobs in the UK were being lost.

evidence.text:
Nokia wins new 5G RAN deal with Virgin Media O2 to accelerate its Mobile Transformation Plan

Nokia wins new 5G RAN deal with Virgin Media O2 to accelerate its Mobile Transformation Plan

Deployment of Nokia's latest AirScale RAN portfolio, including Massive MIMO radios, future‑proof baseband, and energy‑efficient next‑generation radio platforms, will help Virgin Media O2 to accelerate its Mobile Transformation Plan

Significant performance uplift for Virgin Media O2's 5G network, with improvements in capacity, coverage, spectral efficiency, and customer-experienced speeds.

Expansion of long‑term strategic collaboration, including joint innovation programs and pilots focused on network automation, AI‑driven intelligence, and 5G‑Advanced evolution

Espoo, Finland – Nokia announced that it has been selected by Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) for a major new multi‑year 5G Radio Access Network (RAN) deployment and modernization program across the UK. The agreement builds on more than two decades of strategic collaboration between the companies. It marks a significant milestone as Virgin Media O2 continues its mission to deliver the country's most reliable and high‑performance 5G network with its Mobile Transformation Plan.

Under the new deal, Nokia will supply its latest-generation AirScale RAN portfolio, including ultra-capacity modular baseband and energy-efficient, future-proofed Massive MIMO radios. Leveraging Nokia's comprehensive technology roadmap, Virgin Media O2 will benefit from improved spectral efficiency, coverage, capacity, and throughput, ensuring strong 5G performance today while laying the foundation for 5G‑Advanced capabilities.

Transforming the UK 5G experience The deployment will enable Virgin Media O2 to improve network quality and accelerate modernization through optimized spectrum utilization and enhanced energy-saving software features. Nokia's latest GigaSite architecture, Dual‑Band Massive MIMO, and AI‑enabled baseband platforms will support seamless scalability and operational efficiency throughout the rollout. The technology uplift is expected to deliver a more reliable connectivity for Virgin Media O2 customers across the country.

As part of the new engagement, Nokia and Virgin Media O2 will expand their collaboration on joint innovation programs, including pilots and proofs of concept that explore advanced RAN intelligence, automation, and energy-efficient architectures aligned with Virgin Media O2's Mobile Transformation Plan. This new contract extends Nokia's role as one of Virgin Media O2's primary RAN partners, following the previously announced agreement to continue 5G rollout and modernization. "We are delighted to deepen our longstanding partnership with Virgin Media O2 through this important new 5G RAN deal. Our AirScale portfolio is designed to deliver the performance, efficiency, and flexibility required for the UK's future connectivity needs. We look forward to supporting Virgin Media O2 in building one of the most advanced and reliable 5G Advanced networks in the country," said Mark Atkinson, Head of RAN at Nokia.

"As we continue to evolve and enhance our award‑winning mobile network with our Mobile Transformation Plan, Nokia remains a key strategic partner in helping us deliver reliable connectivity to our customers. This new agreement allows us to accelerate our 5G rollout, improve performance, and ensure we meet growing demand for high‑quality mobile services both today and in the future," said Jeanie York, Chief Technology Officer, Virgin Media O2. evidence.title: Orange haalt beste Belgische 5G-dekking, Proximus blijft sterk in 4G
evidence.text:
Itdaily - Orange haalt beste Belgische 5G-dekking, Proximus blijft sterk in 4G

Orange behaalt volgens een nieuw nPerf-barometeronderzoek de hoogste nationale score voor 5G-dekking in België, terwijl Proximus de leiding behoudt op 4G. Brussel biedt de beste 5G-dekking, Wallonië blijft achter.

De nieuwste cijfers van nPerf geven een actueel beeld van de 4G- en 5G-dekking in België. Het gaat om een vergelijking tussen Orange, Proximus en Telenet op nationaal en regionaal niveau. Volgens nPerf bevestigt België een stevig tempo in de uitrol van 5G . “België bevestigt een duurzame dynamiek van 5G-uitrol, gedreven door actieve concurrentie tussen operators die direct de kwaliteit van de verbindingen van gebruikers ten goede komt,” zegt Sébastien de Rosbo, CEO van nPerf. De metingen zijn gebaseerd op tests die gebruikers uitvoeren via de Android-app van nPerf.

Orange staat nationaal op de eerste plaats voor 5G-dekking met een nPerf-index van 84,32 procent. Daarmee haalt de operator de beste score op dit moment voor 5G in België. Het verschil met de dichtste achtervolger blijft beperkt, wat wijst op een relatief gelijk speelveld voor gebruikers.

Proximus volgt immers op korte afstand met een 5G-dekkingsindex van 80,79 procent. Volgens nPerf bedraagt de kloof tussen beide spelers slechts 3,5 punten. Die beperkte marge toont dat geen enkele operator een groot monopolie heeft op 5G-bereik.

nPerf benadrukt dat deze concurrentie rechtstreeks ten goede komt aan de kwaliteit van de verbinding voor eindgebruikers. Hoe dichter de scores bij elkaar liggen, hoe meer druk er is om de dekking verder te verfijnen en uit te breiden. De vergelijking in 5G beperkt zich daardoor tot Orange en Proximus, aangezien er geen beschikbare data zijn voor de 5G-dekking van Telenet, schrijft nPerf.

Orange (en VOO) sleepte recent nog vier van de vijf nationale awards binnen in het nieuwste Fixed Broadband Experience-rapport van Opensignal , dat de connectiviteitservaring van consumenten onderzoekt. Proximus ging aan de haal met de enige award die Orange niet won: uploadsnelheid.

Voor 4G verschuift het beeld. Proximus voert het nationale 4G-klassement aan met een nPerf-index van 97,99 procent. Daarmee haalt de operator de hoogste dekkingsscore in dit segment. Orange volgt op de tweede plaats met een index van 97,94 procent, amper lager dan Proximus.

Telenet neemt de derde plaats in met een 4G-dekkingsindex van 97,74 procent. Het verschil met de twee concurrenten blijft ook hier beperkt. Dat toont aan dat 4G intussen een zeer hoge landelijke dekking heeft bij alle drie de spelers, met slechts fracties verschil in de nPerf-indicator.

Naast de nationale rangschikking bekijkt nPerf ook de situatie per regio. Brussel noteert de beste 5G-dekking met een score van 95,5 procent. De hoofdstad is daarmee de regio waar gebruikers vandaag het meest kans hebben op een 5G-signaal.

Infrabel investeert meer dan vier miljoen euro in de modernisering van zijn spoo…

Wallonië komt uit als regio met de laagste 5G-dekking, met 80,2 procent. Dat wijst op een duidelijk verschil tussen de gewesten, ondanks het algemene beeld van vooruitgang in de uitrol. Vlaanderen zit daar tussenin, al zijn daar geen exacte cijfers van nPerf rond bekend.

Volgens Gartner overweegt de helft van enterpriseklanten te vertrekken uit VMware tegen 2029. Alternatieven staa…

evidence.title: Orange en tête de la couverture 5G en Belgique, Proximus reste solide en 4G
evidence.text:
Itdaily - Orange en tête de la couverture 5G en Belgique, Proximus reste solide en 4G

Selon un nouveau baromètre nPerf, Orange obtient le meilleur score national pour la couverture 5G en Belgique, tandis que Proximus conserve la tête sur la 4G. Bruxelles offre la meilleure couverture 5G, la Wallonie reste à la traîne.

Les derniers chiffres de nPerf dressent un état des lieux de la couverture 4G et 5G en Belgique. Il s’agit d’une comparaison entre Orange, Proximus et Telenet aux niveaux national et régional. Selon nPerf, la Belgique confirme un rythme soutenu dans le déploiement de la 5G . « La Belgique confirme une dynamique durable de déploiement de la 5G, portée par une concurrence active entre opérateurs qui profite directement à la qualité des connexions des utilisateurs », déclare Sébastien de Rosbo, PDG de nPerf. Les mesures sont basées sur des tests effectués par les utilisateurs via l’application Android de nPerf.

Orange occupe la première place nationale pour la couverture 5G avec un indice nPerf de 84,32 %. L’opérateur obtient ainsi le meilleur score actuel pour la 5G en Belgique. L’écart avec le poursuivant le plus proche reste limité, ce qui indique un terrain de jeu relativement équilibré pour les utilisateurs.

Proximus suit en effet de près avec un indice de couverture 5G de 80,79 %. Selon nPerf, l’écart entre les deux acteurs n’est que de 3,5 points. Cette marge étroite montre qu’aucun opérateur ne détient de monopole majeur sur la portée 5G.

nPerf souligne que cette concurrence profite directement à la qualité de la connexion pour les utilisateurs finaux. Plus les scores sont serrés, plus la pression est forte pour affiner et étendre la couverture. La comparaison en 5G se limite donc à Orange et Proximus, car aucune donnée n’est disponible pour la couverture 5G de Telenet, écrit nPerf.

Orange (et VOO) a récemment remporté quatre des cinq prix nationaux dans le dernier rapport Fixed Broadband Experience d’Opensignal , qui examine l’expérience de connectivité des consommateurs. Proximus a décroché le seul prix qu’Orange n’a pas remporté : la vitesse de téléchargement en amont.

Pour la 4G, le tableau change. Proximus arrive en tête du classement national 4G avec un indice nPerf de 97,99 %. L’opérateur obtient ainsi le score de couverture le plus élevé dans ce segment. Orange suit à la deuxième place avec un indice de 97,94 %, à peine inférieur à celui de Proximus.

Telenet occupe la troisième place avec un indice de couverture 4G de 97,74 %. Ici aussi, l’écart avec les deux concurrents reste limité. Cela montre que la 4G bénéficie désormais d’une couverture nationale très élevée chez les trois acteurs, avec seulement des fractions de différence dans l’indicateur nPerf.

Outre le classement national, nPerf examine également la situation par région. Bruxelles enregistre la meilleure couverture 5G avec un score de 95,5 %. La capitale est ainsi la région où les utilisateurs ont aujourd’hui le plus de chances de capter un signal 5G.

Infrabel investit plus de quatre millions d’euros dans la modernisation de sa co…

La Wallonie apparaît comme la région ayant la couverture 5G la plus faible, avec 80,2 %. Cela indique une différence marquée entre les régions, malgré le tableau général de progression du déploiement. La Flandre se situe entre les deux, bien qu’aucun chiffre exact de nPerf ne soit connu à ce sujet.

evidence.title: Ekinops Announces Framework Agreement with Proximus to deploy a nationwide high-speed optical network across Belgium
evidence.text:
Ekinops Announces Framework Agreement with Proximus to deploy a nationwide high-speed optical network across Belgium

PARIS, July 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EKINOPS ( Euronext Paris – FR0011466069 – EKI), a leading provider of optical networking, connectivity and SASE cybersecurity solutions for telecommunications operators and enterprises, today announces the signing of a framework agreement with Proximus, the leading Belgian Tier-1 telecom operator, awarding Ekinops a 10-year supplier contract.

This agreement marks the final step following the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) announced in March. This major strategic project, named NEURON, which stands for Next generation Enhanced Uniform Reliable Optical Network, covers Ekinops' supply of WDM-based optical network equipment and services to deploy a nationwide high-speed optical network across Belgium comprising of over 600 sites.

Proximus has chosen the Ekinops WDM platform for its ability to optimize any types of traffic rate from ultra-low to very high client speeds in a chassis already compatible for 1.6T (terabits per second) rate. Under the long-term agreement containing commitments for future evolutions, Ekinops will provide telecom infrastructure systems supporting 800 Gbit/s (gigabits per second) optical capacity, as well as a broad range of ROADMs (reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers) for Proximus' backbone and metro networks. Ekinops will also provide its network management solution, Celestis NMS, together with associated software and professional services, to support Proximus in building its next-generation, high-performance optical network.

" We have been impressed by the Ekinops' labs and by the quality of their answers to our RFP, as well as the technical expertise demonstrated throughout the selection process ," says Geert Standaert, Network Lead and CTO of Proximus. " Beyond the simplicity and efficiency of the proposed architecture, this collaboration builds on a long-standing partnership with a trusted and reliable partner. Ekinops' expertise will play a key role in supporting our network evolution and delivering on our long-term ambitions. "

" This agreement builds on Ekinops strengths: delivering trusted, flexible, high-capacity optical networking solutions," says Lionel Chmilewsky, CEO of Ekinops. "It highlights how our continued innovation—and the dedication and expertise of our teams serving customers worldwide—are delivering tangible results. We are extremely honored by Proximus' trust in our European technologies and our people. We are fully committed to the success of NEURON and look forward to what we will accomplish together. "

The project plan will include lab and field trials, starting now with first network deployment to start in second half of 2026.

evidence.title: Telenet Business Reclaims Architectural Freedom With Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization
evidence.text:
Telenet Business Reclaims Architectural Freedom With Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization

Belgian service provider collapses infrastructure silos by unifying virtual machines and containers on Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization to accelerate sovereign cloud services

ATLANTA – RED HAT SUMMIT, May 11, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Red Hat , the world's leading provider of open source solutions, today announced that Telenet Business has selected Red Hat OpenShift as the foundation for its modernized private cloud infrastructure. Using Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization , a native feature in Red Hat OpenShift, Telenet Business established a unified and locally-controlled foundation for virtual machines and containers to drive faster innovation for its growing customer base.

From proprietary constraints to a future-ready private cloud

Telenet Business, a managed service provider within the Telenet group (part of Liberty Global), serves more than 10,000 business customers across Belgium. To meet rising demand for localized compute, the provider prioritizes a highly responsive and scalable infrastructure. Market shifts within its legacy virtualization stack led Telenet to adopt open technologies that provide long-term stability and operational control.

By selecting Red Hat OpenShift as its standards-based, open platform, Telenet Business is consolidating virtual machines (VMs) and container workloads. This unified foundation helped Telenet to remove the friction of separate infrastructure stacks and improve operational control without limiting innovation or impacting the customer experience.

One platform, any workload, any infrastructure

By running Red Hat OpenShift on bare metal across two regional datacenters, Telenet Business has established a sovereign private cloud environment. VMs and containerized applications coexist on the same hardware and management layer, providing a consistent operational model that extends to overseeing predictive and generative AI models at scale.

To manage this environment, Telenet Business uses Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes to provide a single management view across both datacenter clusters. This centralized oversight allows the system to automatically spin up VMs at the alternate location if one site becomes unavailable, supporting continuous service availability for Telenet's customers.

This open hybrid cloud approach provides:

Rapid migration with minimal disruption: Using the Red Hat migration toolkit for virtualization , Telenet Business has already migrated close to 200 VMs out of a scope of nearly 1,000. The toolkit automates complex transition tasks and supports 50GB VM transitions in just a few minutes, with near-zero service downtime.

Unified management of VMs and containers: Telenet Business is removing the complexity of separate infrastructure stacks, with engineers managing VMs, containers and the underlying physical hardware through a single interface. This integration helps teams move applications to container deployments faster for increased portability and more efficient operations.

Controllable cloud and sovereign design: All workloads remain hosted within Telenet Business's Belgian datacenters to support strict data residency requirements for government and enterprise clients. Data is replicated four times across two sites to support high availability without reliance on extraterritorial public cloud providers.

Scalable automation: Telenet Business uses Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform to automate VM provisioning and templating. This makes the solution accessible to teams across the company and reduces manual intervention.

Open source flexibility: Red Hat's open source development model was a strategic decision for Telenet to regain architectural freedom and choice from its previous proprietary stack.

Stef Schampaert, Country Manager, Belgium and Luxembourg, Red Hat

"European service providers require the control and transparency of digital sovereignty to remain competitive. By migrating to Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization, Telenet Business can break free from legacy constraints and build modernized platforms that grow with its customers. This transition gives Telenet Business engineering teams the flexibility to support faster business innovation while keeping full control over data and systems."

Dave Van Ingelghem, Technical Product Manager, Datacenter, Telenet Business

"Telenet Business requires a platform that helps strengthen the protection of our data without sacrificing the ability to modernize. Red Hat OpenShift has been a positive step toward a future-ready environment by allowing us to consolidate our workloads onto a single platform and automate recovery across sites. With Red Hat, we have the flexibility to choose our own future as we evolve to serve customers."
