evidence.title: High Prices And Low Sales Could Be Killing Porsche
evidence.text:
Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update

Once the VW Group's profit leader, Porsche has seemingly overnight become its albatross instead. The brand's prices may have soared higher than its customers can reach, but artificial scarcity and expensive options aren't alone in setting Porsche's course.

Some very big and very poorly timed investments are also weighing on the CEO's "value over volume" strategy.

From Massive Moneymaker To Barely Break-Even

For years, Porsche has been a huge source of cash for the VW Group. It had some of the highest margins in the business and generated consistent, reliable profits. Suddenly, it all dried up. Porsche profits fell to effectively break-even and VW just wrote down $6.9 billion on its stake in Porsche... after a $3.3 billion write-down a year ago.

A look at the sales charts show why the profits have disappeared. In the first half of this year, Porsche sold 122,306 cars , down 16% from the first half of 2025. Sales in China, which has been a growing car market, were down 32%.

That decline is against figures that were already down. In 2025, Porsche full-year sales fell 10% from the year before, with a 26% drop in China. 2024 was a 3% drop versus 2023.

Part of the issue is its lineup. Porsche's transition to electric has stalled. Not only has it not launched the replacement for the 718 that has been in development for many years, it doesn't look like one is coming anytime soon.

The Macan, Porsche's bestseller, is also in trouble. Porsche is on track to sell around 30,000 Macan EVs this year, that's fewer than it sold EVs in 2025. The gas Macan made up another 40,000 sales last year, but it went out of production in July. Porsche's electric Taycan, which is on sale, isn't blistering the charts either. Porsche sold 41,000 of those in 2021, but it's not going to reach even half that number this year.

It could be the big expenses that aren't helping. Last year, Porsche listed what it called "extraordinary expenses" of $4.5 billion. Around $1 billion of that was US tariffs , but $2.7 billion was "realignment of the product strategy and the rescaling of the company." The beginnings of the costs of designing both a gas and electric lineup.

Subtract those expenses and suddenly Porsche's profits are back over 10%. Even with tariffs and this year's conflicts in the Middle East, Porsche expects to improve to a 5.5-7.5% margin.

If the company's sales keep falling, it might be impossible to hit the profit margins it wants. Lower sales lead directly to higher costs per vehicle, but if they drop far enough, it doesn't matter what the profit per car is. The total won't pay for the next generation . And Porsche has definitely been raising prices to maximize that per-vehicle profit. We can't be sure if customers are feeling that pinch, but comment threads definitely claim they are.

How dramatic are we talking? Ten years ago, a basic Porsche Cayenne started from around $58,000. Five years ago, that was $67,500. Today it is $90,000 per CarBuzz data. A Cayenne Turbo has jumped from $115,000 to $165,000. Cayenne is a volume seller for Porsche, but inflation is certainly taking a toll.

The Porsche 911 is a niche vehicle, but it's the company's most iconic offering that has millions of fans around the world. The everyday supercar is also leaping and bounding to new highs, and it's not inflation's fault. In 2016, the base price was $84,000, and it hit $99,000 in 2021. Today, the base Carrera will set you back $135,500. And by the time you start plugging in Porsche's notoriously pricey options, you can spec a Carrera upwards of $200,000. A Carrera.

It's at the high end where the prices have truly gone wild, though. Ten years ago, a 911 GT3 was $130,000. In 2022, it started at $161,000. But today, the starting price is around $236,000. That's an increase of over $70,000 in just four years. Are those worse than inflation? If we take the entry-level Cayenne from 2016 and adjust its price for inflation, we get $82,000 – comfortably below today's $90,000 price. The 911 GT3, however, would be $189,000 adjusted for inflation. That amounts to a $47,000 increase.

A 911 GT3 buyer might not care, but for a Cayenne buyer, that can be a big jump. And buyers who were shopping for a $70,000 Boxster are probably not going to stretch to six figures for that 911.

Porsche has gotten the short end of the stick plenty of times over the years, including the near-disaster of 2008 when it tried to take over Volkswagen and ended up becoming owned instead.

Each time, Porsche has recovered and it probably will again. But this time, it can't launch a new model hoping for Cayenne-like success to save it. Or can it?

evidence.title: Porsche electric Boxster prototype spotted at Singapore’s IMM mall
evidence.text:
Porsche electric Boxster prototype spotted at Singapore’s IMM mall

Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Similar prototype cars have been spotted in Europe and the United States.

PHOTO: KENNETH TAN/PORSCHE CAYMAN S 987.2 FACEBOOK GROUP

SINGAPORE - A left-hand-drive electric sports car with German registration plates has been spotted in Singapore.

Photos of the car plugged into an electric vehicle (EV) charger at the IMM mall in Jurong East began circulating on various social media sites on Sept 23.

There are no brand logos on the car, but stickers on the body read “Porsche Research & Development”.

In response to The Straits Times, a Porsche Asia Pacific spokesman confirmed that the vehicle is a prototype of its upcoming electric Boxster 718 sports car being tested in Singapore.

Porsche’s regional office received the car a week ago, and it is due to leave Singapore on Sept 25, according to the spokesman.

Similar test cars have been spotted in California as well as in Europe in recent months.

Mahaendra Gofar, an automotive industry insider who has worked at various car companies in Germany and China, said that although it is common for carmakers to test their pre-production cars oversea s, S ingapore is not a typical testing region.

Gofar said this car is likely being used to test internal components like the battery pack and motor to understand how they perform in the tropical climate. It may also be used to train Porsche Asia Pacific staff.

Subject to approval by the Land Transport Authority, foreign-registered left-hand-drive cars can be driven in Singapore for a limited time period.

The electric sports car was previously scheduled to be launched in 2025 but this was delayed. In August, American automotive news site Road & Track said that Porsche’s chief executive Michael Lieters confirmed that the electric car in convertible Boxster and hardtop Cayman forms remain in development although no launch dates were given.

evidence.title: Rendering: Porsche Octan Comes Out From Behind the CGI Curtain Looking Like a Worthy ICE Macan Heir
evidence.text:
Rendering: Porsche Octan Comes Out From Behind the CGI Curtain Looking Like a Worthy ICE Macan Heir

The Volkswagen Group faces major uncertainties , despite being the second largest automaker in the world, and it’s all due to the constraints plaguing the automotive industry combined with the slowdown in China plus the issues with Porsche’s almost disastrous switch to an EV-focused strategy.

While the Taycan was never the high-profit driver the company hoped for, Porsche implemented an audacious plan a few years ago that involved switching all of its major model series bar the iconic 911 to an EV lifestyle. So far, the company has implemented the switch for the Macan crossover SUV and the Cayenne Electric, and the 718 EV is also incoming.

However, the company was caught with its proverbial pants around the ankle by the sudden anti-EV movement in America and by the slowdown across China, revealing that it was a mistake to kill the ICE-powered Macan in the first place. Now, they decided not to axe the Cayenne and sell it alongside the Cayenne Electric while the 718 series is being reworked to allow both EV and ICE powertrains to live happily together.

Unfortunately, the Macan bit the dust in its ICE -powered form after it was offered for about two years alongside the new second-generation Macan EV . As such, Porsche had to go back to the drawing board and come up with a replacement solution – just recently we saw an Audi Q5 mule posing as an innocent, but our spy photographer partners knew better, signaling that the prototype is most likely a mule for the upcoming Project Octan , the ICE-powered Macan’s successor.

Just like the second-gen Porsche Macan EV shares its PPE (Premium Platform Electric) architecture with the Cayenne Electric but also the Audi Q6 and A6 e-tron, the new Porsche Octan (name not confirmed) will undoubtedly adhere to the PPC (Premium Platform Combustion) used by the third-generation Audi Q5 and Q5 Sportback. Naturally, the Porsche will be more in line with the SQ5 and the upcoming RS Q5 in terms of powertrains, most likely.

It could also get a short development cycle as revealed by the new mules, and Porsche might strive to push for a 2028 model year release window to try and gain back all the lost Porsche Macan ICE customers. As such, it’s no wonder that the rumor mill is paying special attention to the upcoming Porsche Octan, and the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators are also thinking about it when they’re not dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI.

For example, Andrei Avarvarii, the virtual artist behind Avarvarii Automotive Artworks (also known as ' avarvarii ' on social media), has taken a thorough, in-depth CGI look at Porsche's upcoming plans and cooked up an unofficial, hypothetical Octan design project for us to see.

The new Porsche, in his vision, will rely on the new design language showcased by the Porsche Macan and Cayenne EVs but adapted to a coupe- SUV body style like the Audi Q5 Sportback and featuring various ICE-related styling modifications: a gilded air intake integrated into the bumper, classic LED headlights rather than split ones, and quad exhaust tips integrated into the bumper-diffuser assembly. evidence.title: Porsche remains world’s most valuable luxury brand despite $6bn value drop
evidence.text:
Porsche remains world’s most valuable luxury brand despite $6bn value drop

Ferrari climbs to seventh in Brand Finance survey as first electric vehicle debuts

Porsche has yet again ranked number one among the top global luxury brands in the 2026 Luxury & Premium 50 report by Brand Finance .

The German sports car brand was number one among all global luxury brands across all sectors, beating second-placed Chanel and third-placed Louis Vuitton.

Apparel remains the largest luxury and premium segment, with a total of 33 brands in the top 50, said the valuation consultancy.

Brand Finance calculates the values of brands in its rankings using the Royalty Relief approach that involves estimating the likely future revenues that are attributable to a brand by calculating a royalty rate that would be charged for its use, understood as a net economic benefit that a brand owner would achieve by licensing the brand in the open market.

The top four global brands, including the German sports car brand, maintained their positions in the survey two years in a row (2024-2026), but Porsche lost the most ground in terms of brand value over the same period, decreasing 15% to $35.2bn in 2026 from $41.1bn in 2025.

The downturn is accredited to a tumultuous year characterised by a sharp decline in profitability and other challenges, says Brand Finance. Still, the company bolstered its standings with expansion of its electrified models, including hybrid 911s, battery-electric Macan and Cayennes, and interesting projects such as special series including the convertible 911 GT3 S/C.

Among this year’s brands to watch, Jaguar prepares for a major reinvention as an all-electric luxury marque with its highly anticipated Jaguar Type 01, said Brand Finance.

The second most valuable automotive brand was Ferrari, valued at $14.5bn. The Italian brand ranks seventh overall in the survey, up from eighth position in 2025. It reinforced its luxury positioning through a disciplined focus on exclusivity, high-margin models, and product innovation despite heavy criticism when unveiling the Luce, its first fully electric vehicle.

The brand, together with its enduring motorsport heritage and the release of other new products and bespoke models, continued its desirability trajectory.

In third place among motoring brands is Lamborghini, ranked 18th among global luxury brands, up from 19th in 2025. The Italian supercar brand owned by the Volkswagen group had a stellar year transcending its electric era, launching the Revuelto and the Temerario with new and innovative eight and 12-cylinder hybrid engines, including the updated Urus SE hybrid SUV. The brand also marked the 60th anniversary of the Miura in 2026, the defining model of its heritage.

British aristocratic brand Rolls-Royce was the fourth most valuable automotive brand and 24th overall in 2026, up from 28th in 2025. The world’s leading innovator of chauffeured luxury introduced Series II ranges of the Cullinan and electric Spectre, and continued to stun with new levels of exclusive and bespoke design and peerless one-offs.

evidence.title: 1 of 9 factory-built Porsche 962 returns to the track
evidence.text:
1 of 9 factory-built Porsche 962 returns to the track

1 of 9 factory-built Porsche 962 returns to the track

Porsche Motorsport North America breathes new life into chassis 962C-005

There are racecars, and then there's the Porsche 962.

Only a few have achieved the legendary status of the Porsche 962. Built to dominate endurance racing during the 80s and 90s with 19 constructors’ championships and more than 180 overall victories, there’s only one place an icon like this truly belongs: on the racetrack, at full throttle.

That’s exactly what veteran racer and collector Charles Nearburg set out to achieve when he teamed up with Porsche Motorsport North America (PMNA) to restore his rare factory-built 962 with the intention of using it on the racetrack.

With a racing career spanning SCCA, CART, and Le Mans, as well as an FIA World Speed Record of 414 mph at Bonneville, Nearburg knows a thing or two about serious racecars. His rare 962 is undoubtedly one of the most special cars in his collection.

Chassis 962C-005 is one of just nine Porsche 962 prototypes built directly by the factory, with only seven remaining in private hands. Making it even more special, this particular car still wears the iconic Rothmans Porsche livery and also served as a testbed for Porsche’s racing technology.

This explains why the car retains much of its original wiring for Porsche’s early prototype of the Doppelkupplung (PDK) dual-clutch transmission, which made its competition debut in 1986.

The 962 was the first Porsche race car to use the system, with Hans Stuck and Derek Bell taking a PDK-equipped car to victory at Monza during the same year. It was also Stuck’s idea to place the gear selector on the steering wheel. Its period-correct Bosch ECU and ignition system were also preserved.

When Nearburg acquired the car, it was a close-to-running showpiece in need of a serious mechanical revival. Rather than rely on old memories or conflicting technical information, PMNA went straight to Porsche’s archives, using original factory drawings, manuals, and records to guide the restoration.

The 2.8-liter, flat-six, twin-turbocharged powertrain was fully rebuilt and calibrated on PMNA’s engine dyno before the 962 underwent initial shakedown testing at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles.

Six months after arriving at PMNA’s facility in Carson, California, 962C-005 was back with Nearburg. A month later, it returned to its natural habitat at the Circuit of the Americas (COTA), completing a trouble-free session.

Driving a 962, however, remains a very different experience from operating a modern race car. Drivers must anticipate turbocharger response, manage a traditional clutch and shift lever, and stay ahead of the car's reactions rather than relying on modern electronic systems.

"If you are late to the throttle, you simply have to wait," Nearburg explained. "In a more modern car, the electronic boost control is much more linear."

While the safety equipment was updated to modern standards, Nearburg and PMNA went to great lengths to preserve the 962’s original raw, analog driving character.

The 962’s dominance on the track perfectly embodied the old “race on Sunday, sell on Monday” philosophy, helping cement its place as one of the most successful sports prototypes ever built.

For a machine this rare, preserving history doesn’t mean keeping it locked away in storage or a museum. It means letting the 962 do exactly what it was built to do: race.

A certified true gearhead, Francis has been around modified cars for as long as he can remember. He’s our features editor writing all about cars and armed with a keen knowledge of the local automotive aftermarket industry.

evidence.title: Airbus Traces A321neo Stringer Coating Flaw to a Supplier
evidence.text:
Airbus Traces A321neo Stringer Coating Flaw to a Supplier

TOULOUSE — Airbus has confirmed a deviation in the corrosion protection on stringers in the lower forward fuselage of a batch of A321neos, and told The Air Current that the problem originated with an undisclosed second-tier supplier, one that supplies Airbus's direct suppliers. A person familiar with the matter told Reuters on Thursday that the flaw affects about 500 aircraft, roughly 250 already in service and 250 still in production , and that the longer-range A321XLR is not among them.

The Air Current, which first reported the issue on September 24, put the number at more than 500. In a statement Airbus shared with Aviacionline , the manufacturer said: "Aircraft can continue to operate. This is a quality issue, not a safety issue." It added that "the source of the issue has been identified, contained and a remedy is available," and that "all newly coated stringers conform to all requirements."

The timing matters because the A321neo carries Airbus's narrowbody ramp-up. A321s made up roughly three-quarters of the A320 Family backlog at the end of June, as Airways reported when Airbus held its 2026 delivery target in July. Reuters reports that Airbus is pushing for record deliveries this year while trying to raise A320 Family output to 75 aircraft a month.

Stringers run the length of the fuselage and stiffen its skin, while the frames circle it. Airbus's statement places the deviation in the stringers' surface protection "at the lower front section of the fuselage" and says it was found "during some standard rework." The primer and coating are there to protect the structure from corrosion over its service life, and The Air Current reported that the flaw could reduce corrosion resistance inside the fuselage.

In a report published on Friday, Reuters cited two industry sources as saying that a subcontractor to Italy's Leonardo handled the anti-corrosion layer . Leonardo is one of the A321neo's aerostructures suppliers alongside Airbus Atlantic, the in-house unit formerly known as Stelia. Leonardo declined to comment.

Reuters' Thursday source said Airbus first noticed the problem during the summer, with early findings from a closer analysis arriving recently.

Delivered jets and possible regulatory action

"The rework doesn't require any disassembly of the stringers," Airbus said of the fix. "Once rework is applied, the aircraft is considered to be back as if at nominal design."

Reuters' Thursday source also said that Airbus has advised customers there is no immediate requirement to repair, and that customers are still taking deliveries without insisting the work be done first. Reuters added that European regulators could still issue a directive requiring repairs within a set period. People familiar with the matter told The Air Current that aircraft not corrected before delivery will need in-service inspections and rework over the coming years.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) list of recent airworthiness directives and proposed directives , checked on Friday, showed none on the stringer issue. Neither Airbus's statement nor the publicly available reports reviewed for this story identify the affected serial numbers or operators.

Delta Air Lines (DL), which flies the A321neo, said it was continually in contact with manufacturers and would "always take action to meet or exceed operator recommendations and regulator directives," according to Reuters.

The Air Current reported that the affected jets not yet delivered are at various stages of completion within Airbus's supply chain in Europe, the US, and China, and that reworking them is likely to put pressure on medium-term deliveries.

Airbus has not changed its full-year guidance. "Our full-year guidance was formally stated during our first-half results on 29 July—this remains our current public position," a spokesperson told Reuters. That guidance calls for around 870 commercial aircraft deliveries in 2026 . Airbus had delivered 475 commercial aircraft through August, according to Reuters, leaving about 395 for the last four months of the year. In the same July results, Airbus said it expects the A320 Family to reach between 70 and 75 aircraft a month by the end of 2027. Reuters puts the current rate at about 60.

A Jefferies analyst wrote that tracking data showed eight deliveries so far this week, suggesting deliveries were "not meaningfully affected at this stage," Reuters reported. Airbus shares were down just over 1% in early Paris trading on Friday.

Citing industry sources, Reuters reported that the stringer flaw leaves Airbus facing questions over quality control in the biggest part of its factory system for the second time in less than a year. In December 2025, a quality issue with fuselage panels, which Reuters said came from a Spanish supplier, led Airbus to lower its 2025 delivery target from about 820 aircraft to about 790. EASA proposed an airworthiness directive on those panels on December 17, 2025, and issued the final directive on March 13, 2026. It covers A319neo, A320neo, and A321neo aircraft whose serial numbers Airbus listed in an alert operator transmission to airlines, and requires panel inspections on those with certain earlier repairs. The agency said the thickness deviations, in combination with certain repair conditions, could affect structural integrity.

Airbus's statement on the stringers does not say how long the rework takes per aircraft, or whether delivered jets can have it done during scheduled maintenance.

evidence.title: Airbus Sets Date For First A350F Flight After Successful Rejected Takeoff Tests
evidence.text:
Airbus has confirmed that the first test flight of its next-generation widebody twinjet freighter, the Airbus A350F, will take place in Toulouse in the southwest of France on Tuesday, September 29. This milestone is set to mark a key step forward for the type, which successfully completed various non-flying tests at Toulouse-Blagnac Airport (TLS) this week. Airbus has received nearly 120 orders for the type.

Going forward, the Airbus A350F is set to do battle with the Boeing 777-8F from the US planemaker's heavily delayed 777X series, as the pair look to win market share in the next generation of the air cargo market. The A350F is based on the larger A350-1000 passenger model, albeit with a slightly shorter fuselage, and Airbus plans for it to have a 4,700 NM (8,700 km) range at 109 tonnes structural payload.

In four days' time, Airbus plans to make history by operating the first test flight of its prototype A350F out of Toulouse Blagnac Airport. Simple Flying will be there in the south of France to provide live coverage of the event both on social media and here on the website - keep your eyes peeled!

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

As it stands, the Airbus A350F is set to take off on its maiden test flight between 10:30 AM and 10:45 AM local time (04:30-04:45 AM EST) on Tuesday, with the circular trip expected to take four hours or so. Between 2:30 PM and 3:15 PM, Airbus notes that there will be a " flyover, landing, taxiing, technical tests & door opening ," followed by photo opportunities and speeches. However, it does hasten to add:

" This event remains subject to essential operational requirements, including weather conditions. "

The News Follows Successful Engine & Rejected Takeoff Tests

Aside from the announcement of the date for the first test flight, this week has been a big one as a whole for the Airbus A350F . Indeed, as noted by Cargo Facts, yesterday also saw the European planemaker's prototype for the widebody twinjet freighter perform engine tests , as well as two rejected takeoffs. One of these rejected takeoff tests can be seen in the video that is embedded below.

The purpose of these rejected takeoff tests, Cargo Facts notes, is to confirm that, in the event that, for whatever reason, a takeoff needs to be aborted, the aircraft is able to do so successfully and safely. According to Aviation Flights, they followed a pair of engine runs and taxi checks , which took place on September 18 and 22. These came a month after the jet was first spotted in Toulouse in its full paint job.

While the Airbus A350F doesn't match up to quadjet freighters like the Boeing 747-8F in terms of size, it is still inarguably an aircraft of great scale. Indeed, Simple Flying reported back in June of this year that its main cargo door alone is bigger than most regional jet fuselages ! This record-breaking door is the largest of its kind in aviation history , and it even has the ability to 'swallow' jet engines whole .

All pilots receive continuous training, which ensures readiness and equips individuals with the skills needed to handle any situation effectively.

Who Has Ordered The Airbus A350F Thus Far?

Thus far, Airbus's prototype Airbus A350F, which bears the French test registration F-WXLD , according to Aerospace Global News, is the only example of the type to have rolled off the production line. However, there will be plenty more to come, with present fleet data made available by ch-aviation showing that airlines around the world have currently got a grand total of 118 outstanding orders for the type .

21 of these have undisclosed customers, but, of the remaining 97, Atlas Air has made the largest commitment, with 20 firm orders. Elsewhere, double-digit commitments have also been made by Air China Cargo, Etihad Airways, and Starlux Airlines, with 10 orders apiece. Meanwhile, other customers include Air France (three), Cathay Pacific (eight), Korean Air (seven), and Singapore Airlines (seven).

evidence.title: Airbus A350F will make first flight on 29 September after high-speed tests
evidence.text:
Sign up for our newsletter and get our latest content in your inbox.

Airbus is only a few days away from flying its new A350F freighter for the first time. The manufacturer has confirmed the maiden flight will take place on 29 September in a post on X.

Ready for a special delivery? 📦 Tune in to our X live broadcast of the A350F maiden flight: 📆 29 September 2026 ⌚️10:20 GMT+2 Note: this event remains subject to essential operational requirements, including weather conditions. pic.twitter.com/2qrSSk2qBg

The prototype completed two high-speed rejected-takeoff tests in Toulouse on Thursday. The tests hinted that the first A350F, MSN700, registration F-WXLD, had entered the final stages of preparation for its maiden flight.

Two rejected takeoff tests for the #Airbus #A350F prototype this morning! The first flight is scheduled for early next week.✈️ #Toulouse #FWXLD #Avgeek pic.twitter.com/p7wIdQYVZE

Airbus said earlier this month that it planned the A350F’s maiden flight for late September, subject to variables including the weather.

Videos and images of the runs have also appeared on social media.

A350F has moved rapidly through final ground testing

The rejected-takeoff runs follow a series of milestones that Airbus must complete before committing a new aircraft to the air.

MSN700 conducted its first taxi test at Toulouse on 18 September, according to aircraft tracking and production records.

Aviation Flights Group’s production record identifies the aircraft as MSN700, registration F-WXLD, powered by two Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines. Its timeline traces the prototype from completion of major structural components through final assembly, engine installation, and its appearance in full Airbus colours.

Airbus has also confirmed that the aircraft has passed several much more substantial engineering milestones.

The aircraft completed Ground Vibration Testing in June . Engineers mechanically excited the airframe and measured its response to validate the structural and aeroelastic models that will be used during flight testing.

Airbus described the test as a “key enabler” for first flight , because it provides evidence needed to begin opening the aircraft’s flight envelope.

Other ground work has included tests of the main-deck cargo door , cargo loading system and aircraft pressurisation.

The A350F has an unusually large electrically actuated main-deck cargo door, with a clear opening measuring 4.3 metres wide and 3.15 metres high. Airbus completed the first production door earlier this year before integrating it into the test aircraft.

Airbus has already flown the A350F virtually

Another significant milestone came before MSN700 started its recent taxi tests.

Airbus has begun the countdown after completing what it calls its Virtual First Flight programme , comprising 13 simulator sessions lasting about five hours each.

The development simulator is connected to real aircraft avionics test benches, including the flight controls and digital engine control systems. Airbus says the setup is approximately 90% representative of the actual aircraft.

The programme cleared systems, validated flight-control laws, rehearsed the first-flight profile and trained crews to respond to failures.

“The only significant variable left to prove in the sky is the freighter’s specific aerodynamic model,” A350F lead flight test engineer Laurent Bussiere said.

The A350F is more than an A350-1000 with its passenger cabin removed. It combines the forward fuselage length of an A350-900 with the rear fuselage length and wings of the A350-1000. Its different proportions and landing-gear geometry require Airbus to validate a new aerodynamic model and ground-handling characteristics.

First flight will deliberately use Direct Law

Airbus says MSN700 will conduct its maiden flight entirely in Direct Law, rather than the A350’s normal flight-control mode. Normal Law provides the flight-envelope and stability protections familiar to A350 pilots. Direct Law provides much more direct pilot control.

Airbus says around 10% of the derivative aircraft’s aerodynamic characteristics remain based on an unverified model until they can be confirmed in flight. The first crew has trained for the Direct Law flight profile in the simulator.

The five-person crew will comprise two pilots, one test flight engineer and two flight test engineers.

The maiden flight of MSN700 will focus on aerodynamic performance, handling qualities and autopilot testing. The aircraft has also been fitted with a special tail skid and bumper for later takeoff-performance testing.

Two A350Fs will conduct around 400 flight-test hours

The first flight will begin a planned roughly 400-hour flight-test programme involving two aircraft.

MSN700 will lead aerodynamic and handling work and will progressively clear the A350F’s flight-control laws.

A second prototype, MSN701, registration F-WCGO, will concentrate on systems testing, including air conditioning, fire and smoke testing and hot- and cold-weather trials.

Airbus expects the overall certification flight-test campaign to last around nine months.

One of the early priorities after first flight will be flight vibration, or flutter, testing. Engineers will progressively expand the aircraft’s permitted envelope towards its maximum dive speed and Mach number, building on the structural models established during June’s ground vibration tests.

The maiden flight of MSN700 will mark the most critical phase yet for a cargo plane Airbus launched in 2021 to challenge Boeing’s longstanding dominance of the large dedicated freighter market. Airbus is targeting certification in 2027, followed by first customer deliveries in the second half of the year.

evidence.text:
Airbus sets date for first A350F flight with livestream access

Airbus has set the date for the first A350F cargo aircraft flight, promising a livestream broadcast to enable the public to be part of the occasion.

On September 25, 2026, Airbus confirmed on social media that the first A350F flight will take off on September 29, 2026, at 10:20 (GMT+2).

Airbus said that the maiden flight comes following five years of “detailed planning, component and demonstrator testing”.

Earlier this month, the European planemaker confirmed that the final countdown had begun, moving from the ‘Virtual First Flight’ milestone to the real thing.

Laurent Bussiere, Lead Flight Test Engineer for the A350F program, explained that, despite the A350F being built on the A350-1000 needs, the aircraft still requires extensive testing.

“The A350F presents unique dimensions due to the freighter’s specific fuselage configuration – which is equivalent to an A350-900 forward fuselage [length] mated to an A350-1000 rear fuselage [length] and A350-1000 wings,” Bussiere said. “In turn, this creates a new aerodynamic model which affects flight control, while the new geometry for the landing gear affects ground maneuvering.”

He added: “It’s not an A350-1000 and it’s not an A350-900, but rather it’s between both. So, we need to look at the behavior of the whole system with this unique model. That’s why we go into the development simulator to prepare for the first flight and the subsequent 400 flight-hour flight test campaign.”

In recent weeks, a test A350F has been seen performing high-speed rejected takeoffs in Toulouse, France.

There will be a five-person crew on board the first test flight, comprising two pilots, one test flight engineer (TFE), and two flight test engineers (FTE).

The certification campaign is expected to take around nine months and will involve two test A350Fs, namely MSN700 and MSN701.

evidence.title: Airbus Identifies A321neo Defect Affecting 500 Aircraft
evidence.text:
Parts already moving through standard rework on the production line brought the nonconformity into view. Airbus confirmed a surface protection deviation on stringers at the lower front section of the fuselage, affecting a number of A321 aircraft. The parts are made by Stelia, the company’s in-house aerostructures unit.

The defect affects about 500 aircraft. Roughly 250 already operate in airline fleets and 250 remain in production.

Airbus first spotted the problem over the summer. Only recently did the first results from closer analysis come back.

In a modern airliner the fuselage is the main body that carries crew, passengers and cargo. Most large jets use a semi-monocoque design: formers set the cross-section shape, then lightweight longitudinal members called stringers join those formers and stiffen the aluminum skin that covers them. The stringers run the length of the lower forward fuselage. Any shortfall in the protection applied to them stays hidden until the structure is opened again for other work.

What slipped was the coating. Airbus described a “deviation” in the surface protection applied to those stringers—the thin barrier of primers and surface treatments that delays corrosion in alloy exposed to moisture, condensation and the contaminants that collect beneath the cabin floor and in the cargo hold. That layer is not structural metal. When the protection falls short of specification, corrosion resistance inside the structure is reduced. The shortfall does not mean an immediate loss of integrity. It shortens the durability margin the airframe is built to carry over years of pressurized service.

Airbus said the finding is a quality issue that does not pose a safety risk. The aircraft may keep flying. The company has identified and contained the source of the issue, and a remedy is available. The same deviation does not affect the A321XLR.

Those airframes are A321neos, Airbus’s largest and most popular single-aisle jet. The airplane seats up to 244 passengers and is designed to fly routes of up to 4,000 nautical miles (7,400 km). That combination of capacity and range has made it the flagship workhorse for major airlines on high-density domestic routes and longer single-aisle sectors, some of them transatlantic. It stands at the top of the A320neo family, the re-engined narrow-body development of the earlier A320 series. New engines and sharklet wingtip devices improve fuel burn by 15 to 20 percent; the A321neo stretches that shared structure to its longest form, packing the highest passenger count into a single aisle while still reaching distances the shorter models cannot.

The finding is the second fuselage quality issue to reach the model in nine months. In December 2025 Airbus reported defects with fuselage panels. The company described that earlier episode as a quality problem with no safety implications, yet unravelling it still caused several months of delivery delays.

Airbus began alerting its customers and told them there was no immediate requirement to repair. Customers continued taking deliveries without insisting that any extra work be carried out in advance. Industry publication The Air Current first reported the issue on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters and other outlets followed the same day.

The timing pressed against a production climb already under way. Airbus is pushing narrow-body output toward 75 jets a month from about 60, a rate pursued after earlier years when neo-family production sat near fifty aircraft a month and subsequent targets stepped through the low sixties. Delivery numbers showed the distance still open: 475 aircraft handed over through the end of August 2026 against a full-year target set between 850 and 890. September shipments had not yet been reported, and the fourth-quarter surge that customarily fills the annual books still lay ahead. Shares fell 0.33 percent to 194.38 euros in Paris.

European regulators may issue a directive requiring the defects to be repaired within a certain period. Production jets still incomplete would be reworked before delivery, the coating restored on the line so each airframe meets specification by handover. Airbus does not expect any change to its full-year delivery guidance.

Delta Air Lines operates the A321neo. The carrier said it would always take action to meet or exceed operator recommendations and regulator directives.

The remaining unfinished A321neos keep moving down the line under the contained fix.

evidence.title: Airbus flags corrosion-protection deviation on the A321neo: more than 500 aircraft under review, with no safety risk
evidence.text:
Airbus confirmed on Thursday that it has identified a quality defect that can reduce corrosion resistance in the internal fuselage structure of A321neo aircraft. The manufacturer, however, was explicit: this is a quality issue and not a safety one , so the aircraft can remain in service . The news was first reported by The Air Current , which estimated that the finding could affect more than 500 aircraft , including units already delivered and jets still on the production line. Airbus did not deny the general scope of the report and added that the source of the problem has already been identified, contained, and that a remedy is available .

The constructor shared a statement with Aviacionline:

Airbus identified a surface protection deviation on stringers in the lower forward fuselage section that can reduce corrosion resistance in the internal fuselage structure.

Yes. Airbus says it is a quality issue, not a safety issue, and aircraft can continue to operate.

More than 500 aircraft are under review, including about 250 still in production and the rest already in service.

A rework is available; it does not require disassembly of the stringers, and once applied the aircraft is considered back at nominal design.

No. No PAD or AD from EASA or the FAA has been published yet.

No. This case concerns corrosion protection on A321neo stringers, while the earlier case involved forward fuselage panel thickness deviations across the A320neo family and was linked to supplier Sofitec.

Airbus has not published a list of serial numbers, registrations, or operators, so it is not confirmed which Latin American aircraft are in the batch.

Aircraft in service can keep flying; engineering should cross-check serial numbers against the Airbus bulletin, and any affected units will be scheduled for rework during maintenance windows.

"We can confirm that during some standard rework a surface protection deviation on stringers located at the lower front section of the fuselage was identified affecting a number of A321 aircraft. The source of the issue has been identified, contained and a remedy is available. All newly coated stringers conform to all requirements. Aircraft can continue to operate. This is a quality issue, not a safety issue. The rework doesn’t require any disassembly of the stringers. Once rework is applied, the aircraft is considered to be back as if at nominal design."

The company's shares traded in Paris with a moderate decline of 0.33%, at 194.38 euros, a contained reaction for an alert that touches the most in-demand narrowbody on the market. What went wrong, and where According to the technical reconstruction that circulated based on The Air Current 's report , the deviation is not in the outer fuselage skin, but in the surface protection of the stringers located in the lower forward section . Airbus reportedly detected the non-conformity during routine rework and attributed it to a second-tier supplier (Tier 2) that was not identified. In structural terms, stringers are the longitudinal reinforcements that work alongside the frames to stiffen the fuselage. Surface protection (treatments, primers and coatings) is the barrier that delays the onset of corrosion in aluminium alloys exposed to moisture, condensation and contaminants from the cargo hold or the lower cabin. A deviation in that process does not mean an immediate failure , but it can shorten the durability margin if it is not corrected.

That nuance explains the message from Toulouse: the aircraft does not lose structural integrity overnight, but the affected fleet will have to enter an inspection and rework programme to restore the specified protection. Of the more than 500 aircraft mentioned, about 250 are said to be still in production . On those airframes the extra work will be done before delivery. The rest are aircraft already in service, which will have to schedule the correction during maintenance windows. According to the same report, Airbus did not change its annual delivery plan . Not the same problem as December 2025 It is important not to confuse this alert with the earlier S12 panel alert. In late 2025, EASA opened a process (PAD 25-196) over thickness deviations in forward fuselage panels of the A320neo family (A319neo, A320neo and A321neo), a case linked to Spanish supplier Sofitec that did lead to regulatory inspections because, combined with certain previous repairs, it could affect structural integrity.

Thursday's episode is different in three respects: It affects the A321neo for now, not the entire neo family. The finding concerns corrosion protection on stringers, not panel thickness. Airbus classifies it as a quality issue, not an unsafe condition, and no airworthiness directive has been published yet. That distinction does not play down the issue. It shows, rather, that pressure on the A320neo/A321neo supply chain keeps generating non-conformities as the manufacturer tries to raise the build rate. The A321neo is Airbus's flagship product. By August 2026 the programme had accumulated some 2,226 deliveries and a backlog of more than 5,600 orders . In July there were around 1,911 active aircraft with 96 operators and in 2026, of the 369 neo family deliveries counted through August, 230 were A321neos .

That commercial weight explains the sensitivity of the alert. Every day of rework in Finkenwerder, Toulouse, Mobile or Tianjin multiplies when the model concentrates the bulk of the ramp-up toward the 75 aircraft per month Airbus is chasing for the A320 family in 2027. In July, CEO Guillaume Faury had already spoken of a quality “moonshot” to halve non-quality problems, after the 2025 panel episode “created a lot of disruptions in the system”. What it means for airlines in the region Airbus has not yet published the list of registrations or operators. Therefore, it is not confirmed which Latin American aircraft are part of the batch of more than 500. What is clear is that the model is no longer marginal in the region.

LATAM took on A321neos throughout 2026 (four in the first half and more units via leasing, including five A321-271NXs from CDB Aviation delivered through September) and uses them to add seats and range on medium-haul routes. JetSMART operates a growing fleet of 240-seat A321neos in Chile, Argentina and other group markets. Both carriers also have the A321XLR on the roadmap for 2027. As long as there is no MSN list, the most likely scenario for regional operators is operational, not a grounding: Aircraft in service keep flying. Engineering will have to cross-check serial numbers against the bulletin Airbus sends to customers. If there are affected units, the rework will be scheduled during checks or short stops, not a mass grounding. That sets this case apart from the GTF engine crises, which did leave aircraft on the ground because of a lack of powerplants.

At this hour, there is no public: List of serial numbers. Name of the Tier 2 supplier. Exact scope for the A321LR and A321XLR. A PAD or AD from EASA or the FAA. Standard rework times per aircraft. What did become clear is the triad the manufacturer cites when it detects a quality deviation: source identified, problem contained, solution available . The question that remains for the coming hours is not whether the A321neo is safe, since Airbus says it is and there is no evidence to the contrary, but how much extra work this deviation implies for a line that was already stretched and how many operators will have to inspect their fuselages.

The agreement, signed at Safran Landing Systems' Singapore facility during MRO Asia-Pacific, covers China Airlines' entire fleet of Airbus Airbus A350-900 aircraft and will support the airline's landing gear maintenance requirements from 2026 through 2031.

China Airlines already relies on Safran Landing Systems for landing gear maintenance services for its Airbus A330 fleet, while other members of the CAL Group, including Tigerair Taiwan and Mandarin Airlines, also partner with Safran Landing Systems on their respective fleets.

The agreement further reinforces Safran Landing Systems' commitment to supporting airlines across Asia-Pacific through a comprehensive network of landing gear maintenance services. It also highlights the strategic role of the company's Singapore MRO facility, which serves operators throughout one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets.

evidence.text:
Safran launches US$22 million landing gear MRO facility in Singapore

The Republic is now the aviation company’s second-largest location for such services globally

[SINGAPORE] Aviation company Safran Landing Systems Services Singapore (SLSSS) launched a major new site on Tuesday (Sep 22), expanding the French aviation giant’s Asia-Pacific maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) capabilities. The US$22 million, 7,500 square metre (sq m) development was supported by the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB).

Benoit Graby, managing director of SLSSS, said the move reflects “our confidence in the future of aviation, in the growth of our customers across the Asia-Pacific region, and in Singapore’s role as a leading aerospace hub”.

Cindy Koh, executive vice-president of EDB, said: “Global players like Safran are in Singapore to tap our vibrant aerospace and advanced manufacturing ecosystems, and access the growth potential of the Asia-Pacific – a region expected to become the largest aviation market globally in the next 20 years.”

The new site is located at 66 Loyang Way, around 250 metres from the existing SLSSS facility at 21 Loyang Crescent, and increases SLSSS’ footprint to a total of 20,500 sq m.

With the addition, Singapore becomes Safran’s second-largest MRO site for landing gear in the world, and its largest in Apac.

The company will create 100 new roles by 2030, taking SLSSS’ headcount in Singapore to around 460.

Get insights into businesses across South-east Asia

Started in 1979, SLSSS specialises in the repair and overhaul of aircraft landing gear.

In 2000, it formed a joint venture with SIA Engineering Company (SIAEC), where Safran holds a 60 per cent stake and SIAEC has 40 per cent.

The new site is expected to begin full operation in October. It will focus on the assembly of landing gear, while the 21 Loyang Crescent facility will carry out repair and manufacturing work.

At around twice the size of the previous assembly line, it is expected to ship 2.5 complete sets of landing gear per week.

With this, SLSSS will be able to service and overhaul the landing gear on several aircraft types, including Boeing 787, 737, Airbus A380, A350, A320, A321, and models from ATR.

SLSSS’ Graby said that the expansion will allow the company to increase its capacity by 40 per cent.

It will also introduce new processes and technology in the future, including the repair of titanium parts and advanced coating and plating techniques.

EDB and SLSSS also announced training for 300 existing employees and 100 new hires in MRO services for new aircraft, including on-the-job training, mentorships and attachments at Safran sites abroad.

evidence.text:
This Small-Cap Stock, engaged in providing cloud-based enterprise software solutions across aviation, logistics, transportation, payroll, and human capital management sectors globally, hit a 5 percent upper circuit after signing an MoU with Safran Helicopter Engines to integrate engine data with Ramco Aviation Software.

With a market capitalization of Rs. 2,312.01 crores, the shares of Ramco Systems Limited hit a 5 percent upper circuit of Rs. 615.65 per share on Friday, up from its previous closing price of Rs. 586.35 per share. Since then, the stock has retreated and is currently trading at Rs. 614.95 per equity share.

Ramco Systems has signed an MoU with Safran Helicopter Engines to integrate engine data with Ramco Aviation Software. The partnership will automate data transfer, reduce manual work, improve accuracy, and support better maintenance planning. The collaboration is expected to strengthen Ramco’s aviation software business and expand its digital aviation capabilities. Here are 5 key points investors should know about the deal:

MoU with Safran Helicopter Engines: Ramco Systems has signed an MoU with Safran Helicopter Engines, a leading manufacturer of helicopter engines, to integrate Safran’s engine data directly with Ramco Aviation Software.

Automatic Engine Data Integration: Engine information such as configuration, operating hours, usage metrics, and maintenance events can be automatically transferred into Ramco’s Maintenance Information System (MIS), reducing manual data entry.

Benefits for Helicopter Operators: The integration is expected to save time, improve data accuracy, and reduce manual work for operators. It can also support better maintenance planning and aircraft airworthiness management.

EngineLife® Connect Label: The collaboration is expected to result in Safran awarding Ramco the EngineLife® Connect label, which recognizes connectivity solutions compatible with Safran’s products and services.

Strengthens Ramco’s Aviation Business: The partnership strengthens Ramco’s position in the aviation MRO software ecosystem by connecting aircraft operators with OEM data. It could also support Ramco’s growth in digital aviation services through AI and automation-driven solutions.

Ramco Aviation Software: Driving Digital Transformation in Aviation

Ramco Aviation Software is a trusted solution used by more than 24,000 users across over 4,000 aircraft globally. With more than 90 aviation organisations onboard, it serves airlines, third-party MROs, helicopter operators, defence companies and emerging urban air mobility businesses. Its cloud-based platform helps customers access aviation solutions from anywhere, improving efficiency and flexibility.

Ramco is also using AI and automation to modernise aviation software. Features such as intelligent voice-enabled services, digital task cards, offline maintenance tools, conversational chatbots, and cognitive solutions help reduce manual work and improve productivity. These capabilities position Ramco to benefit from the growing demand for smarter, faster and more connected aviation maintenance solutions.

Commenting on the partnership, Sam Jacob, Executive Vice President & SBU Head-Aviation, Aerospace and Defense, Ramco Systems, said, “With several of the world's largest helicopter operators on our platform, Ramco sits at a unique intersection of the aviation MRO ecosystem-connecting OEMs and operators through a single digital backbone. We're delighted to partner with a leader like Safran Helicopter Engines to enable this seamless digital exchange:

Safran gains richer engine maintenance data to strengthen reliability, while operators receive OEM information directly into their systems, cutting manual work and improving productivity. Powered by AI and agentic automation, Ramco Aviation Software is built to make exactly this kind of connected, intelligent ecosystem possible.”

Ramco Systems Limited is an enterprise software company based in Chennai that offers its customers aviation, logistics, and human resource management applications hosted in the cloud. A part of the Ramco group, this company provides enterprise applications that automate complicated business processes.

The major products of the company are aviation software, including airline and MRO, logistics and transportation, and payroll and HR. Ramco Systems concentrates on cloud, mobile, and AI-based technologies to help companies become more modernized.

Looking at the company's financial highlights, Ramco Systems Limited's revenue has increased from Rs. 161.32 crore in Q1 FY26 to Rs. 172.77 crore in Q1 FY27, which has grown by 7.08 percent. The net profit has decreased by 48.15 percent from Rs. 1.08 crore in Q1 FY26 to Rs. 0.56 crore in Q1 FY27.

Ramco Systems Limited’s revenue and net profit have grown at a CAGR of 13 percent and 32 percent, respectively, over the last five years. In terms of return ratios, the company's ROCE and ROE stand at 19.7 percent and 18.1 percent, respectively. Ramco Systems Limited has an earningsper share (EPS) of Rs. 11.1, and its debt-to-equity ratio is 0.12x.

evidence.title: Thales in ‘quite advanced’ talks with NATO countries on AI-powered command software
evidence.text:
PARIS — French defense-technology firm Thales is "quite advanced" in discussions with a number of NATO countries about using its artificial intelligence-powered command-and-control system HexaForce, said the company's vice president for multi-domain operations, Patrick Moreau.

Thales announced the availability of HexaForce last week, after testing it during NATO's Coalition Warrior Interoperability Exercise, or CWIX, in Poland in June. The company is positioning the system as a multi-domain C2 "overlay" that can plug into legacy and national systems from the strategic to the tactical level, while allowing users to choose their own AI models and avoid vendor lock-in.

NATO is increasingly turning to AI to harness growing amounts of data in command and control, and already operates a C2 system supplied by United States-based Palantir Technologies. Meanwhile, the European Union is looking to accelerate development and deployment of European capabilities amid concern about sovereign control of the technology underpinning them.

"I don't want to go too much into detail. but we are quite advanced in some discussions with some NATO countries so far," Moreau told Defense News in a Sept. 24 interview.

As European and NATO militaries look to scale operations from brigade-level formations to army corps of more than 100,000 troops, AI will be key to processing more complex data, shortening planning cycles and improving situational awareness, Moreau said.

France to test its own AI-powered battlefield command in June NATO exercise

HexaForce is aimed at providing command and control from the army corps level down to the battalion, according to the executive. Thales defined a goal with end users to be able to plan 1,000 target missions a day, a tenfold increase.

The system has an open architecture built around NATO standards, allowing countries to plug in existing systems for tasks such as mission planning, or use the large language model of their choice, according to Moreau. In addition to the LLM component, HexaForce includes agentic AI for tasks such as targeting mission preparation.

It has a fully distributed architecture designed to rely on mesh capability, allowing the system to be spread over different data hubs within different command posts, in line with new operational concepts to not rely on central computing, according to Moreau.

By interfacing with legacy solutions, HexaForce can add "AI-powered capability" to systems already in use by the armed forces, according to Moreau. HexaForce is a command-and-control system, and users still need dedicated tactical systems to provide sensor data, he said.

The executive said the aim at CWIX was for end users to test HexaForce and its interoperability with existing and legacy systems. The system implements NATO standards related to the Data-Centric Security and Federation Mission Networking frameworks, he said.

For threats identified at the strategic command level, HexaForce can propose different courses of action, including firing options using air or land forces, according to Moreau. The operator can then choose a course of action, with the system sending the targeting mission to the tactical level.

"Of course it remains up to the operator to choose to push the button, and to choose the best option proposed by HexaForce," Moreau said. "There is no automated action."

In addition to connecting to systems that provide tactical awareness, Hexaforce could include commercial ship-tracking data or cyber threats to provide a more complete picture, Moreau said.

While developed with input from the French Army, the executive repeatedly stressed that the Thales system is designed as a NATO solution rather than a France-specific system. Asked how it compares with existing systems such as Systematic's SitaWare or Airbus's Multi-Domain Combat Cloud, Moreau instead focused on the interoperability of the Thales system.

Moreau said HexaForce is ready and already in the hands of the armed forces, with the first version taking nine months from design to making it available to the French Army.

France is developing its sovereign C2 system Arcadia, and Moreau said that while Hexaforce could be "a cornerstone" of the French system, the decision is not up to Thales.

evidence.text:
Jakarta. Sovereign wealth fund Danantara and the French defense giant Thales have sealed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) that could unlock investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and military equipment.

The MoU covers AI, defense systems, digital technologies, and cybersecurity, according to Danantara. Both sides have agreed to discuss possible investments in Indonesian defense technology manufacturing, airport security, AI use cases, cybersecurity operations centers, and post-quantum technologies.

However, Danantara said on Thursday that the signed document was only an “initial framework”. In other words, actual investments will be subject to “further evaluations, applicable governance, and definitive agreements”.

Danantara managing director Ricardo Irwan Rei said that investments in such sectors could speed up “technology transfer, create high-skilled employment, [and] strengthen local industrial capability”.

Guy Bonassi, the senior vice-president for Asia of Thales Group, said the company was “honored” to work with the fund on “ambitious projects that would foster economic growth”.

Danantara signaled that Thales could team up with the state-owned enterprises (SOEs) under its wings, while avoiding naming specific companies.

Amid the scant details, the fund is now responsible for all Indonesian SOEs, some of which are no stranger to Thales.

The telecommunications giant Telkom had even clinched a Thales digital security and smart city deal in 2025. Jakarta has procured Thales' long-range air surveillance radars in partnership with the electronics firm Len Industri. Indonesia has received the first two GM403 radars earlier this year amid a huge appetite for military upgrades.

Thales has operated in Indonesia for decades, and is even behind the launch of the Satria-1 satellite that has helped connect the country’s remote areas to the internet.

evidence.title: Thales cuts the ribbon on new Flight Safety Center in Bordeaux
evidence.text:
Thales cuts the ribbon on new Flight Safety Center in Bordeaux

As the civil and military aviation sectors enter a new era – one marked by increasing global air traffic and the growing demand for fighter aircraft, the arrival of ever more connected systems, the growing automation of operations, and heightened cybersecurity requirements – flight safety remains the aviation industry’s top priority.

To successfully meet these challenges, Thales has this week inaugurated a new “Flight Safety Center” at its Bordeaux campus – an immersive space entirely dedicated to understanding, sharing and advancing air safety culture.

More than just a demonstration centre, this new facility is intended to be a global centre of excellence where employees, customers, partners, suppliers, authorities and experts can learn about and receive training on air safety challenges. They will be able to share best practices and explore cutting-edge technologies that make aviation one of the safest modes of transportation in the world.

Through a unique educational journey combining interactive experiences, technology demonstrations, and real-world operational feedback, the new Flight Safety Center provides an understanding of how safety is built throughout the lifecycle of an aviation system – from design and development, to certification, operation and maintenance.

Located at the Bordeaux Campus, one of Thales’ leading centres of excellence for aeronautics, the facility marks the first step toward a broader ambition to roll out this concept across several strategic sites in order to support the skills’ development of its 21,000 employees in civil and military aviation activities worldwide.

Yannick Assouad, Thales’ Executive Vice-President Avionics, said: “Flight safety is the foundation of trust in aviation. Behind every safe flight are advanced technologies, rigorous processes, a culture of transparency and learning from experience, and, above all, dedicated women and men. Our Flight Safety Center was designed to bring this safety culture to life, share it with our entire ecosystem and work together to prepare for the challenges of tomorrow’s aviation.”

evidence.title: Thales strengthens data protection amid AI and quantum risks
evidence.text:
AI adoption, expanding data volumes and the emerging threat posed by quantum computing are prompting enterprises to reassess their cybersecurity strategies. Growing demand for platform consolidation is also encouraging organisations to integrate data security, application security and identity and access management capabilities.

In an interview with TahawulTech.com at GISEC Global 2026, Sébastien Pavie, Vice President of Sales – SEMEA at Thales , discusses the company’s latest data protection and quantum-safe security developments. He also examines the dual role of AI in strengthening cyber defence and enabling more sophisticated attacks, highlighting the importance of protecting sensitive data throughout its lifecycle.

How did you find GISEC Global 2026 compared with previous editions?

The new venue at Expo City Dubai brought fresh energy to GISEC Global 2026. The event was extremely busy, which reflected strong engagement from the cybersecurity community. GISEC continues to provide an important platform for Thales to connect with customers and partners, discuss evolving security priorities and present our latest product developments.

What did Thales demonstrate at GISEC Global 2026?

Thales showcased capabilities across data security, application security, and identity and access management. Customers increasingly want to consolidate products and vendors, so we continue to combine complementary solutions within integrated platforms. One of our latest developments brings data protection capabilities together within a single platform, covering the discovery, visibility, protection and control of sensitive information. We also introduced a next-generation, quantum-ready hardware security module designed to help organisations prepare for the potential impact of quantum computing on current encryption methods.

What should guide enterprises when selecting AI-powered cybersecurity technologies?

Enterprises should first recognise AI’s dual role in cybersecurity. Attackers can use AI to increase the scale and sophistication of threats, while defenders can apply the technology to strengthen detection, protection and response. AI adoption also creates and processes significantly larger volumes of data, making data-centric security more important than ever. evidence.text:
Thales Opens Flight Safety Center to Connect Training, Technology and Operational Experience Across Aviation

Thales Opens Flight Safety Center to Connect Training, Technology and Operational Experience Across Aviation

(IN BRIEF) Thales has opened a new Flight Safety Center at its Bordeaux campus to provide immersive training, demonstrations and industry collaboration focused on civil and military aviation safety. The facility is open to employees, customers, partners, suppliers, authorities and other aviation stakeholders and is designed to illustrate how safety is integrated throughout the lifecycle of aviation systems, from design and development through certification, operation and maintenance. The initiative comes as the sector faces higher air traffic volumes, increased demand for military aircraft, expanding automation, greater connectivity and growing cybersecurity requirements. Thales plans to use the Bordeaux centre as the first step toward extending the concept to other strategic sites and ultimately training all 21,000 employees involved in its global civil and military aviation activities. Executive Vice-President Avionics Yannick Assouad said the centre will support a safety culture based on technology, rigorous processes, transparency, operational learning and collaboration across the wider aviation ecosystem.

(PRESS RELEASE) LA DÉFENSE, 24-Sep-2026 — / EuropaWire / — Thales has inaugurated a new Flight Safety Center at its Bordeaux campus , creating an immersive training, demonstration and collaboration environment dedicated to strengthening safety culture across civil and military aviation.

The facility has been designed for use by Thales employees as well as customers, partners, suppliers, aviation authorities and other industry stakeholders. It will provide a venue for training, technical demonstrations and exchanges on the technologies, processes and operational practices that contribute to flight safety.

Thales said the initiative responds to an increasingly complex aviation environment characterised by rising global air traffic, stronger demand for military aircraft, greater connectivity between systems, increasing automation and heightened cybersecurity requirements.

Against this backdrop, the company aims to reinforce understanding of how flight safety is established and maintained throughout an aviation system’s complete lifecycle.

Visitors to the Bordeaux centre will follow an educational programme combining interactive experiences, technology demonstrations and lessons drawn from real-world operations.

The programme is intended to show how safety considerations are incorporated from the earliest stages of system design and development through certification, operational deployment and maintenance.

Thales described the Flight Safety Center as more than a conventional product demonstration facility, positioning it instead as a global centre of excellence where participants can examine aviation-safety challenges, share operational experience and explore technologies relevant to future civil and military aircraft systems.

The facility is located at the company’s Bordeaux campus, one of Thales’ principal centres of expertise for aeronautics.

The opening represents the first stage of a broader programme under which Thales intends to extend the Flight Safety Center concept to additional strategic locations.

The company’s longer-term objective is to support the development of safety skills across its worldwide aviation workforce and ultimately provide flight-safety training to all 21,000 employees working in Thales’ civil and military aviation activities.

The programme is intended to promote a common safety culture across functions, geographies and business areas while encouraging greater sharing of experience between engineering, certification, operational and maintenance communities.

Thales said this approach is particularly important as aircraft and aviation systems become increasingly connected and automated, creating new interactions between software, hardware, human operators and digital networks.

Cybersecurity is also becoming more closely intertwined with conventional aviation safety as aircraft, avionics and supporting infrastructure incorporate greater levels of connectivity.

The Flight Safety Center is therefore intended to give participants a broader understanding of the technical and organisational factors that contribute to safe operations rather than focusing only on individual products or technologies.

Yannick Assouad, Executive Vice-President Avionics at Thales , said flight safety underpins confidence throughout the aviation sector and depends on the combination of advanced technology, rigorous processes, transparency, learning from operational experience and the expertise of the people involved.

She said the new Bordeaux centre is designed to make that safety culture tangible, extend it across Thales’ wider aviation ecosystem and create an environment where stakeholders can work together on the challenges facing future aviation.

The centre will also provide an opportunity for customers, regulatory bodies and industry partners to discuss safety practices and compare approaches across different phases of aircraft and system development.

By combining technical demonstrations with training and operational feedback, Thales intends the facility to help participants understand how individual safety measures interact across the broader aviation system.

The opening forms part of the company’s effort to maintain safety as a central consideration while aviation evolves through increased automation, connectivity and digitalisation.

Through the Bordeaux centre and its planned expansion to other locations, Thales aims to strengthen a shared flight-safety framework spanning its civil and defence aviation activities worldwide.

Thales (Euronext Paris: HO) is a global leader in advanced technologies for the Defence, Aerospace, and Cyber & Digital sectors. Its portfolio of innovative products and services helps address several major challenges: sovereignty, security, sustainability and inclusion.

The Group allocates €4.5 billion per year in Research & Development in key areas, particularly for critical environments, such as Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Quantum and Cloud technologies.

Thales has more than 85,000 employees in 65 countries. In 2025, the Group generated sales of €22.1 billion.

evidence.title: Dassault Systèmes stock trades 30.96 percent below its yearly high
evidence.text:
Dassault Systèmes stock was trading at EUR 20.96 on Euronext Paris on September 25, 2026, down 0.99 percent from the prior close of EUR 21.17. The price stood 30.96 percent below its 52-week high of EUR 30.36, putting valuation and earnings delivery at the center of the investor debate.

On September 24, 2026, Ideal Investisseur reported that Oddo BHF raised its price target from EUR 22.00 to EUR 23.50 while maintaining a neutral rating. The new target is 12.12 percent above the September 25 intraday price, using the reference price of EUR 20.96.

The more cautious counterpoint came on September 17, 2026, when Ideal Investisseur reported that BNP Paribas Exane cut its rating from market perform to underperform and set a EUR 17 price target. That target is 18.89 percent below the September 25 price, creating a clear gap between broker views.

First-half revenue reaches EUR 3.065 billion

Dassault Systèmes reported first-half 2026 revenue of EUR 3.065 billion, down 1 percent, and net income of EUR 611.8 million. These figures are tied to the reporting period ended June 30, 2026, rather than to the September share price.

The company confirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of EUR 6.356 billion when it published its half-year results on July 23, 2026, according to Ideal Investisseur . The guidance gives investors a concrete benchmark against which to measure the second half of the year.

The market data show a wide range between the 52-week low of EUR 15.82 and the high of EUR 30.36. At EUR 20.96, the stock was 32.49 percent above its yearly low, but still materially below the upper end of that range.

For investors, the central tension is visible in the numbers: management is targeting EUR 6.356 billion in 2026 revenue, while the stock remains 30.96 percent below its 52-week high and broker targets span EUR 17.00 to EUR 23.50.

SYSTRA and Dassault Systèmes partner to advance rail infrastructure through virtual twin technology

Global engineering and consulting specialist SYSTRA has announced a strategic collaboration with Dassault Systèmes aimed at accelerating innovation across the rail and transport infrastructure sector through the use of advanced virtual twin technology.

As rail projects become increasingly complex, the industry is under growing pressure to improve collaboration, reduce risk, optimise performance and make better-informed decisions throughout the lifecycle of critical assets. The partnership seeks to address these challenges by harnessing the capabilities of virtual twins and integrating them within Dassault Systèmes' 3D UNIV+RSES platform.

Virtual twins are rapidly emerging as a transformative tool for the infrastructure sector, enabling organisations to digitally design, simulate, test and optimise assets before implementing changes in the real world. Unlike traditional digital models, the 3D UNIV+RSES environment connects multiple virtual twins together and links them to their operating environment using real-world data, engineering models and artificial intelligence.

The initiative aims to help the rail sector move away from fragmented analysis methods towards more connected and collaborative digital ecosystems. By bringing together data, models and expertise from across project teams and stakeholders, organisations can gain a clearer understanding of project challenges, assess options earlier and improve decision-making from concept through to operation and maintenance.

The approach is also expected to enhance cooperation between the many stakeholders involved in rail infrastructure delivery, supporting more effective planning and helping teams anticipate the potential impacts of key decisions before they are implemented.

Prisca Flattot, Senior Vice President Technical & Operational Performance, SYSTRA, said:

“Through this initiative, SYSTRA reaffirms its ambition to be a driving force in digital innovation for rail and infrastructure alongside major technology partners. The virtual twin is a powerful tool for better design, better decision-making, and supporting our clients throughout the lifecycle of their assets. With Dassault Systèmes, we want to accelerate the development of high value-added digital services for infrastructure that is even safer, more reliable, and more sustainable.”

By combining SYSTRA's extensive rail and infrastructure expertise with Dassault Systèmes' digital engineering and AI-driven technology capabilities, both organisations are already developing innovative digital solutions designed to deliver greater value for infrastructure owners and operators.

The partnership comes at a time when data governance, digital trust and technological sovereignty are becoming increasingly important considerations for both public and private sector organisations responsible for critical transport infrastructure.

As the rail industry continues its digital transformation journey, the collaboration has the potential to support the development of smarter, more resilient and more sustainable infrastructure networks, while enabling project teams to make better decisions based on connected, data-driven insights.
