evidence.title: Carrefour uses Fortnite to make food careers feel playable
evidence.text:
There is a reason brand worlds in games keep showing up around back-to-school season: younger audiences are already spending time in these spaces to hang out, compete, and explore identity, not just to “play a game.”

Carrefour is tapping that behaviour by using Fortnite as a way to make its behind-the-scenes food jobs feel like something you can try on, not something you read about. The company outlined the experience on its official page for the activation, including an island code (6671-9497-0398) and related video content.

Why a grocery retailer is showing up inside Fortnite

Carrefour is entering Fortnite at a moment when gaming platforms function like social spaces. People do not just consume content there, they spend time there with friends, watch creators stream it, and treat in-game worlds as places to explore.

The activation is designed to reach younger audiences and introduce the brand through the jobs and roles that “make food more accessible and more responsible,” tying the experience to Carrefour’s Act for Food mission.

This also frames recruitment as culture, not corporate messaging. Instead of telling students what retail and food ecosystem work looks like, it lets them experience a version of the pressure, speed, and coordination those roles involve.

What players actually do in Carrefour’s four mini-games

Carrefour built a bespoke Fortnite map with four mini-games, each tied to a profession:

Taken together, the mini-games are doing something specific: turning abstract job descriptions into a set of familiar Fortnite-style mechanics (timed runs, vigilance, defending objectives) that players already understand.

How this blends employer branding with culture marketing

Carrefour’s bet is that the easiest way to be memorable to younger audiences is to meet them in a format they already share, stream, and talk about. The company describes the activation as having “strong viral potential,” and it is built on a platform where creator-led discovery is a default behaviour.

The campaign also has a broader distribution plan across France, Spain, Brazil, and Belgium, supported by a wider comms mix that includes a 30-second trailer, digital and social content, DOOH, CRM, and in-store materials. Each market is expected to tailor amplification locally, including influencer activations, student fairs and events, and partnerships.

For a retailer, that mix matters because it connects the in-game moment to real-world touchpoints. It is not just a “cool map,” it is an attempt to make a brand story travel from Fortnite to feeds to physical stores and then into hiring conversations.

The most interesting part of this move is not that a retailer used Fortnite. It is that Carrefour treated “jobs” as something that can be experienced like content, in the same spaces where culture already spreads.

1. Make the message playable, not readable A list of roles rarely travels on social. A mini-game can. When you turn work into an experience with stakes, timing, and feedback, people understand it faster and remember it longer.

2. Use creator and community behaviour as distribution, not an add-on The plan includes influencer activations and events, but Fortnite itself is already designed for sharing. If your campaign format naturally fits streaming and clips, it reduces the need to force attention later.

3. Treat recruitment as brand storytelling By centering the “food ecosystem” professions, Carrefour positions its commitments and mission through human roles, not just corporate claims. That is often more credible because it shows who does the work.

4. Design one core world, then localise how it travels Carrefour’s approach mixes a consistent international platform with local amplification. That is a practical way to keep the idea coherent while still matching different market habits and channels.

In the long run, this is a signal that employer branding is moving closer to entertainment formats, especially for younger audiences who expect brands to show up where they already spend time. The campaigns that land will be the ones that feel native to the platform’s behaviours, not just visually present inside it.

It also hints at a shifting baseline for “explaining” work. For Gen Z, it can be more intuitive to understand a job through a simulation, creator stream, or shared clip than through a webpage. Brands that can translate complex roles into simple, familiar mechanics will have an advantage in both attention and talent.

evidence.title: Carrefour intensifies its commitment to artificial intelligence
evidence.text:
Carrefour has reached 11 million active members in its loyalty program in Spain, a figure that means the French retailer is present in more than half of the country’s households and reinforces the strategic importance of customer loyalty in its trajectory for the coming years.

The company celebrated this milestone by unveiling its new Club 2030 strategy in Palma, a plan designed to transform its customer program into an ecosystem of services and benefits that goes beyond food distribution. The event took place last Tuesday aboard the Ciudad de Sóller , operated by Trasmed, a Grimaldi Group shipping company, in a gathering that brought together business partners and collaborating companies.

According to the company, the program is currently available in 58% of Spanish households and has become one of the group’s key assets for customer loyalty. Carrefour now aims to expand the reach of this platform through new alliances and greater integration of services linked to everyday shopping .

The Club 2030 strategy envisions expanding the partner network, which currently includes more than 25 companies and which the company aims to double by the end of the decade. The goal is to introduce new benefits in areas such as energy, transportation, travel, leisure, insurance, and financial services.

In this context, Carrefour has announced the renewal of its agreements with Trasmed and Iberdrola, as well as the expansion of customer benefits in collaboration with Moeve. The company also plans to intensify savings initiatives aimed at program members , including specific promotions such as the so-called “Club Day.”

The development of the program reflects a growing trend in the retail sector, where loyalty programs have become key tools for increasing purchase frequency, improving customer understanding, and developing new revenue streams through third-party partnerships.

Artificial intelligence is at the heart of the strategy.

One of the cornerstones of the new plan will be the use of artificial intelligence technologies to personalize the shopping experience and optimize offers tailored to each customer.

The company plans to double the number of personalized interactions with its customers by 2030, using systems capable of tailoring coupons, promotions, and recommendations to individual shopping habits.

As part of this initiative, Carrefour has launched ClubIA , a generative artificial intelligence-powered assistant that will allow users to use natural language to inquire about available promotions, personalized discounts, or information related to their regular purchases.

The tool, which integrates data on the energy consumption of customers who consent, aims to simplify access to the program’s benefits and help customers save money through personalized recommendations based on their individual profiles.

“Customer loyalty is no longer limited to a card or a QR code at checkout. We want to establish a more personalized and conversational relationship with our customers, leveraging the capabilities offered by artificial intelligence,” said Élodie Perthuisot, Managing Director of Carrefour Spain.

evidence.title: Club Carrefour contará con ClubIA, el primer asistente de inteligencia artificial integrado en un programa de fidelización
evidence.text:
Club Carrefour contará con ClubIA, el primer asistente de inteligencia artificial integrado en un programa de fidelización

María Quintín anuncia en el Congreso de la Asociación Española del Retail "Horizonte 2028" la estrategia del Club Carrefour para alcanzar los 12 millones de socios y llegar al 75% de los hogares españoles en 2030.

María Quintín, directora de Comunicación, Club Carrefour y Servicios Comerciales en Carrefour España, ha avanzado en el Congreso AER, celebrado hoy con el título "Horizonte 2028", las principales líneas estratégicas que marcarán la evolución del Club Carrefour hasta 2030, con un objetivo claro: alcanzar los 12 millones de socios y estar presente en el 75% de los hogares españoles.

Actualmente, el programa de fidelización de la compañía ya tiene presencia en más del 58% de los hogares del país y constituye, según Quintín, "la primera razón de visita para nuestros clientes".

Durante su intervención, la directiva desgranó los cuatro grandes pilares sobre los que se asentará la evolución del Club Carrefour en los próximos años: captar más clientes activos y aumentar la frecuencia de visita; ofrecer una propuesta más generosa con mejores precios gracias a acuerdos con proveedores y partners; desarrollar una experiencia más inteligente mediante el uso de inteligencia artificial; y reforzar la dimensión emocional y aspiracional de la relación con los socios.

ClubIA, la asistente IA del Club Carrefour

La gran novedad anunciada por Quintín fue ClubIA , que aspira a convertirse en el primer asistente de inteligencia artificial integrado en un programa de fidelización.

Según explicó, esta herramienta estará diseñada a partir de las necesidades y preferencias de los más de once millones de socios actuales del Club Carrefour y permitirá ofrecer un nivel de hiperpersonalización sin precedentes.

"Va a ser el primer asistente de IA dentro de un club de fidelidad. Ayudará a nuestros socios y tendrá incluso presencia en redes sociales: va a tener su propio mundo", señaló.

La nueva plataforma permitirá evolucionar hacia cupones inteligentes adaptados a los hábitos y experiencias de compra de cada cliente, reforzando así la personalización de las promociones y recomendaciones.

"La inteligencia artificial nos va a ayudar a gestionar nuestros datos y a hacerlo todo más fácil, pero los datos son de los clientes y de nadie más", subrayó Quintín.

Elodie Perthuisot, CEO de Carrefour España, presentó el asistente IA ClubIA en 2025.

La responsable de fidelización de Carrefour destacó también el papel diferencial que juega la gamificación dentro de la estrategia de Carrefour.

"Carrefour y el Club Carrefour son los reyes de la gamificación", afirmó, recordando que se trata del club de fidelización más grande de Europa.

De cara a 2030, la compañía pretende reforzar aún más la conexión emocional con sus socios a través de experiencias exclusivas desarrolladas junto a partners y proveedores nacionales, regionales y locales.

"La parte emocional es la que realmente te va a fidelizar", defendió Quintín.

Asimismo, Carrefour mantendrá programas específicos y ventajas diferenciales para algunos de sus colectivos prioritarios, como los clientes menores de 30 años -"nuestros clientes del futuro"-, las familias numerosas y los mayores de 65 años, a quienes otorgará condiciones especiales.

Con esta hoja de ruta, Carrefour España, con Elodie Perthuisot a la cabeza como gran experta en tecnología y digitalización, busca consolidar el Club Carrefour como uno de los principales activos de su estrategia comercial y avanzar hacia un modelo de fidelización cada vez más personalizado, experiencial y apoyado en la inteligencia artificial.

evidence.title: Carrefour launches Europe’s first AI shopping on ChatGPT
evidence.text:
Carrefour launches Europe’s first AI shopping on ChatGPT

French shoppers can now browse, select, and order groceries directly through ChatGPT

Carrefour has introduced its AI-powered grocery shopping service through ChatGPT, which enables customers to access all their products through a chatbot in their first implementation as a major European retailer.

The service, which launched in France this year, enables users to search and plan and shop through a conversational interface which represents a transition to AI-based retail shopping experiences.

The new feature reflects the growing trend of “AI shopping” and conversational commerce. Consumers can now use ChatGPT to find recipes, check product availability, build shopping baskets and choose delivery options before completing purchases on Carrefour’s platform.

The buying process becomes easier through this method because it matches the new shopping behaviour of consumers who use AI tools for their daily activities. Carrefour uses artificial intelligence technology as its main strategic element for future business development.

Chief Executive Alexandre Bompard showed during the Carrefour 2030 strategy presentation that artificial intelligence creates better operational results and helps companies connect with their customers.

The retailer supported Google, which created the Universal Commerce Protocol as an open standard that enables better communication between AI systems and retail systems. Carrefour plans to create a shopping experience which provides customers with both personalised service and seamless shopping.

evidence.title: Carrefour : le distributeur intègre l’intelligence artificielle de ChatGPT pour les courses en ligne
evidence.text:
Toute l'actualité de votre région en continu sur notre application

Carrefour : le distributeur intègre l’intelligence artificielle de ChatGPT pour les courses en ligne

Le groupe français lance une application sur ChatGPT permettant aux utilisateurs de composer des paniers et de planifier leurs achats via le robot conversationnel d’OpenAI

Carrefour a lancé une application sur ChatGPT permettant de composer des paniers de courses à partir de son offre, une première pour un distributeur alimentaire européen, a annoncé jeudi 26 mars le groupe français qui mise sur l’intelligence artificielle pour gagner des parts de marché.

Deuxième distributeur alimentaire en France, Carrefour a fait son apparition sur le catalogue d’applications de l’outil d’IA générative d’OpenAI, aux côtés d’autres acteurs comme Booking ou encore, le mois dernier, le site français Leboncoin . Les utilisateurs de ChatGPT, une fois connectés à cette appli Carrefour, pourront échanger avec le robot conversationnel « pour obtenir des idées de recettes, vérifier la disponibilité d’un produit en rayon », composer un panier de courses ou encore « choisir un mode de livraison », précise l’enseigne dans un communiqué. En revanche, la commande devra être finalisée et réglée sur Carrefour.fr, où un compte personnel doit être créé.

Le paiement via ChatGPT n’est pas au programme, OpenAI ayant récemment « abandonné » cette fonctionnalité, a précisé Emmanuel Grenier, directeur commerce en ligne, données et transformation numérique du groupe Carrefour. Le distributeur souhaite ainsi « toucher les 26 millions d’utilisateurs de ChatGPT en France et leur proposer une expérience d’achat plus fluide, rapide et personnalisée », assure le groupe.

L’IA est l’un des principaux piliers du plan stratégique dévoilé en février par le PDG de Carrefour, Alexandre Bompard, qui vise 25 % de parts de marché en France en 2030, contre 22 % actuellement selon Kantar Worldpanel. « Partout où on a des contacts clients, on y met de l’intelligence artificielle », résume Emmanuel Grenier, rappelant que Carrefour a lancé dès 2023 sur son site un robot conversationnel (le chatbot Hopla) adossé sur ChatGPT.

Le groupe a également annoncé début 2026 un partenariat majeur avec Google, qui doit permettre à terme aux clients de faire leurs courses via l’agent IA de ce groupe (Gemini). Selon une étude Odoxa pour la Fédération de l’e-commerce (Fevad) dévoilée en février, un tiers des « cyberacheteurs » français utilisent l’IA lors d’achats en ligne.

Tesco has announced a multi-year deal with WSL Football to become the official supermarket partner of the Barclays Women’s Super League and Barclays Women’s Super League 2.

This business partnership aims to drive more visibility of the free fruit & veg for schools programme and improve access to healthy food for children.

evidence.title: WSL Football partner with Tesco
evidence.text:
With the start of the new season, WSL Football have agreed a new multi-year deal with Tesco, Britain’s favourite supermarket*, to become the Official Supermarket Partner of the Barclays Women’s Super League and Barclays Women’s Super League 2.

The partnership has a common goal of making healthy eating more accessible to children through the Tesco Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme, as well as encouraging more people to attend and engage with the Barclays WSL and Barclays WSL2.

Tesco's Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme helps schools provide children with access to free fruit and vegetables during the school day, supporting healthy eating habits from an early age. Tesco has set an ambition to help one million children access free fruit and veg through its school and community programmes, with this partnership providing a new platform to grow awareness, participation and impact.

Every fan matters in this partnership. Every attendance at a Barclays WSL and Barclays WSL2 match this season will contribute towards a donation from WSL Football to Tesco’s Fruit & Veg for Schools programme**. The bigger the crowds, the bigger the impact.

By combining WSL Football's ambition to grow match attendance and engage more fans with supporting Tesco’s ambition to support schools and community programmes, the partnership will help drive greater awareness of the Free Fruit & Veg for Schools programme and improve access to healthy food in schools to help build lifelong healthy eating habits and deliver meaningful benefits for communities across the country. Additionally, Tesco will bring its product development, supplier base and nutritional expertise to support WSL Football with its Health and Nutrition agenda.

This partnership with Tesco reinforces the positive momentum around women’s football and adds to WSL Football’s world-leading roster of partners who share the collective ambition to create positive impact both on and beyond the pitch.

Suzanne Quinn, Customer Director, Tesco, said:

“We’re very excited to partner with the WSL Football to help support our Free Fruit and Veg for Schools programme, while driving attendance at matches this season. We’re committed to supporting the health of communities around the country, and we know that keeping active and making healthier choices are fundamental to this mission. We’ve set an ambition to help one million children access free fruit and veg through our school and community programmes, and this partnership is a brilliant opportunity to raise awareness of that work through the growing popularity of women’s football.

“It is such an exciting time for the game, and we’re proud to collaborate with WSL Football to not only support the women’s football, but also inspire the next generation of players and fans.”

Zarah Al-Kudcy, Chief Revenue Officer, WSL Football, says:

“We are thrilled that our final Official Partner is one of the most recognisable names in the country. Tesco's decision to come on board is a real endorsement of the direction of travel and a testament to the momentum behind the women’s game.

A key priority for WSL Football and our clubs is driving attendance, and this unique collaboration with Tesco offers real mutual benefit. From working with local communities and schools to ensure more children are making healthier choices to unlocking a partnership which will benefit the health and nutrition of our players.

The partnerships we have built are helping to transform women’s football, and we hope this partnership can go some way towards transforming society too, by helping to build healthy habits for children across the country.”

evidence.title: Lidl owner joins race for Tesco’s Central European business
evidence.text:
Lidl owner joins race for Tesco’s Central European business

Lidl owner Schwarz Group is among a string of grocery giants circling Tesco’s Central European operations as it pushes ahead with a potential exit from the region.

The German retail group, which owns both Lidl and Kaufland, is expected to make an offer for Tesco’s Czech and Slovakian businesses.

Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Albert supermarket chain in the Czech Republic, and Biedronka, owned by Portuguese retail giant Jerónimo Martins, have also been linked to the sale process.

Tesco is understood to be planning to sell its Czech and Slovak operations separately from its Hungarian business, with initial bids expected by the end of September.

It is working with Goldman Sachs and Citi on the potential disposal. Tesco, Schwarz Group and the other prospective bidders have declined to comment on the process.

Retail Gazette reported in July that Tesco was exploring a sale of the division, which represents its only sizeable operation outside the UK and Ireland.

The grocer operates 561 stores across the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia and employs more than 22,000 people in the region.

Its Central European arm generated £4.49bn in sales during its 2025/26 financial year, up 3.7 per cent at constant exchange rates, although adjusted operating profit slipped 0.9 per cent to £115m.

The division contributed less than four per cent of Tesco’s £3.15bn group adjusted operating profit during the year.

A sale would mark the latest step in Tesco’s long-running retreat from international markets as it concentrates investment on its core UK and Ireland operations.

It has disposed of the bulk of its overseas empire over the past decade, including its businesses in South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia.

Tesco has instead ramped up investment in its home market under chief executive Ken Murphy, focusing on price, loyalty through Clubcard and its store estate as it battles traditional rivals and discounters including Aldi and Lidl.

Aldi and Sainsbury's cut Quality Street and Heroes prices

The great Christmas chocolate price war has begun, with Aldi cutting the price of Quality Street 500g and Cadbury Heroes 475g to £3.85 a tub.

That makes Aldi's tubs the cheapest on the market, according to the supermarket, as shoppers begin stocking up for Christmas.

And the timing could hardly be earlier, with festive food shoppers already looking for ways to spread the cost of Christmas. But Aldi isn't the only supermarket making a move.

Sainsbury's cuts price of Quality Street and Cadbury Heroes

Sainsbury's is currently selling its 550g Quality Street tub for £3.95, meaning Aldi's 500g tub is just 10p cheaper despite containing 50g less chocolate.

Sainsbury's is also offering Cadbury Heroes for £4.95 to Nectar card holders, putting Aldi's 475g tub £1.10 cheaper.

For shoppers stocking up on several tubs, the difference could quickly add up.

The race is on for the big Christmas supermarket shop

Aldi's latest move means the annual Christmas chocolate price race is already gathering pace, with supermarkets competing to tempt shoppers with some of the most recognisable tubs of the festive season.

The £3.85 price is available from today, giving early Christmas shoppers the chance to get their chocolate stash sorted before the festive rush.

And for families planning ahead, buying a few Christmas favourites now could also help spread the cost of the big day rather than leaving the entire food bill until December.

With Quality Street and Heroes among the traditional Christmas favourites, the latest reductions could be just the beginning of the supermarket battle over festive chocolate prices.

The big question now is whether other supermarkets will follow Aldi's £3.85 move - and who will eat the last of the strawberry and orange creams?

evidence.title: M&S, New Look, Sainsbury's and Oxfam Join Forces to Boost the UK’s Circular Textile Economy
evidence.text:
M&S, New Look, Sainsbury's and Oxfam Join Forces to Boost the UK’s Circular Textile Economy

New Look, M&S, Sainsbury’s, Oxfam and Circle-8 today announce The Circuit, a new collaborative model bringing together retailers, textile recovery partners, automated sorting, recyclers, digital innovators and manufacturers to help build new circular textile value chains and transform UK generated post-consumer textiles into future circular raw materials. The first phase of the initiative will focus on testing, learning and developing the operational frameworks needed to support future scale-up.

In 2024, approximately 1.4 million tonnes of post-consumer textiles were generated across the UK, reinforcing the need for greater investment in the infrastructure required to recover, reuse and recycle valuable textile resources. It’s estimated nearly half of this is made up of non-reusable textiles , highlighting the need for new solutions to recover and recycle textiles at scale. Demand for recycled textile materials is growing, but the systems needed to create them from post-consumer textiles are still emerging. The Circuit has been established to close that gap.

The Circuit is designed to create new pathways through which UK generated non-reusable end-of-use textiles can be recovered, sorted and pre-processed into input materials for the existing and emerging fibre to fibre recycling industry. By bringing together organisations from across the value chain, The Circuit aims to create the scale, consistency and commercial conditions needed accelerate future textile to textile recycling viability. The initiative also supports the broader UK economy by enabling job creation and manufacturing. Automated sorting and pre-processing, close to the source of where textiles that have reached end of use are generated and turned into feedstock for regional and global supply chains.

The partnership supports the development of both mechanical and chemical recycling processes capable of transforming UK generated post-consumer textiles into raw materials for regional and global textile manufacturing. By creating multiple routes to market and products for recovered materials, participating retailers will help shape the value chains that support future circular materials.

Circle-8, the development company behind The Circuit, is developing the infrastructure, partnerships and commercial frameworks required to connect post-consumer textile recovery with future circular material supply. This includes the development of Automated Textile Sorting and Pre-processing facilities, which create feedstock for existing and emerging textile recyclers.

The first phase of The Circuit will begin in January 2027, bringing together retailers and partners at Oxfam’s site in Batley, Yorkshire. The initial phase will focus on automated textile sorting, combined with developing reporting frameworks to improve traceability, identifying circular material opportunities, building relationships with recyclers and exploring operational models that could support further scaling of the initiative. Oxfam will play a crucial role in separating the reusable and non-reusable textiles and operating the automated textile sorting equipment, building on its longstanding expertise in textile recovery and reuse.

Lynda Petherick, Chief Executive Officer at New Look, said: “Building a more circular fashion industry requires collaboration right across the value chain. The Circuit gives retailers an opportunity to play an active role in developing the systems that could turn non-reusable textiles already in circulation into the raw materials of the future. For New Look, this is about looking at how we can help create more resilient, circular supply chains over the longer term. We’re pleased to be part of The Circuit, to help demonstrate what can be achieved at scale.”

Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability & Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S, said: "At M&S, we believe the most sustainable clothing is clothing that is worn and loved for longer. Through Plan A for Another Life, we have an ambition to give 5 million items Another Life by 2030 through rewear, repair, resale and recycling. However, when textiles reach the end of their usable life, we need better solutions to recover and recycle the materials they contain. The Circuit is an important step forward, bringing together organisations from across the retail industry to help create viable routes for non-reusable textiles and support a more circular future for fashion.”

Ben Smith, Managing Director of Sainsbury's Tu Clothing, said: "Creating a more circular future for textiles will take collaboration and innovation across the whole industry. The Circuit is an exciting opportunity to work alongside partners from across the value chain to explore how post-consumer textiles generated here in the UK can be given a new life as valuable raw materials. For Tu at Sainsbury's, it's about learning, testing practical solutions and helping shape a more circular textiles economy for the future."

Rachel Cosgrove-Pearce, Retail Director at Oxfam, said: “Oxfam has been giving clothes a second life for almost 80 years, and our experience tells us that keeping clothing in use for as long as possible is one of the most effective ways to reduce fashion’s impact on our planet. But we also urgently need better solutions for textiles that can no longer be worn or reused. Developing the infrastructure to recover valuable fibres from end-of-use textiles is an important part of building a fashion system that uses fewer virgin resources and creates less environmental harm, and The Circuit brings together the expertise and investment needed to move this forward at scale. We’re proud to be playing our part, building on Oxfam’s long history of textile recovery and our work at Batley.”

Cyndi Rhoades, CEO and Co-Founder of Circle-8 Textile Ecosystems said: The retailers who help build circular textile value chains today will be best positioned to influence and benefit from them tomorrow. Through The Circuit, we’re powering the relationships, infrastructure and commercial frameworks needed to make that possible. No one organisation can create a circular textile value chain alone, and we look forward to welcoming others to The Circuit.

1 [WRAP Textiles Market Situation Report 2024]

All press enquiries to [email protected] and [email protected]

Borne as a follow on from the Innovate UK funded ACT project, The Circuit is a collaborative initiative designed to build circular textile value chains from UK-generated post-consumer textiles. It brings together retailers, textile recovery partners, automated sorting, recyclers, digital innovators and manufacturers to create pathways through which end-of-use textiles can be transformed into future raw materials. The Circuit aims to create the scale, infrastructure and commercial conditions needed to support circular material production and fibre-to-fibre recycling.

Founding participants in The Circuit include: M&S, New Look, Sainsbury's, Oxfam and Circle-8. Development Partners: Biffa and Ekman Group; Recycling Partners: Usha Yarns, Kipas, Reju and Worn Again Technologies. The Circuit’s first wave of partners welcome wider industry participation from other retailers, recyclers and value chain partners.

New Look is a leading fashion retailer operating in the clothing and footwear market in the UK, with a strong online presence. New Look offers products, and a shopping experience based on excitement, value and newness. The New Look brand is distinct and trusted in the UK, catering to a broad customer audience. New Look ranked No. 2 for overall Womenswear market share in the 18 to 44 age range.

Marks & Spencer (“M&S”) is a leading British retailer with a presence across the UK and more than 70 international markets. M&S serves 32 million customers every year with exceptional quality products at value they can trust. Behind M&S is over 60,000 colleagues who bring passion and expertise to everything they do.

For more than 140 years, M&S has built trust by doing the right thing by its colleagues, customers and the communities. Underpinning this commitment is Plan A – M&S’ sustainability programme – a promise to always source and make products with care. Plan A is also an integral enabler of M&S’ strategy to reshape for sustainable, profitable growth and to become a net zero business across its value chain by 2040.

Tu has been inspiring fashion confidence since its launch in 2004, offering design-led, excellent quality and great value fashion across womenswear, menswear and childrenswear. Tu helps customers fulfil their clothing missions every day by offering everything from a broad range of lingerie, lounge and nightwear, the latest denim fits alongside key fashion pieces, everyday essentials and school wear. Tu also offers a range of specialist sizes with its own brand Petites and Maternity offers, as well as working with selected partners to keep the whole family's wardrobe updated with fashion that makes you feel good. Tu clothing is available to buy online at Tu and Argos as well as in over 400 selected Sainsbury's stores.

Oxfam is a global community of people who believe in a kinder, and radically better world, where everyone has the power to thrive not just survive. Oxfam has more than 500 shops across the UK and by buying and donating through Oxfam shops, people can help to protect our planet, while helping raise life-saving money to tackle poverty around the globe.

Circle-8 has developed The Circuit to power the partnerships and infrastructure needed to create future circular textile value chains, with UK-generated end of use textiles as the source. Through The Circuit, retailers drive the recovery, sorting and recycling systems that transform end-of-use textiles into future raw materials for regional and global manufacturing. Alongside the development of Automated Textile Sorting and Pre-processing Facilities (ATSPs), Circle-8 is creating commercial frameworks and networks that connect textile recovery with future circular material supply, thereby establishing the next generation of transparent, traceable and scalable textile value chains.

​​​Sainsbury's full-year earnings preview: what to watch as the supermarket reports amid economic headwinds​​​

​​Sainsbury's will release its full-year 2024-25 results on 17 April, with analysts expecting EPS of 11.9p for Q4 amid challenging economic conditions.​

Sainsbury's full-year 2024-25 earnings expectations

J Sainsbury ​ is set to release its preliminary full-year results for the fiscal year 2024-25 on Thursday, 17 April 2025. The UK's second-largest supermarket chain will be reporting at a time of continued economic uncertainty for British retailers and consumers alike amid US President Trump’s ever shifting tariff policy.

​Analysts anticipate an earnings per share (EPS) of 11.76p for the fourth quarter (Q4), up from 11.3p in the same period last year. This modest growth reflects the company's resilience despite ongoing cost pressures affecting the retail sector as a whole.

​The company has maintained its guidance for underlying retail operating profit between £1.01 billion and £1.06 billion, representing a 5-10% year-over-year (YoY) increase. This guidance suggests management confidence in their ability to navigate the challenging economic landscape.

​Market participants using online trading platforms will be closely watching whether Sainsbury's can meet or exceed these expectations, as the results could trigger significant share price movements in either direction. The grocery sector remains highly competitive, with thin margins and constant pressure to deliver value to consumers.

Sainsbury's recent performance highlights

​In the first half of the fiscal year, Sainsbury's reported an encouraging 5% increase in food sales, boosting its market share to 15.2%. This growth trajectory in its core business has been a bright spot amid broader retail challenges.

​The success has been driven largely by the popularity of its premium Taste the Difference range, which has resonated with consumers seeking affordable luxury during economically constrained times. The company has also seen an increased number of customers opting to shop at Sainsbury's, suggesting effective customer acquisition strategies.

​However, the Argos division has faced significant headwinds, with a 5% decline in sales due to tough market conditions and weaker demand for big-ticket items. This performance disparity highlights the two-speed nature of UK retail, with non-food items suffering as consumers prioritise essentials.

​For investors considering whether to buy shares , these contrasting performances within Sainsbury's business divisions will be a key consideration. The company's ability to manage this internal divergence while maintaining overall growth will be scrutinised in the upcoming results.

​Strategic initiatives and cost management

​The company has focused on investing in its product range and pricing strategies to attract and retain customers in a fiercely competitive grocery market. One of the most notable initiatives has been the Aldi price-match programme, designed to combat the continued threat from discount retailers.

​Sainsbury's has also introduced 600 new products in its convenience stores, recognising the growing importance of this format as shopping habits evolve. This expansion demonstrates a commitment to meeting customers where they are and adapting to changing consumer preferences.

​On the cost front, Sainsbury's has announced ambitious plans to cut £1 billion in structural costs over the next three years. This aggressive target underscores the pressure on margins across the retail sector and the necessity of operational efficiency to maintain profitability.

​The company is additionally aiming for £500 million in retail free cash flow for the year, which would provide valuable financial flexibility for future investments or shareholder returns.

​Investors using trading platforms will be monitoring whether these targets remain on track in the full-year announcement.

​Despite strong performance in the grocery segment, Sainsbury's faces significant economic headwinds that could impact future growth. One immediate challenge is a £140 million increase in its tax bill following changes in national insurance contributions implemented in the latest budget.

​These additional costs are expected to impact profit margins and may ultimately lead to higher prices for consumers at a time when affordability remains a key concern. The company's approach to absorbing or passing on these costs will be watched closely by market analysts.

​Broader inflationary pressures, while moderating, continue to affect both operational costs and consumer spending power. Sainsbury's ability to manage its supply chain and procurement strategies efficiently will be crucial in maintaining competitiveness.

​The uncertain UK economic outlook for 2025-26 presents another layer of complexity for Sainsbury's strategic planning. With consumer confidence remaining fragile, the company must balance value offerings with the need to protect margins – a delicate equilibrium that few retailers have mastered.

​Competitive landscape and market position

​Sainsbury's continues to operate in one of the UK's most competitive retail environments, with traditional rivals Tesco, Asda and Morrisons all pursuing aggressive growth strategies. The ongoing expansion of discounters Aldi and Lidl further intensifies the battle for market share.

​The company's current market share of 15.2%, up from 14.6% reported in 2024, represents a modest gain, but maintaining this position requires continuous investment in both price competitiveness and shopping experience. Any commentary on market share trends in the full-year results will be closely scrutinised.

​Online grocery shopping remains a key battleground, with Sainsbury's competing not only with traditional rivals but also with pure-play online retailers and rapid delivery services. The company's digital performance metrics will be an important indicator of future competitiveness.

​For investors using trading signals to guide their decisions, understanding Sainsbury's competitive positioning relative to peers will be essential for assessing the stock's prospects beyond the immediate reaction to the results.

​Investor sentiment and analyst perspectives

​Analysts have expressed cautious optimism about Sainsbury's resilience in the current economic climate, with the company's focus on value and customer satisfaction contributing to its market share gains. However, sentiment remains mixed given the challenging operating environment.

​The Sainsbury share price has experienced volatility in recent months, reflecting broader uncertainty in the UK retail sector. Current analyst recommendations span the spectrum from 'buy' to 'hold', indicating diverse perspectives on the company's near-term prospects.

​According to LSEG Data & analytics, 2 analysts have a ‘strong buy’ recommendation on Sainsbury’s, 6 a ‘buy’, 3 a ‘hold’ and 2 a ‘sell’ recommendation (as of 15/04/2025).

​Sainsbury has a TipRanks Smart Score of ’6 Neutral’ and is rated as a ‘buy’ by analysts with 4 ’buy’, 1 ‘hold’ and 1 ‘sell’ recommendation (as of 15/04/2025).

​Technical analysis on Sainsbury’s share price

​The Sainsbury’s share price, down 12% year-to-date, is trying to recover from its 223.40 pence four-month low.

​For the bulls to be back in control, a rise and daily chart close above the 200-day simple moving average (SMA) and last Monday’s high at 260.3p-to-264.8p needs to be seen.

​Even in such a scenario, further range trading in the 310p-to-240p zone may then be witnessed, as has been the case since January 2023.

​Were last week’s low at 223.4p to give way, though, the June 2016 low at 211.6p would be back in the firing line.

​Current yield projections of around 5.5%, versus 3.9% for the broader market average, place Sainsbury's among the more attractive dividend payers in the FTSE 100.

​Investors considering share investing in Sainsbury's will be watching not just the financial results but also management's tone and forward guidance. Any signs of confidence or caution regarding the coming fiscal year could significantly influence market sentiment.

​Beyond the headline financial figures, several key metrics will deserve investor attention in the full-year results. Like-for-like sales growth remains the primary performance indicator, with food and non-food comparatives providing insight into divisional strengths and weaknesses.

​Gross margin performance will be particularly important given the inflationary pressures and competitive pricing environment. Any erosion in margins could signal difficulties in passing increased costs to consumers without losing volume.

​Cash generation and balance sheet strength will also be scrutinised, especially given the company's ambitious cost-cutting targets. Strong cash flow would provide reassurance about Sainsbury's ability to weather continued economic uncertainty while investing for growth.

​The performance of newer initiatives, including the expanded convenience store product range and digital services, will offer clues about future growth drivers. Success in these areas could partially offset challenges in more mature segments of the business.

evidence.title: Marks & Spencer, New Look and Sainsbury’s join Oxfam to build UK textile recycling network
evidence.text:
British retail giants Marks & Spencer, New Look and Sainsbury’s have joined UK charity Oxfam in partnering with textile development company Circle-8 to launch The Circuit, an initiative designed to develop circular textile supply chains using clothing collected in the UK.

The initiative brings together retailers, textile recovery organisations, automated sorting specialists, recyclers, manufacturers and digital innovators to develop routes for end-of-use textiles to be recovered and converted into raw materials for future textile production.

Around 1.4 million tonnes of post-consumer textiles were generated across the UK in 2024, according to an associated report, with almost half estimated to be non-reusable. The Circuit is intended to address the infrastructure gap around these textiles and help develop the commercial conditions needed to make fibre-to-fibre recycling viable at industrial scale.

Rachel Cosgrove-Pearce, retail director at Oxfam, stated: “Developing the infrastructure to recover valuable fibres from end-of-use textiles is an important part of building a fashion system that uses fewer virgin resources and creates less environmental harm, and The Circuit brings together the expertise and investment needed to move this forward at scale.”

Circle-8, the development company behind the project, is working on the infrastructure, partnerships and commercial frameworks required to connect textile recovery with future recycled material supply. This includes Automated Textile Sorting and Pre-Processing facilities, which will sort and prepare recovered textiles for existing and emerging recycling technologies.

The first phase of The Circuit will begin in January 2027 at Oxfam’s site in Batley, Yorkshire, and will focus on automated textile sorting, developing reporting and traceability frameworks, identifying opportunities for recovered materials and establishing relationships with recycling partners, supporting both mechanical and chemical recycling processes.

The founding participants are inviting further retailers, recyclers and value-chain partners to join the initiative as it develops. Development partners include Biffa and Ekman Group, while recycling partners include Usha Yarns, Kipas, Reju and Worn Again Technologies.

In a statement, Katharine Beacham, Marks & Spencer's head of sustainability & materials in fashion, home and beauty, said the retailer needs “better solutions to recover and recycle the materials” in clothing once it reaches the end of its usable life.

“The Circuit is an important step forward, bringing together organisations from across the retail industry to help create viable routes for non-reusable textiles and support a more circular future for fashion,” she added.

Sainsbury’s Tu Clothing managing director Ben Smith commented that the project would allow the retailer to “explore how post-consumer textiles generated here in the UK can be given a new life as valuable raw materials”.

Circle-8 CEO and co-founder Cyndi Rhoades said retailers involved in developing circular textile value chains would be positioned to influence their future development, before adding: “No one organisation can create a circular textile value chain alone, and we look forward to welcoming others to The Circuit."

evidence.title: Levi Strauss & Co. and Marks & Spencer launch the Fashion Renewable Collaborative to turn climate commitments into renewable electricity action
evidence.text:
Levi Strauss & Co. and Marks & Spencer launch the Fashion Renewable Collaborative to turn climate commitments into renewable electricity action

Posted by Editorial Team | Sep 25, 2026 | Global

Levi Strauss & Co. and Marks & Spencer (M&S), in partnership with SE Advisory Services, Schneider Electric’s global consulting practice, today launched the Fashion Renewable Collaborative (“FRC”) and are inviting fashion brands across the industry to join the effort. Announced at New York Climate Week, the FRC is designed to help interested suppliers adopt renewable electricity at scale through coordinated brand engagement and practical implementation support. By modeling a shared approach to supplier engagement, the collaborative aims to facilitate renewable electricity adoption across global fashion supply chains and help manufacturers understand, access and implement renewable electricity solutions at scale.

The launch comes as fashion brands seek new ways to translate their individual climate commitments into measurable, durable emissions reductions across complex global supply chains. While many companies have established ambitious climate goals, supplier adoption of renewable electricity remains a critical challenge due to market barriers, limited resources, fragmented engagement efforts, and differing requests from multiple customers. The opportunity is significant: textile processing, the fabric mills and dye houses at the heart of global fashion supply chains, accounts for more than half of the apparel industry’s emissions, according to the Apparel Impact Institute, making supplier adoption of renewable electricity one of the fastest and most scalable paths to progress.

The FRC was established to address this challenge through a comprehensive framework that can reduce the burden on interested suppliers while accelerating impact across the fashion industry. According to the Roadmap to Net Zero from the World Resources Institute and the Apparel Impact Institute, shifting manufacturing to renewable electricity is the single largest decarbonization lever, representing roughly two-thirds of the sector’s identified emissions-reduction potential.

Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability and Materials in Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S, said: “At M&S, we know that real change happens when we collaborate. Through our sustainability programme, Plan A, we’re committed to becoming a net zero business across our value chain by 2040, and that means working with others to make the transition to renewable electricity easier for our supply partners. Building on the work already underway through Re:Spark, our supply chain decarbonisation programme, the Fashion Renewable Collaborative will provide practical support, resources and greater access to renewable electricity, helping suppliers take action and facilitating change in the fashion supply chain.”

The FRC is one of the first fashion industry initiatives focused on providing real renewable electricity solutions. Unlike programs primarily focused on commitments or a roadmap, the FRC gives suppliers the opportunity to access the tools, knowledge and support to accelerate their energy transition. This includes digital education, powered by Resource Advisor+, SE Advisory Services AI-native energy and sustainability intelligence platform, market guidance, and significant support in assessing and procuring renewable electricity.

The FRC is built around a structured implementation model that helps suppliers first learn and then execute through digital education modules. Participating brands benefit from a common approach, while suppliers gain access to support designed to reduce complexity and improve access to credible renewable electricity solutions, including power purchase agreements (PPAs), energy attribute certificates (EACs), on-site and distributed renewable generation, energy storage, and other proven procurement and deployment pathways.

At New York Climate Week and beyond, the Fashion Renewable Collaborative is inviting additional fashion brands to join as sponsors and members to broaden the reach and impact of renewable electricity education, resources, and support among participating suppliers.

“It’s become abundantly clear that the most effective way forward on emissions reduction is working in partnership with suppliers,” said Jennifer DuBuisson, Senior Director, Sustainability, Levi Strauss & Co. “Initiatives like this create better working relationships and a more effective path forward. The Fashion Renewable Collaborative enables greater support of suppliers that want to access or would like to increase use of renewable electricity but haven’t been able to so far, helping facilitate adoption while reducing unnecessary duplication. It’s a natural extension of work we’ve already been doing with our own suppliers, and we’re glad to bring that experience into this effort with M&S and SE Advisory Services.”

The FRC initiative builds on successful engagement efforts already underway. Together, the two programs registered nearly 500 supplier facilities, demonstrating growing interest among suppliers seeking practical pathways to decarbonization.

The FRC is supported by SE Advisory Services, which will serve as the program’s global implementation partner. Schneider Electric brings extensive experience in designing and managing large-scale supply chain decarbonization programs, including more than 20 active initiatives globally involving over 3,100 supplier companies and 16 multi-buyer renewable energy cohorts. As a global energy technology leader, Schneider Electric combines deep energy markets expertise, digital platforms, and on-the-ground implementation support to help suppliers move from commitment to execution.

“Many fashion brands have made their individual commitments. Now the focus must be on helping suppliers deliver against them,” said Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President, SE Advisory Services. “The Fashion Renewable Collaborative is designed to provide suppliers with practical support and engagement that can help accelerate renewable electricity adoption at scale. We’re excited to support Levi Strauss & Co. and M&S, and future participating brands as they work together to drive meaningful supply chain decarbonization.”

The FRC will leverage SE Advisory Services’ Resource Advisor+ for Supply Chain product to support supplier onboarding, engagement tracking, readiness assessments, and progress monitoring. Together, these capabilities help create a consistent, digitally scalable experience for both brands and suppliers.

By participating, brands can directly support suppliers’ ability and desire to adopt renewable electricity while reducing supplier fatigue, expand renewable electricity access, and helping brands achieve their individual supply chain decarbonization goals.

evidence.title: Marks & Spencer Fall 2026: Let the Games Begin
evidence.text:
After decades of lagging behind the high-street fashion giants, Marks & Spencer has stepped into its power, staging a slick see-now, buy-now fashion show at the Design Museum during the London Fashion Week spring 2027 showcase.

The food-to-fashion retailer, which has nearly 400 stores and 50 websites around the world, used the show to mark its 100-year anniversary in the clothing business and its push into international markets. Earlier this year it began selling at Nordstrom stores, and online, in the U.S., and has partnered with Zalando in Europe.

Who knew the retailer best known for its cotton knickers, and cozy thermal underwear, could behave like a fashion brand? It tapped Erin O'Connor, Lara Stone, Jodie Kidd and Karen Elson to walk in the show and dressed them in sleek black tuxedos and herringbone suits, embroidered kimono jackets, va-va-voom V-neck sweaters and fluid, wide-leg corduroy trousers.

It had a gilded front row to match its ambitions: Joan Collins, Zandra Rhodes, Katherine Jenkins, David Gandy and Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch, a stylish politician who could well be Britain's next prime minister.

They watched as models swished by in kilts and kitten heels, houndstooth puffers, shearling coats and knee-high leather boots, and straight after the show they could buy it all online and at 10 flagship stores across the country.

The store wants to compete on a price level with the fast-fashion retailers, too. Some 50 percent of the new-season collection is 50 pounds or under, which during a cost-of-living crisis here counts for much.

And while this show may be the first, it won't be the last. A source told WWD that M&S plans to be a regular fixture on the London Fashion Week calendar going forward. It's not just about knickers anymore.

evidence.title: Marks & Spencer Adds Automated Fulfillment Hub Amid Push to Double Online Fashion Sales
evidence.text:
Marks & Spencer (M&S) has acquired a warehouse from fellow U.K. retailer Asos as the department store seeks to double its online fashion business.

The fully automated 437,000-square-foot logistics hub in Lichfield, U.K. is expected to become operational by 2027. The warehouse is expected to employ 600 people, according to a company press release.

M&S acquired the space for 67.5 million pounds ($91 million), which is designed to add capacity across the retailer’s distribution network and process orders more quickly to serve customers faster. The company said the warehouse will enable customers to order items online later in the day, while making more sizes and styles available. Related Stories Industry News Levi's, M&S Join Forces on Supplier Renewable Energy Industry News AutoScheduler.AI Platform Orchestrates All Functions in a Warehouse

“We’ve always said that we’ll deliver our transformation with highly disciplined capital investment, always mindful of spending shareholder money wisely,” said John Lyttle, managing director for fashion, home and beauty at M&S. “This acquisition does just that, delivering tangible business benefits that move our transformation forward, at a much lower cost compared to a new build option.”

According to M&S, supply chain transformation is a strategic priority for the retailer as it reshapes for growth, with shortening the time it takes for product to move from supplier to distribution center and then into stores or customers is a key focus. The company consider the move as another lever to pull to drive online growth and improve profit margin in the long term.

The warehouse acquisition complements M&S’ three-year, 120-million-pound ($160 million) investment in automation to increase capacity and reduce complexity across its supply chain that began last year.

That is part of a much wider overhaul, in which M&S is spending 600 million to 650 million pounds ($806 million to $873 million) on capital investment in the 2025-26 fiscal year of which between 200 million and 250 million ($269 million to $336 million) is being invested in technology infrastructure, store maintenance and upgrades to its logistics fleet.

Marks & Spencer has five non-grocery national distribution centers across England, with the company investing in robotics technology designed to speed up sorting “click-and-collect” parcels. The technology has helped extend cut-off times for next-day delivery to nearly midnight.

Further investments at the 900,000-square-foot Central Donington site and another in Bradford will increase the company’s boxed storage capacity by more than 30 percent.

Last November, at its annual shareholder meeting, the retailer unveiled a goal to double online fashion sales over 2025 numbers to roughly 2.8 billion pounds ($3.8 billion) with the help of its automation push.

In its third quarter, M&S saw sales in its fashion, home and beauty segment contract 2.5 percent year over year to roughly 1.3 billion pounds ($1.7 billion). On a comparable store basis, sales declined 2.9 percent.

The unit is the second largest across all Marks & Spencer segments, covering 25.5 percent of sales at the wider business as of the company’s third quarter. The M&S grocery unit is its largest revenue driver, generating 2.7 billion pounds ($3.7 billion) in the three-month period, or 54.5 percent of total sales.

As M&S seeks to expand its supply chain square footage, former owner Asos has taken the opposite approach in recent years to strengthen its balance sheet and cut costs.

The fast-fashion retailer began to sunset the facility in late 2023, with the company saying that over the past three years, improvements in stock turn and the launch of its Asos Fulfillment Services (AFS) in the 2025 fiscal second half have resulted in lower capacity requirements.

“The disposal of our Lichfield fulfillment center represents a further step in strengthening Asos’s balance sheet and improving our capital efficiency,” said Jose Antonio Ramos, CEO of Asos in a statement. “This transaction enables us to unlock value from one of our non-core assets while reducing our ongoing cost base, consistent with the actions we have taken over the past three years to simplify the business and enhance financial resilience. Asos is a well-invested business and we have significant capacity to support future growth. We will continue to maintain a disciplined approach to capital allocation as we execute our strategy.”

In the absence of the Lichfield location, Asos says its two other U.K.-based fulfillment centers in Barnsley and Berlin provide sufficient capacity to support future growth.

Asos also closed an Atlanta-area distribution center in the U.S. in January last year, opting to serve American customers via the automated Barnsley fulfillment center . The closure was expected to cost the fashion seller roughly 190 million pounds ($256 million) in one-off expenses, before freeing up 20 million pounds ($27 million) in cash flow for the 2026 fiscal year.

evidence.title: Kingfisher Dojo #001
evidence.text:
On Yumeume Koume's note, I have written three series so far. The photography journal "Chasing the Blue Flash." The "Talk About Gear" series, where I write about the equipment I actually use. And the "Kingfisher Photo Gallery," where I share the wild birds I've photographed. One of those, "Chasing the Blue Flash," recently came to a conclusion. Now, the Wednesday and Saturday slots have opened up lol So— I'm starting a new series. Its name is,

You want to photograph kingfishers, right?

The fact that you're reading this article means... You want to photograph kingfishers, right? lol Kingfisher photos that pop up when you look at Instagram or X. The moment they spread their blue wings and dive into the water. The moment they emerge with a fish, along with a splash. Things like this.

You've started wanting to take them, haven't you? lol If so— let's take them. That longed-for shot of a kingfisher at the water's edge.

In this "Kingfisher Dojo," I intend to explain things step-by-step for those who want to try photographing kingfishers, from the very beginning to completing a single photo. What kind of bird is a kingfisher? Where are they? What kind of equipment is needed? How should the camera be set? How do you photograph a dive? How can you increase your success rate even a little? And once you've successfully taken the shot, we'll do some simple RAW development to finish it into a single photo. Finally, we'll post the finished photo to Instagram or X. Let's do all of that together. I'm planning for about 10 episodes in total. In theory, anyway lol Even before I start writing, I don't really feel like it's going to end in 10 episodes lolol Well, let's think about that as we go 🤣 What I want to aim for in this dojo is not to master everything about kingfisher photography. First, I want to try photographing a kingfisher. Starting from there, I did it, I photographed a kingfisher! reaching that point. I'll leave out the difficult parts as much as possible and move forward one step at a time.

I'd like to get straight to the shooting methods... but before that, there is one thing I want to talk about first in this dojo. That is, to cherish the shooting location. I feel this strongly while photographing kingfishers, but kingfishers themselves are surprisingly present in familiar bodies of water. Rivers, ponds, and waterways. When you look for them, you might think, Oh, they're even in a place like this. However, the place where a kingfisher lives and the place where it is easy to photograph a kingfisher are not the same thing. If the body of water is too large, it's hard to tell where they will dive. Photos are easier to take in places where bright sunlight enters rather than in places that are dark all day. Added to that are the distance to the kingfisher, your standing position, the background, and so on. When you think about it that way, the places where kingfishers are present and where it is also easy to take photos are surprisingly limited. That is exactly why. If you find a good spot, I want you to cherish it.

Even if you find one, don't easily spread the word

You found a kingfisher yourself. That's happy, isn't it? lol But even so, I don't recommend easily spreading the word about the shooting location. When I post photos to SNS, I am careful about information that could identify the location. When I'm shooting in places like parks, people often ask me, "What are you photographing?" Even then, I usually say, "I came here hoping there might be a kingfisher... it's quite difficult, though lol" I usually brush it off like that. It's not that I'm being mean and keeping it a secret. Even without malice, if people know a kingfisher is there, the number of people coming to see it may increase. Some people might even chase the kingfisher with a smartphone in hand 😅 I don't think there is any benefit to spreading the location more than necessary, both for the kingfisher and for myself, who wants to continue shooting there in the future.

Cherish not just the kingfisher, but the location too

Of course, don't leave any trash behind. Don't enter restricted areas. Don't cut branches or grass on your own. Let's follow these basic manners. And there is one more thing I cherish at shooting locations. Greetings. The locals. People taking a walk. People who are already shooting. When I see them, I try to greet them as much as possible. Good morning. Hello. That's all. But I believe that just by doing that, unnecessary trouble can be avoided.

Don't get angry even if your shooting is interrupted lol

This is also important. The kingfisher is about to dive. You hold up your camera, It's coming... It's coming... It's coming... And just at that moment, someone walks in front of you. A dog comes by. The kingfisher flies away. Ahhhhhhhhh 😭 It happens lol But don't get angry there. Parks and riverbeds are not places that exist for us photographers. There are people walking. There are people walking their dogs. Children are playing. Locals are living their lives. Kingfishers are living there too. And we, with our cameras, are just there among them. Ultimately, we are being allowed to take the photos. Toward the kingfisher. And toward that location. I want you to never forget this feeling, even after you get used to shooting.

You want to start shooting soon, right? lol

Now then. After talking so much about etiquette, I bet you're thinking, "Let me shoot kingfishers already!!" I get it lol. But don't worry, there's no need to rush. In my kingfisher photography, the real season is winter. Roughly from December to the end of February. I feel this period is the easiest time to aim for good photos in many ways, such as the lighting and the conditions at the water's edge. So, until then, it's practice time. Let's take it slow. Find a kingfisher. Watch its movements. Try tracking it with your camera. Fail. Try tracking it again. That's perfectly fine. Actually, I'm the same way right now lol. From mid-summer through the lingering summer heat, my shooting pace slows down a bit. This time of year, just after the break, is for me a period to get my senses back. If I try tracking one after a long time, I miss them just like anyone else lol. So, let's practice together. Read this dojo, prepare little by little, actually shoot, fail, and shoot again. And when winter comes— let's seriously aim for that one shot of a kingfisher at the water's edge you've always dreamed of.

Now then. Now that we've covered the dojo's code of conduct, the training officially begins next time lol. Next time, kingfisher habits, how to find them, and how to look for shooting spots. Where are kingfishers? What kind of places do they like? When you go to the river, where should you look? And among the places where kingfishers are, how do you find a spot suitable for photography? Before worrying about camera settings, nothing starts if you can't find a kingfisher lol. Next time, I'll talk about what I usually look for when searching for kingfishers, incorporating my own actual experience. See you next time. Let's go find some kingfishers.

Thank you for reading until the end. ※ This site participates in the Amazon Associates Program. If you purchase products through the links above, a portion of the sales may be returned to me as a referral fee. The purchase price will not increase.

evidence.title: Kingfisher shares rocket after B&Q owner lifts profit target
evidence.text:
Home improvement group Kingfisher saw its shares rocket after the group lifted its profit target, despite summer heatwaves pushing down sales at B&Q.

The FTSE 100 retailer , which also owns Screwfix, said it now expects to make a pre-tax profit of between £595m and £635m, having previously guided between £565m and £625m. Last year, the group posted a £560m profit.

Kingfisher’s shift towards “trade” customers – builders, plumbers and electricians – has driven this boost in forecasts, the group said . Its shares jumped by more than eight per cent to 332p in early trading.

The firm returned a pre-tax profit of £400m in the six months to July, improved by more than 18 per cent from last year. Like-for-like sales across the group edged up by 0.1 per cent.

But the group’s forecast was dragged down by the performance of B&Q, which suffered a 2.9 per cent drop-off in like-for-like sales, driven by a five per cent decline in the sale of “big ticket” items like kitchens and bathrooms.

Kingfisher said its bathroom ranges have “underperformed subdued markets,” adding that it has launched a “comprehensive” review into these products.

The group said sales fell at B&Q because record summer heatwaves drove customers away from shops and towards online shopping. The retailer’s market share remains “broadly stable,” it added.

B&Q recently launched its first trade-only store. Kingfisher said sales in this market remained “resilient,” gaining 0.2 per cent to £490m. The group has said it wants to reach £5bn in trade sales across its retailers.

Trade customers visit Kingfisher stores more often and spend more than retail customers, the group has found.

Sales at Screwfix jumped by 5.6 per cent in the six months to July, owing to a 7.3 per cent uplift in its seasonal ranges. The heatwaves boosted the sale of cooling products and garden seating, Kingfisher said.

The group saw a 2.2 per cent uplift in sales in its Polish market, while sales dipped by 2.3 per cent in France.

Kingfisher chief executive Thierry Garnier, who is set to leave the business, said the group’s shift towards trade customers and e-commerce is “creating new growth opportunities and strong financial discipline supporting performance across the business.

Kingfisher lifts profit outlook as pros keep spending and e-commerce clicks higher

Pros kept building even as DIYers took a breather, and that was enough for Kingfisher to lift its outlook. The home-improvement group now sees adjusted pretax profit landing between £595 million and £635 million, compared with a prior range of £565 million to £625 million. Investors liked it, pushing the shares up as much as 11%.

What did the heavy lifting? A busy Screwfix and solid performances in Poland, Spain and Portugal. Those gains offset weaker demand at B&Q and Brico Dépôt France, with high temperatures reducing store traffic.

The reset comes after many expected a tougher summer as extreme heat and tight household budgets weighed on the sector. UK rivals Topps Tiles and Wickes both missed estimates amid weather-related pressure.

Comparable sales ticked up 0.1%, matching expectations. Gross margin improved to 38.4%, helped by the company's scale in purchasing and sourcing and by expansion of its online marketplace. Digital kept humming too: e-commerce revenue was up 11% to £1.6 billion, making up 22% of group sales compared with 20% a year earlier.

"Much stronger than expected," is how RBC Capital Markets analyst Richard Chamberlain summed it up. Bloomberg Intelligence's Charles Allen and Darja Lema said the combination of standout trade demand and broad e-commerce reach could lift consensus estimates by about 6%.

Kingfisher, meanwhile, is targeting trade revenue of more than £5 billion annually in the medium term and is returning cash: a third £50 million share buyback tranche begins this week and is slated to finish by December, after two completed rounds totaling £125 million.

For your money, this is a snapshot of a retailer leaning into resilient trade customers, a bigger online basket, and steady buybacks, with policy and wage costs as the wild cards to watch.

Kingfisher is raising its full-year profit guidance after first-half earnings increase and sales edge higher across its home improvement operations. The upgrade comes as the retailer says it wins market share in the UK, Poland and Spain, despite weaker trading at Brico Dépôt France during heatwaves.

First-half performance supports guidance upgrade

evidence.title: Kingfisher Screws Its Profit Guidance Higher
evidence.text:
Kingfisher Screws Its Profit Guidance Higher

Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.

Kingfisher's broader DIY markets are hardly booming, but Screwfix is doing enough heavy lifting to make the group look considerably healthier. Strong trade demand, better margins and tighter cost control pushed first-half profits higher and gave management the confidence to raise guidance despite a still-mixed consumer backdrop.

Kingfisher shares jumped around 9% after the home-improvement retailer upgraded its full-year outlook following a stronger-than-expected first half.

Adjusted pretax profit rose 9.9% to £404 million (about $539 million) in the six months to July, while statutory sales increased 0.8% to £6.86 billion and underlying like-for-like sales edged 0.3% higher.

The standout performer was Screwfix, where like-for-like sales climbed 5.6% as stronger volumes, higher spending from trade customers and continued market-share gains offset softer consumer demand elsewhere in the group.

Trade customers now account for 74% of Screwfix sales, giving the chain greater exposure to professional builders, plumbers and electricians whose purchasing tends to be more frequent and less discretionary than that of ordinary DIY shoppers.

Digital engagement is also becoming increasingly important. E-commerce penetration at Screwfix reached 60%, while app sales increased 18%, helped by stronger loyalty-program usage and a broader range of branded products.

Kingfisher's wider digital strategy continued gaining ground too. Group e-commerce sales excluding Screwfix rose 16%, while marketplace gross merchandise value jumped 42% to £372 million and contributed £13.4 million of profit.

Profitability improved faster than sales, with gross margin expanding 70 basis points due to sourcing gains, marketplace growth and disciplined cost management. A £14 million UK business-rates refund also helped the first-half result.

Management now expects adjusted pretax profit of £595 million to £635 million for the full year, up from its previous £565 million to £625 million range. Free-cash-flow guidance was also increased to £480 million to £520 million from £450 million to £510 million.

The stronger outlook comes even though trading remains uneven across the portfolio, particularly in France, where weak consumer confidence and softer demand for larger renovation projects continue to weigh on performance.

Kingfisher's results show why exposure to professional tradespeople can be particularly useful when ordinary consumers are nervous about spending.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

Large discretionary projects such as bathrooms, kitchens and major decorating work remain softer in several markets because households are still dealing with expensive borrowing, higher energy bills and generally cautious sentiment.

A plumber replacing a boiler or an electrician finishing a contracted job has less flexibility to postpone buying tools and materials, which gives Screwfix a more dependable demand profile than much of traditional DIY retail.

That distinction is becoming increasingly valuable for Kingfisher because Screwfix is no longer just another banner inside the group. It is becoming one of the main engines behind customer growth, digital adoption, market-share gains and earnings resilience.

The same logic explains why Kingfisher has been pushing harder into trade customers across B&Q and its European businesses. Trade sales excluding Screwfix grew 16% in the half, lifting group trade penetration to 31%, and management sees professional customers as a way to generate more frequent and predictable purchases.

Margins are improving at the same time, which makes even modest sales growth more valuable. Group revenue barely moved, yet adjusted pretax profit increased almost 10%, demonstrating how sourcing improvements, marketplace income and cost discipline can amplify relatively small top-line gains.

The marketplace model adds another attractive layer because Kingfisher can increase product availability without carrying all of that inventory itself. If third-party sellers can broaden assortment while Kingfisher collects commissions and service income, digital growth becomes less dependent on adding more stock and warehouse capacity.

The weak point remains France, where Brico Dépôt has been hit by softer project spending while Castorama has produced less exciting growth. B&Q also continues to see pressure in some larger-ticket categories, making Screwfix's performance particularly important to the upgraded group outlook.

The main question is whether Screwfix can maintain mid-single-digit growth once comparisons become tougher, particularly if construction activity and consumer confidence remain uneven.

Investors will also watch whether Kingfisher can keep converting marketplace and e-commerce growth into higher profits rather than simply generating additional digital volume. Marketplace GMV is already growing much faster than group sales, suggesting more of the range can expand without Kingfisher owning the inventory itself.

France remains the biggest operational challenge, and any sustained recovery there would make the group less dependent on Screwfix and UK trade demand for earnings growth.

Leadership will become another focus as chief executive Thierry Garnier prepares to leave for Ahold Delhaize. His successor inherits a business where the overall DIY market remains difficult, but Screwfix, trade sales, digital channels and better margins are providing enough momentum to keep the profit outlook moving in the right direction.

evidence.title: Kingfisher delivers profit upgrade despite flagging B&Q sales

Kingfisher delivers profit upgrade despite flagging B&Q sales

B&Q like-for-like sales in the UK and Ireland dropped 1.8% over its second quarter, with sales of so-called big ticket items plunging 8.1%.

B&Q owner Kingfisher has hiked its annual profit outlook despite flagging half-year sales in the DIY chain as Britons held off from splashing out on bigger purchases.

The group said B&Q like-for-like sales in the UK and Ireland dropped 1.8% over its second quarter, with sales of so-called big ticket items plunging 8.1%, driven largely by lower demand for bathroom ranges.
