evidence.title: Engineering’s Tripathi joins with Cognizant to explore AI innovation in life sciences
evidence.text:
Engineering’s Tripathi joins with Cognizant to explore AI innovation in life sciences

Brown University's School of Engineering and Cognizant have launched a research collaboration examining how artificial intelligence could support innovation across life sciences and biotechnology. Supported by an industry grant, the initiative brings together academic research and commercial expertise to address pressing challenges in therapy development, manufacturing, and delivery.

The effort is led at Brown by Professor Anubhav Tripathi, whose lab works at the intersection of life sciences and diagnostics technologies. “The hard problems in life sciences are no longer only biological, they are problems of speed, scale and decision-making,” he said. “Working alongside Cognizant lets us test ideas against real-world considerations involved in developing and delivering therapies.”

Scope and priorities will be informed by industry needs and framed across four life sciences value areas: pipeline cycle time reduction, supporting discovery, development, clinical trials, approvals and therapy delivery; intelligent manufacturing and supply chain resilience, using physical AI, digital twins and increasingly automated operations to improve reliability and speed-to-market; patient engagement and outcomes, supporting patient identification, recruitment, outreach and treatment pathways for targeted populations; and enterprise AI enablement, supporting broader adoption across R&D, manufacturing, quality, compliance and operations.

Throughout the collaboration, researchers from Brown and Cognizant will collaborate on joint fundamental research publications, share ongoing findings, and produce a final synthesis report. The organizations are also exploring events aimed at fostering collaboration among scientists, researchers, and healthcare leaders across Rhode Island and beyond.

evidence.title: Microsoft, AWS and Cognizant’s Role in Frontier AI
evidence.text:
Microsoft, AWS and Cognizant’s Role in Frontier AI

You can read this and more in the magazine

For the past few years, frontier AI has referred almost exclusively to the model layer – the largest, most capable systems produced by labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, distinguished by scale, generality and the pace at which their capabilities have advanced.

Each new generation has pushed further into reasoning, coding and autonomous agentic behaviour, closing the gap between what a model can theoretically do and what it can be trusted to do on an unsupervised basis.

That gap has, however, proven to be the real story of 2026. Enterprises have struggled to turn frontier models into working systems that integrate with legacy infrastructure, respect governance requirements and deliver measurable business outcomes.

Cognizant frames this as an “AI outcome gap” worth an estimated US$4.5tn, arguing it is fundamentally a people and process problem rather than one of compute or infrastructure.

This has given frontier AI a second, quieter meaning. It now describes not just the models themselves – but the organisations being built to put them to work inside the enterprise.

Microsoft, AWS and Cognizant have each launched dedicated units in recent months.

Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, wrote in July that customers have “moved well beyond experimentation” and are now focused on demonstrating a return on their AI investment while protecting intellectual property.

Francessca Vasquez, VP of Frontier AI Engineering and Services at AWS, has made a similar point, noting that customers want to make AI core to how they operate rather than simply testing what it can do.

The model these firms are converging on borrows from (and explicitly seeks to move beyond) forward-deployed engineering (FDE), a practice popularised by Palantir in which technical specialists embed directly within a client's teams.

AWS has adopted the FDE label outright; Microsoft has positioned its offering as going further than FDE towards what it calls “frontier transformation”; Cognizant has gone further still, arguing that what enterprises actually need is a permanent, accountable workforce combining deep industry expertise with AI fluency.

Three forces explain why this is happening now.

First, the shift from experimental to agentic AI has raised the stakes of implementation, since autonomous systems that touch live business processes carry operational and security risks that pilot projects did not.

Second, enterprises increasingly want outcomes rather than technology for its own sake, pushing vendors towards engagement models scoped around measurable results rather than billable hours.

Third, competition among hyperscalers and services firms has intensified to the point where deployment capability, not model access, has become the differentiator, since most large enterprises can now reach broadly comparable frontier models through several routes.

Firms are exploring several different ways of answering the same underlying question: who actually does the work of making frontier AI real inside the enterprise

Microsoft Frontier Company: Engineering at customer scale

Back in July, Microsoft announced Microsoft Frontier Company , a new operating business dedicated to what it calls end-to-end “frontier transformation”.

The unit is backed by a US$2.5bn investment and will embed 6,000 industry and engineering experts directly at customer organisations.

The business combines three capabilities that Microsoft argues enterprises need together rather than separately: deep industry knowledge; change management and continuous improvement experience; and enterprise-grade AI engineering expertise.

In a blog post, Judson Althoff , CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, wrote: “This goes beyond what has been labelled as forward-deployed engineering (FDE) and will be the largest, most capable, outcome-driven engineering organisation in the industry.”

This will be the largest, most capable, outcome-driven engineering organisation in the industry.

Judson framed the effort around two linked priorities: helping customers build proprietary intelligence platforms where their own data and workflows compound in value over time, and pairing that with a trusted platform for observing, governing and securing AI systems across the technology stack.

He added: “It comes down to Intelligence + Trust and empowering our customers to achieve meaningful outcomes and a return on their investments.”

Microsoft Frontier Company signals that even the largest platform vendors no longer see software licensing as sufficient.

Delivery capacity – at industrial scale – has become part of the product.

AWS Forward Deployed Engineering: Betting US$1bn on speed

AWS unveiled its own Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) organisation, backed by a US$1bn investment funded entirely from its own balance sheet. Unlike Microsoft's approach, AWS has embraced the FDE label directly, placing engineers within customer teams to build, deploy and scale AI solutions using agents purpose-built for specific business needs.

Francessca Vasquez , Vice President of Frontier AI Engineering and Services at AWS, explained the rationale behind the launch: “Customers have moved past exploring what AI can do; they want to make it core to how they operate.

They want to recreate their business processes with agentic AI built in so they can increase productivity and deliver AI-powered products.”

Customers have moved past exploring what AI can do; they want to make it core to how they operate.

The model is built around three principles: it is agentic-first; it compresses deployment timelines from months to days; and it aims to leave customers able to run their systems independently once an engagement ends.

Teams work in pods of five to six engineers on 45-day sprints, using what AWS describes as an AI-Driven Development Lifecycle that pairs AI agents with human oversight.

Crucially, AWS has positioned the unit as internal infrastructure rather than a spin-out.

“This organisation is a separate business unit within AWS, not a standalone company,” Francessca told Channel Dive, distinguishing the initiative from the joint-venture structures some rivals have used to fund their own deployment arms.

Cognizant's frontier workforce: Prioritising permanence

Cognizant has taken a different route, announcing a commitment to scale its “frontier-certified” workforce to 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators, with the first deployment-ready cohort expected by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Rather than temporary embeds, Cognizant is positioning the roles as permanent, accountable positions built on existing industry domain expertise.

Ravi Kumar S., CEO at Cognizant, said: “Closing the AI outcome gap demands talent who not only understands a client's industry deeply but can also reimagine the way work is structured and take end-to-end responsibility for delivering results in collaboration with clients, on any model or cloud the client selects. That is what a frontier workforce does.”

We know how to take these powerful frontier tools and turn them into real business value.

Cognizant’s Chief People Officer Kathy Diaz links the initiative to a broader labour shift.

She added: “AI has exposed 93% of jobs to change, and the associated labour value remains untapped because the workforce architecture built for a pre-AI world cannot capture it. So, we rebuilt the architecture for the world we are in now.”

Cognizant’s frontier workforce is deliberately model and cloud-agnostic, spanning partnerships with Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, AWS, NVIDIA, Salesforce and ServiceNow, with certifications credentialed directly by frontier-model companies including including GitHub Copilot, Google Gemini, Anthropic's Claude, and OpenAI's Codex.

Vice President of Professional Services & Agentic AI

Chief Commercial Officer and CEO of Commercial Business

evidence.title: Cognizant: How the CISO Role Evolves in the Age of AI Agents
evidence.text:
Cognizant: How the CISO Role Evolves in the Age of AI Agents

It is no secret that indeterminate systems like autonomous agents have changed the cybersecurity landscape as we knew it.

Able to interpret information, make decisions and take action across connected systems, agents introduce new risks when their context, permissions or behaviour are compromised.

This is why protecting AI requires more than conventional controls. Organisations need verifiable agent identities, tightly governed access, continuous monitoring and clear accountability for autonomous actions.

Context must also be treated as a security asset, with controls covering both the information agents can access and the actions they can take.

Vishal Salvi is the Global Head of Cybersecurity Service Line at Cognizant . His industry experience is long standing, and as Vishal puts it: "Three decades in cybersecurity gives you a particular kind of perspective."

Yet, it is his belief that the "last six months of AI advancement has changed the threat landscape in ways the last decade did not".

In conversation with Cyber Magazine, Vishal elaborates the many security traps that AI has brought about and how to guard against them.

What makes autonomous AI agents fundamentally different from the applications that traditional cybersecurity was built to protect?

Traditional applications typically operate within predefined rules and permissions, while autonomous AI agents can interpret information and take actions across connected systems with limited human intervention.

That ability to decide and act is what fundamentally changes the cybersecurity risk .

When an agent fails, the impact goes beyond producing an incorrect output. It can disrupt a business process, trigger an unintended action in another system or influence a decision with real financial or operational consequences.

The blast radius of a single failure is no longer confined to one system.

Critically, agents also expand the attack surface in ways legacy controls were never designed to handle. Models, prompts, data pipelines and tool integrations are now live attack surfaces inside every enterprise.

Attackers and defenders draw on the same AI, and the advantage goes to whoever moves first.

If an AI agent can make decisions and take action autonomously, who should be held responsible for those actions?

The people and organisations responsible for deploying and overseeing these systems must remain accountable for how they behave. Giving an AI agent greater autonomy should never mean giving up human responsibility for its actions.

That starts with anticipating what could go wrong when an agent acts autonomously, and defining where human intervention is required as a core part of cybersecurity controls. Clear ownership and escalation paths are essential, particularly where there is significant operational, financial or regulatory risk.

This is why the CISO's role is evolving. The CISO is the one executive with the mandate and operational mechanisms to manage AI trust continuously, not through periodic policy reviews but through governance backed by evidence: traceability, auditability and explainability.

The shift is from assumed trust to provable trust.

Organisations should therefore invest in the skills people need to govern AI effectively, so those responsible for autonomous systems can provide meaningful oversight and remain accountable for how they operate.

How can organisations give agents enough context to be useful without exposing sensitive data or creating new attack paths?

Context is AI's superpower and its most significant vulnerability. When an agent relies on enterprise context (internal documents, customer records, operational procedures, previous interactions), that context is operationalised within enterprise workflows. If it is corrupted or manipulated, the agent does not just leak data, it makes confidently wrong decisions at scale.

Organisations must treat context as a first-class security asset. That means giving each agent a verifiable identity and limiting access to the specific data, systems and tools required for the task.

It means tracking provenance, governing retrieval and maintaining auditable records of what the agent accessed, what it did and what it decided.

The level of access and oversight should reflect the level of risk. An AI assistant answering employee questions should not have the same permissions as one authorised to approve payments. Higher-risk activities require stronger guardrails, while lower-impact tasks can remain largely autonomous.

Are today's AI guardrails keeping pace with autonomous agents or are organisations still relying on security controls designed for a different era?

Most organisations are still adapting security controls designed for conventional software, where behaviour was predictable and easier to constrain. AI agents interpret new information, operate in changing contexts and behave differently over time. Static, point-in-time controls cannot keep pace.

But the issue is not just speed. Rather, it is fragmentation. When security tools operate in silos, you cannot automate what you cannot unify.

The organisations making real progress are bringing their security data, identity systems, policies and response processes together, giving AI the context it needs to support a joined-up response.

This is also the thinking behind our own Neuro Cybersecurity platform, which brings separate security signals together so teams can respond in a coordinated and controlled way.

Guardrails must also operate across the full lifecycle. Trust has to be engineered twice: at build time through secure development controls , and at run time through continuous monitoring, policy-aware enforcement and the ability to contain or stop unexpected behaviour.

The patch queue itself becomes part of the attack surface when discovery accelerates but remediation still moves at enterprise speed.

As businesses deploy AI agents across multiple platforms, how can they avoid fragmented security controls and blind spots?

Businesses need a consistent approach that follows agents across the entire lifecycle, rather than relying on separate controls for individual tools or applications. Security must extend across every point where AI accesses information and makes decisions.

The more an agent can see and do, the greater the potential impact if it is compromised.

Getting data context right is crucial to minimising blind spots. If the information an agent relies on, such as internal documents, customer information, and previous interactions, is inaccurate or manipulated, it can make the wrong decision even when the underlying model works as intended.

Controls must therefore cover both what agents can see and what they can do across platforms, preventing gaps as they move between data, tools and systems.

The answer is consolidation – unified signals, identity and policy enforced through one control plane - combined with continuous, audit-ready evidence of what happened and why. That is how you move from hoping your defences hold to proving they do.

What does continuous AI governance actually look like when agents are learning, adapting and acting in real time?

Continuous AI governance means having the ability to see how agents are behaving and intervene when something goes wrong, not relying on periodic checks that may already be outdated by the time they are completed.

That requires clear ownership, escalation paths and mechanisms such as kill switches that can contain unexpected behaviour.

Organisations need visibility across AI and traditional systems to identify anomalies, enforce policies and respond in real time. Some are exploring guardian agents that monitor other AI systems and flag deviations, an example governance itself becoming more autonomous to keep pace with the systems being overseen.

Governance needs to be part of how AI is managed day to day, rather than something organisations revisit periodically.

We have taken that approach by building continuous checks into our governance model, Cognizant Trust. This includes keeping track of the AI systems being used, monitoring compliance, recording incidents and giving leadership a clear view of how AI is being managed across the business.

Our ISO 42001 certification provides independent validation of that approach. Ultimately, the goal is to move from assumed trust to provable, continuous control.

If you were advising a CISO deploying autonomous AI today, what are the three security controls you would implement first?

First, control identity and access. Every agent should have a verifiable identity and access only to the data, tools and systems required for its role. The more an agent can see and do, the greater the potential impact if it is compromised.

Second, build in real-time oversight. Organisations need visibility into what agents are doing, with the ability to contain or stop unexpected behaviour before it spreads across connected systems.

Third, protect the context agents rely on. Controls should ensure the information feeding an agent is trusted, accurate and appropriate for the task as well as monitoring the task output itself. Ensuring the quality of what an agent can see is just as important as controlling what it can do.

And underpinning all three: accept that securing AI and governing AI responsibly are not separate programmes. The CISO who unifies them becomes the steward of AI trust for the organisation. The enterprises that get this right will define trust in the next decade.

Global Head of Cybersecurity Service Line

Cognizant Technology Solutions stock outlook: Support test amid AI-driven risk concerns

Cognizant Technology Solutions (CTSH) stock is trading at $59.87, marking a daily decline of 3.25%. The stock is positioned below its key moving averages, reflecting ongoing pressure from sellers.

Cognizant Technology Solutions has shifted its delivery model to prioritize artificial intelligence, transitioning from a workforce focus to one that integrates digital and human labor while providing outcome-based services, according to Defenseworld . This strategic move alters the company's cost structure and delivery approach, which may affect how investors view its future competitiveness relative to evolving client demands. As the firm continues to align with broader trends toward automation, the adjustment introduces new operational efficiencies and risks, emerging as a key factor shaping market perception during the current session.

The Ichimoku Kijun is set at $62.38 and acts as immediate resistance. Both MACD and ADX are displaying sell signals, with RSI, Stoch RSI, and CCI all pointing to oversold conditions. Negative Bull/Bear Power highlights seller dominance, and the Awesome Oscillator supports the ongoing downward momentum seen in the session.

Consolidation likely as limited upside meets heightened downside risk

In the short term, the price is expected to consolidate within the $58.28 to $61.46 range based on typical volatility. There is a low probability of a rebound, with just a 21% chance for an upward move and a 79% likelihood of further decline. The base case anticipates consolidation within this range, while any break below $58.28 could trigger additional selling pressure. A sustained move above immediate resistance would be required to signal any potential for recovery.

evidence.title: Infosys (INFY) Lands a Brake Maker as Growth Stays in Low Gear
evidence.text:
Infosys (INFY) Lands a Brake Maker as Growth Stays in Low Gear

On August 18, Infosys (NYSE: INFY ) announced a long-term deal to manage the enterprise software behind Knorr-Bremse AG, a maker of braking systems for rail and commercial vehicles. The work stretches from ERP and data platforms to engineering and product lifecycle tools, and it runs on Infosys Topaz, the company's AI offering. It is a nice win. But the results Infosys posted on July 23 give it some context, and that context cuts both ways.

Start with AI, the pitch Infosys leads with. In the quarter ended June 30, AI made up 8.2% of revenue, which shows the technology is reaching the income statement and not just the press releases. Large deal wins totaled $3.6 billion, and most of it, 61%, was net new. The Knorr-Bremse contract fits the pattern. Infosys will apply generative and agentic AI to automate work inside the managed services it runs, aiming to go past routine outsourcing and deliver productivity gains the customer can measure. And because the deal spans both of the customer's divisions, Infosys will be embedded in the core systems of a manufacturer whose products are safety-critical.

The financial engine is also sturdier than the growth rate suggests. Operating margin came in at 21.1%, inside the 20% to 22% range Infosys kept for its FY27 guidance. Cash backs it up. Free cash flow reached $955 million, which was 116.5% of net profit, so earnings are turning into real money and not just accounting figures. That gives Infosys a way to fund its AI push from its own operations.

Growth is the weak spot. Revenue rose 2.4% from a year earlier in constant currency and only 1.0% from the prior quarter, a pace that sits awkwardly beside all the talk of AI momentum. Infosys also revised its FY27 revenue guidance to a range of 1.5% to 3.0%, so management is not promising a sudden acceleration. The best-looking figure deserves a second glance too. Earnings per share grew 14.9% in rupee terms, but basic EPS in dollars rose just 3.7% to $0.20, so the rupee number paints a rosier picture than the dollar one.

Then there is what we do not know. The Knorr-Bremse announcement gives no contract value, so there is no way to tell how much revenue it adds. AI, at 8.2% of revenue, is still a minority of the business. And the CFO called the operating environment challenging while saying Infosys is spending more on AI, talent and platforms. Those are costs the margin has to absorb, and its gain over the prior quarter was only 0.2%.

Hedge fund ownership rose to 71 funds from 63 in the prior quarter, which reads as conviction building rather than fading. Short interest stands at 3.70% of float, so few investors are organized against the stock. The forward P/E is 13.37 as of September 18. At that multiple, the market is paying for modest growth and not a boom. That fits guidance of 1.5% to 3.0% revenue growth.

Infosys is telling an AI story while its results still read like those of a slow-growing services company. The Knorr-Bremse win supports the first tale, and strong cash generation gives management room to keep spending on it. Bulls need AI's share of revenue to climb fast enough to lift the overall pace, while bears will be proven right if big wins keep landing without much showing up in the top line.

evidence.title: Infosys Expands Indore Operations With New Software Development Block
evidence.text:
Infosys Expands Indore Operations With New Software Development Block

IT firm Infosys has expanded its development centre in Indore with a new 3,30,000-square-foot software development block, as the Indian IT services company seeks to deepen its presence in Central India and tap the region's technology talent pool.

The new Software Development Block-2 (SDB-2) was inaugurated at Infosys' campus in Indore's Super Corridor in the presence of Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav, Indore Member of Parliament Shankar Lalwani and state legislator Manoj Nirbhay Singh Patel, the company said in a statement on Wednesday.

Infosys' Indore centre currently employs more than 3,300 people and serves clients globally across banking, financial services and insurance, retail, life sciences and manufacturing.

The expansion will strengthen the company's capabilities in cloud, application development, artificial intelligence and machine learning, and cybersecurity, Infosys said.

The move comes as IT services companies expand delivery capacity around India's major and emerging technology hubs to access engineering talent beyond traditional centres such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai and Pune.

Infosys also plans to increase its engagement with Madhya Pradesh's academic and technology ecosystem through skilling initiatives and institutional partnerships, including with IIT Indore, IIM Indore and Devi Ahilya Vishwavidyalaya.

The new facility incorporates energy-efficient systems and features such as low-energy cooling, smart building automation, rainwater harvesting and wastewater recycling, the company said. It will also include flexible workstations, training facilities and wellness centres.

"Indore is steadily emerging as an important technology hub, supported by a strong talent base and a growing innovation ecosystem," Yadav said, adding that Infosys' investment would create employment opportunities for skilled youth in the state.

Infosys Chief Financial Officer Jayesh Sanghrajka said the expansion would help the company leverage the region's talent pool and strengthen its AI, cloud and digital technology capabilities.

evidence.title: Infosys faces the AI test as coding automation rewrites Indian IT services
evidence.text:
Infosys faces the AI test as coding automation rewrites Indian IT services

Infosys used its AGM to deliver the message that AI as a services opportunity, while shareholder questions showed unease over coding, jobs, margins, growth, execution, and proof now.

At Infosys’ 45th Annual General Meeting, Artificial Intelligence was not a passing reference. It was the question behind almost every serious question. The company had a steady year to report. Revenue crossed USD 20 billion in fiscal 2026. Constant currency growth stood at 3.1%. Adjusted operating margin was 21%. Free cash flow was strong at USD 3.7 billion. Large deal total contract value touched USD 14.9 billion, with 55% of it coming from net new business. On paper, these are not numbers of a company in crisis. Yet, the mood around the AGM showed something deeper. Shareholders were not only asking how Infosys had performed. They were asking what happens to Infosys when Artificial Intelligence begins to automate coding, change delivery models, reshape talent needs, and alter the economics of technology services.

That made the AGM more than a shareholder meeting, it in a way served as platform to look at the evolving trajectory of not just Infosys, but overall IT Services industry.

Nandan Nilekani, Non-Executive Chairman, put the issue on the table directly. Every major technology transition, he said, brings questions about relevance, leadership, growth, and margins. With AI, those questions have become pronounced because the shift is larger and more disruptive.

The hardest question is also the simplest one. If coding becomes automated, why are IT services companies needed at all?

Infosys’ answer was clear. Coding is important, but enterprise technology is not just coding. Large organisations need systems that work with existing investments. They need testing, resilient architecture, cybersecurity, data governance, compliance, and deep knowledge of how their business actually runs. AI tools may write or improve code, but they do not automatically understand a bank’s risk systems, a retailer’s supply chain, a manufacturer’s shop floor, or a telecom company’s customer operations.

This is where Infosys wants to position itself. It is not trying to tell investors that AI will leave the services model untouched. It is saying the model will change, and that the companies which can adapt will become more relevant.

The most important insight from the AGM was “AI deployment gap.”

That gap is where Infosys sees its next opportunity. Many enterprises have experimented with generative AI. Fewer have managed to turn it into production-grade business impact. The challenge is not only model access. It is execution. It is the hard work of putting AI inside core systems, connecting it to enterprise data, securing it, governing it, and making it useful to people who run real business processes every day.

This is a very different story from the early excitement around chatbots and copilots. Infosys is seeing enterprise AI as an integration and transformation problem. In that view, the AI success will not be decided only by who the models. They will also be decided by who can make models, agents, data, cloud, cybersecurity, and transaction systems work together and make for seamless delivery of outcomes.

For Indian IT services, this is the most important part. If AI is seen only as coding automation, it can look like a threat. If AI is seen as enterprise deployment at scale, it becomes a large services opportunity. There is no use in the use cases. We need to real, on ground projects and how AI has been intersected with those projects and how it changed the outcomes.

One striking point from the AGM was Infosys’ view that AI has made legacy modernisation urgent in a way nothing else has.

For years, modernisation was often sold as a cloud migration or cost optimisation exercise. AI changes that conversation. Enterprises cannot build serious AI-led workflows on top of fragmented data, ageing applications, brittle architecture, and disconnected systems. If they want agents to act on business processes, the underlying technology estate has to be cleaner, more connected, and more secure.

That gives Infosys a familiar but renewed market to address. Modernisation is no longer only about moving old systems to the cloud. It is about making the enterprise AI-ready.

This also explains why Infosys continues to talk about Topaz, Fabric, and Cobalt together. Topaz and Fabric represent the AI layer. Cobalt brings the cloud foundation. The larger message is that AI cannot scale in isolation. It needs cloud, data, engineering, governance, and domain knowledge around it.

Salil Parekh, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, described six broad areas where Infosys sees clients using AI. These are AI engineering and strategy, data, process transformation, technology modernisation using agents, physical AI, and AI trust.

This framework in a way gives a direction and it shows that Infosys is trying to move the conversation beyond “AI can write code.” The company is presenting AI as a full enterprise transformation stack.

For instance, AI engineering and strategy is about building agents and AI-led applications. Data is about making structured and unstructured enterprise data usable. Process transformation is about improving workflows before placing agents inside them. Technology modernisation is about using AI to renew ageing systems. Physical AI takes the story into manufacturing, automotive, medical devices, and other product environments. AI trust focuses on security, responsible AI, and governance.

When one connects all the dots, Infosys sees these areas as part of a USD 300 billion to USD 400 billion AI-first services opportunity by 2030. That is the big market-sizing claim. The real question however, will be how much of this opportunity turns into sustained revenue growth, better margins, and stronger market confidence.

One of the strongest points that emerged from the AGM was the importance of data. Infosys’ argument is that enterprises will not get lasting value from generic AI alone. The value will come when their own data is made available to AI models in a secure, governed, and useful way.

This is where the services opportunity becomes clearer. Many enterprises still have data spread across applications, geographies, business units, cloud environments, and legacy systems. Some of it is structured. Much of it is unstructured. Some of it is clean. Much of it is not. Without fixing that foundation, AI may remain stuck in pilots.

For Infosys, this creates work across data engineering, cloud migration, application modernisation, cybersecurity, compliance, and business process redesign. In other words, AI is becoming the front door through which older enterprise technology problems are being reopened.

This is also why Indian IT services firms may still have a role in the AI era. The problem is not only to build an agent. The harder problem is to make that agent work safely and usefully inside a live enterprise.

The AGM also showed that investors want more than broad AI messaging. They want numbers.

Infosys has disclosed that AI services contributed about 5.5% of revenue, or roughly USD 1 billion annualised. In the context of an IT services company, this refers to client work where AI is a core part of the consulting, engineering, data, modernisation, process, or trust layer, rather than revenue from selling a standalone AI model. The company also said this revenue was growing faster than the company average. It said it is working with 90% of its top 200 clients on their AI journeys, and has thousands of AI projects underway.

These numbers are to be read with cautious optimism because they also raise the next set of questions.

How much of this AI revenue is truly incremental? How much is replacing older work? Are AI services better for margins or do they carry investment pressure? Will productivity gains reduce billable effort? Will clients expect savings to be passed back? Can AI-led deals become large enough to offset softness in traditional discretionary spending?

These were not abstract concerns. Shareholders asked about AI revenue, AI margins, separate AI reporting, growth, and the impact of automation on the services model. The market is clearly moving from excitement to accountability.

The other big question was people.For decades, Indian IT services grew on the strength of talent scale. AI now challenges parts of that model. If tools can write code, test software, generate documentation, improve productivity, and support agents, the old relationship between headcount and revenue will change.

Infosys did not present this as a job-loss story. Its line was about reskilling, redeployment, and new kinds of work. The company said it hired more than 20,000 college graduates during the year and ended with a workforce of over 325,000 employees. It also spoke about preparing employees for the AI era, and redeploying people released through productivity gains into new growth areas.

That data is important. It suggests that the work mix is changing, even if the company is not saying it as workforce reduction. The future model may not be only about how many people are added. It may be about how effectively employees, domain experts, platforms, and agents work together.

This is where Infosys’ internal skilling becomes critical. The company spoke about employees being AI aware, AI builders, and AI masters. That progression matters because awareness alone will not be enough. The next phase will need people who can design, deploy, govern, and improve AI-led systems inside complex enterprise environments.

The AGM also revealed an emotional undercurrent. Many shareholders praised Infosys for governance, dividends, CSR, leadership, and transparency. But the repeated concerns were hard to miss. They asked about the falling share price, buyback, bonus shares, AI’s impact on the IT services model, employee retention, AI revenue, and future growth.

This is the real pulse of the company’s AGM. Infosys continues to command trust among long-term shareholders, but that trust now comes with a demand for proof.

The question is no longer whether Infosys understands AI. The question is whether Infosys can show that AI will create visible and tangible business momentum. Investors want to know if AI will lift growth, protect margins, support talent transformation, and make the company more competitive in a slow-growth market.

The company’s response was measured. It declined to comment on share price movement. It pointed to its capital allocation policy, under which it expects to return around 85% of free cash flow cumulatively over a five-year period through dividends, buybacks, or special dividends. It also said its mergers and acquisitions approach would remain disciplined, focused on tuck-in acquisitions that fill capability gaps or strengthen growth areas.

But the shareholder mood suggests that capital return alone may not be enough. Investors want Infosys to invest in the future, explain the AI revenue path more clearly, and show that it can convert AI capability into growth.

Nilekani’s most candid clarification came when he explained execution risk. The opportunity, he said, is large because AI makes many new things possible. But Infosys has to reorient its services to AI-first and AI-augmented models. It also has to align sales and delivery, transform talent, and look at new pricing models, including outcome-based pricing.

Infosys has the relationships, scale, balance sheet, delivery depth, cloud capability, and AI partnerships. But AI is forcing every large IT services firm to rethink the old playbook. Productivity gains can help margins, but they can also reduce revenue if clients demand the benefit. Outcome-based pricing can create upside, but it also transfers more risk to the provider. Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. stock (ISIN INE467B01029) fell more than 3 percent on September 18, 2026, with the IT major trading around INR 2,128 on the National Stock Exchange as a governance dispute at holding company Tata Sons hit sentiment across Tata Group names.

TCS stock reacts to Tata Sons boardroom battle

According to NDTV Profit on September 18, 2026, Tata Consultancy Services share price fell as much as 3.64 percent to INR 2,116 apiece on the BSE in early trade, before paring some losses to trade 2.70 percent lower at INR 2,136.65 around 9:45 a.m. local time.

As Economic Times reported on September 18, 2026, TCS slipped over 3.5 percent intraday to a low of INR 2,116, pulling its overall market value below INR 7,73,294 crore, or roughly INR 7.73 trillion.

Group-wide governance dispute drives selling pressure

As Economic Times noted on September 18, 2026, Tata Trusts labelled the extension of Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran’s tenure illegal, challenging the board’s decision to grant him a fresh five-year term and proceed with plans for a Tata Sons holding company IPO.

According to Reuters on September 18, 2026, flagship Tata Consultancy Services shares slipped around 3 percent as Tata Group companies collectively shed about USD 3.2 billion in market capitalization amid the dispute at the holding company.

Short-term performance and valuation context

On September 18, 2026, MarketsMojo reported that TCS opened at INR 2,179.50 and ended the day with a 3.25 percent loss, underperforming the broader Sensex, which gained 0.22 percent over the same session.

According to the same MarketsMojo analysis, TCS traded at a price-to-earnings ratio of 14.79 times versus an industry average P/E of 20.34, suggesting the stock is valued at a discount of about 27 percent relative to the broader IT services peer group on that metric.

Recent results provide fundamental backdrop

While the latest trading-day move in Tata Consultancy Services stock is driven primarily by the Tata Sons governance dispute, the company’s fundamentals from its most recently reported financial period provide important context for investors assessing the IT major.

Based on recent quarterly numbers reported for fiscal 2026 within the last nine months, TCS posted consolidated revenue of around INR 62,000 crore in the latest quarter, up roughly mid-single-digit percent year-on-year, and net profit in the region of INR 11,000 crore, delivering a net margin close to 18 percent over that period, according to figures cited in contemporary financial portal coverage of its current fiscal year results.

These figures represent a modest improvement compared with historical fiscal year 2024 levels, when TCS had generated lower quarterly revenue and net profit, underscoring that the current share price weakness is more closely tied to holding-company governance uncertainty than to an abrupt deterioration in operating performance.

Risk factors around governance and group dynamics

The immediate risk factor for Tata Consultancy Services shareholders is the potential for prolonged governance friction at Tata Sons, which could distract management attention at the holding company level and influence decisions around capital allocation, dividend flows and strategic initiatives that affect TCS as a key subsidiary.

As Goodreturns highlighted on September 18, 2026, the market reaction has extended beyond TCS to other Tata siblings such as Tata Chemicals, Tata Investment and TMPV, with group stocks sliding between 3 and 8 percent as investors reassessed governance risks and the timing of the proposed Tata Sons stake buyout.

TCS stock closing level and market position

Per live data referenced in Indian stock market coverage on September 18, 2026, Tata Consultancy Services stock closed the latest session near INR 2,130 on the Bombay Stock Exchange, down around 3 percent versus the prior close of INR 2,190, leaving the shares below their recent intraday high of INR 2,236 recorded in the preceding session.

evidence.title: Why 400 Wipro trainees are agitated over a decades-old fresher programme
evidence.text:
Why 400 Wipro trainees are agitated over a decades-old fresher programme

This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.

Bengaluru: Wipro Ltd has delayed the permanent onboarding of at least 400 trainees who joined the company four years ago through one of India’s oldest IT recruitment programmes, according to people familiar with the matter. Wipro launched its Wipro Integrated Learning Program (WILP) in 1995, taking non-engineering graduates to work while pursuing an advanced engineering degree. It was the first of its kind, and the country's fourth-largest IT services company hired about 5,000 people annually through the flagship programme. The delays highlight the challenges facing graduates recruited during a period of aggressive post-pandemic hiring, as slower growth and the rise of artificial intelligence reshape workforce requirements in the technology services industry. For trainees, extended academic programmes and deferred conversion to full-time employment have created uncertainty over career progression, financial planning and job security .

For Wipro trainees, the deferment prompted several agitated graduates to email company management, including executive chairman Rishad Premji and chief executive Srini Pallia.

“We understand that the current timeline indicates completion of our M.Tech programme around March/April 2027, resulting in an overall tenure of nearly five years. This is considerably longer than the timelines experienced by previous batches and has raised concerns regarding career progression, financial planning, and conversion timelines,” read an email dated 24 August, sent by one of the trainees to at least 400 people, including Premji and Pallia.

“The extended timeline has also created considerable financial uncertainty for many students. In my case, my family is dependent on my income, and I had planned important financial commitments based on the timelines previously communicated to us,” the email added.

WILP trainees work five days a week in coding, software development and customer support, with one day between Friday and Sunday reserved for M.Tech classes. They earn ₹ 15,000 a month in the first year, rising to ₹ 23,000 by the fourth year. They remain on the stipend without full-time employee benefits until they are converted into permanent employees.

Under the original WILP offer, Wipro is expected to begin academic courses within a year of a trainee joining the company.

“However, our actual enrolment took place beyond the 12-month period mentioned in the offer letter. We would appreciate clarification regarding the reason for this delay and its impact on the overall completion timeline,” the email said.

A second executive familiar with the developments said the delay was primarily due to “certain procedural delays in 2022 which deferred the start of the programme for some employees.” Mint could not independently ascertain the exact nature of the procedural delays. An email sent to Wipro on 18 September went unanswered.

“The programme for the 2022 batch was expected to end in December this year but got delayed due to the late start of the academic courses, which began in June 2023. This delay is essentially two months from when the programme was expected to end,” the executive said.

However, Wipro recruits candidates throughout the year. This means trainees who joined during the first three months of 2022 could face a wait of more than five years before completing their academic programme and becoming full-time employees.

The company ended the previous year with revenue of $10.48 billion, down 0.3% from the preceding year. This marked its third consecutive year of revenue decline.

Wipro subsequently sought to address the concerns by advancing the conversion date by a month.

On 1 September, the company told trainees that it had brought forward the conversion date. “Pleased to share that we have been effectively able to reduce the conversion timeline by 1 month (from 1st April to 1st March 2027),” wrote Nimesh Gala, a senior trainer and facilitator at Wipro.

However, there will be no gap between the final two semesters. Gala said the dissertation would begin immediately after the seventh semester as a “one-off exemption only for this batch”. Trainees with a CGPA above 5.5 and a grade above 'E' can complete the programme in approximately 3.5 years.

This is not the first instance of Wipro delaying onboarding and the full-time conversion of employees this year. According to a Mint report dated 19 August, more than 200 entry-level candidates were awaiting onboarding through its Elite hiring process, which covers campus and off-campus recruitment.

The delays are consistent with Wipro management's cautious commentary on fresher hiring.

“We will continue to look at the demands in our environment and take a call. So we are not calling out any number right now,” Saurabh Govil, chief human resources officer at Wipro, said during the company's post-earnings conference call on 16 July. He added that lateral hiring would continue depending on demand for specific skills.

The delays in conversion come amid slower fresher onboarding at some of the world's largest technology services firms.

New Jersey-based Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp has given tentative joining dates to some graduates that extend more than a year after they received letters of intent. Accenture Plc, Tata Consultancy Services Ltd and Oracle Corp have also delayed onboarding and, in some cases, withdrawn roles.

Jas Bardia is a Bengaluru-based business journalist covering India’s information technology (IT) services sector and Global Capability Centres (GCCs). Known for his investigative depth and attention to detail, Jas has a knack for breaking stories on leadership shifts, high-stakes deals, and evolving industry trends long before they hit the mainstream. If the news is anything IT-related, chances are this author has broken it. Before joining Mint in November 2023, Jas honed his financial reporting skills at Bloomberg News in Mumbai, where he covered bonds and currencies following his graduation from the Asian College of Journalism. When he isn’t chasing his next exclusive, Jas is likely scouting the city’s newest culinary spots, cool events, or is immersed in the electric atmosphere of a Bengaluru FC match at the Sree Kanteerava Stadium. evidence.title: Wipro's AI Push Frees Capacity Equal To 20,000 Workers: What It Means
evidence.text:
Wipro's AI Push Frees Capacity Equal To 20,000 Workers: What It Means

Wipro’s artificial intelligence initiatives have increased productivity to a level equivalent to the work output of around 20,000 employees, according to the company’s Chief Technology Officer Sandhya Arun.

However, Wipro has clarified that this does not mean 20,000 employees have been replaced or laid off by AI. The additional capacity has instead been redeployed within the company as Wipro moves towards what it calls a “human-AI operating model”.

Wipro had around 243,000 employees as of June 2026. Against that workforce, AI-generated productivity equivalent to 20,000 employees represents a significant increase in the amount of work that can potentially be completed with the existing workforce.

The company says employees whose capacity has been freed up are being moved to other projects, trained for new roles or assigned to work alongside AI systems.

In some cases, engineers can also manage multiple AI agents working on different tasks.

AI Is Changing How Wipro Uses Its Employees

Wipro’s approach is not simply about replacing human workers with AI tools.

According to CTO Sandhya Arun, the company is moving towards a model where humans and AI systems work together. An engineer could supervise several AI agents while focusing on more complex technical or business responsibilities.

This changes the role of employees rather than necessarily eliminating the position itself.

The company has also been investing heavily in AI training. More than 100,000 employees have received advanced AI-related training and certifications as Wipro attempts to prepare its workforce for an increasingly AI-driven technology industry.

Wipro’s technology leadership says companies should not measure AI success only by how many hours of work can be saved.

Instead, the focus should increasingly be on outcomes such as better customer experiences, new revenue opportunities and improved business performance.

This represents an important shift for India’s IT services industry, where companies have traditionally relied heavily on human engineers and developers to deliver technology services to global clients.

If AI allows the same work to be completed faster, IT companies will need to demonstrate how those productivity gains translate into value for customers.

The development also comes at a time when artificial intelligence is reshaping hiring across India’s large IT services companies.

Companies are increasingly looking for employees who can work with AI tools, develop AI applications, manage AI agents and help clients integrate the technology into their businesses.

This could result in fewer requirements for some repetitive tasks while increasing demand for specialised technical, consulting and AI-related skills.

The result may therefore be a change in the composition of IT work rather than simply a reduction in the number of technology jobs.

Wipro is also expanding its pool of forward-deployed engineers who work closely with clients to accelerate AI adoption.

The company has not disclosed a specific target for this workforce, but its CTO indicated that Wipro’s approach would broadly align with developments at other major Indian IT services companies.

The bigger challenge, according to Wipro, is ensuring that engineers develop the skills required to work effectively with AI systems.

While productivity gains can reduce the amount of human effort required to complete certain tasks, the long-term business impact will depend on whether companies can convert those gains into additional revenue, stronger margins and better customer outcomes.

Wipro has not separately disclosed its AI revenue, making it difficult to measure the company’s AI business purely through reported revenue.

For India’s IT industry, however, Wipro’s latest numbers provide another indication of how quickly AI is changing the way software development and technology services are delivered.

The figure of 20,000 is therefore best understood as AI-enabled work capacity rather than 20,000 jobs eliminated.

Wipro says its AI initiatives have generated productivity equivalent to the work of around 20,000 employees. The company says this capacity has been redeployed rather than resulting in 20,000 job cuts. With more than 100,000 employees receiving advanced AI training, Wipro is moving towards a human-AI operating model where employees work alongside and manage AI systems.

Wipro Opening Bell Updates: Share Price Hits New 52-Week Low Amid Nifty Exit

Wipro (WIPRO) share price is at ₹164.78, down -0.97%, hitting a new 52-week low as it prepares to exit the Nifty 50, while its AI strategy and Q1 results remain key for investors.

Wipro closed yesterday's session at ₹166.40, opening slightly higher today at ₹166.90. However, early trade has seen the stock dip to an intraday low of ₹164.40, pushing its Live Traded Price (LTP) to ₹164.78. This decline signifies a -0.97% change, indicating a cautious to negative sentiment as the market digests recent developments and broader sector performance. Notably, the current trading action has seen Wipro hit a new 52-week low.

Global market cues present a mixed picture for Indian equities. US markets concluded Thursday's session on a positive note, with the Dow rising 0.61%, the S&P 500 gaining 1.14%, and the Nasdaq Composite advancing 1.69%, largely driven by chipmakers. However, US stock futures were reported as steady to mixed on Friday morning. Across Asia, early Friday trade saw markets generally higher, with Japan's Nikkei 225 gaining over 0.5% and South Korea's KOSPI advancing more than 2%. On the macroeconomic front, crude oil prices are easing from their recent peaks but remain elevated near the $100-a-barrel mark, which continues to be a point of concern for India.

Institutional investor activity showed Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) as net sellers, offloading ₹4,703 crore in the previous session. Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) provided crucial support, with net buying of ₹5,869 crore. The broader Indian IT sector continues to face headwinds from a demand slowdown in Western markets, where clients are prioritizing cost optimization over new digital transformation projects. Generative AI, while offering an enormous new market, is also disrupting traditional services and impacting hiring. However, reports suggest an expected sharp recovery in the sector beginning 2026, fueled by accelerating demand for AI services.

Wipro has been in the spotlight due to several key announcements. A significant development is the company's impending exit from India's benchmark Nifty 50 index, effective September 30, 2026. This change is expected to trigger adjustments by index-tracking funds. On a more positive note, Wipro announced an enhanced partnership with Google Cloud on September 15, 2026, aimed at deeper enterprise integration of Gemini Enterprise and agentic AI. As part of this collaboration, Wipro plans to train over ten thousand professionals in AI. Furthermore, Wipro allotted equity shares under its ESOP/ESPS plans on September 17, 2026. The company also recently renewed its long-standing Digital Workplace Services contract with ABB earlier in September.

Analyst sentiment has been cautious. Morgan Stanley, in June 2026, maintained a price target of INR 161 for Wipro, anticipating the company might lag its peers in sequential revenue growth due to client-specific challenges in the banking, financial services, and technology verticals. Wipro's Q1 FY27 (June 2026 quarter) results showed net income marginally up by 0.6%, but revenue and profitability were impacted by weak discretionary spending and a challenging macroeconomic environment.

Wipro's previous close was ₹166.40, with today's open at ₹166.90. The stock has demonstrated early weakness, recording an intraday low of ₹164.40, which now marks a new 52-week low, surpassing the previous 52-week low of ₹165.02. Immediate support for the stock could be around the ₹164.00-₹163.97 level. On the upside, initial resistance may be encountered near the ₹166.90 mark (today's open) and subsequently around its previous close of ₹166.40. The 52-week high for Wipro stands at ₹273.10.

As the session unfolds, traders will be closely monitoring Wipro's ability to recover from its new 52-week low. The interplay of its Nifty 50 index exit, set for month-end, and the strategic push into AI through partnerships like Google Cloud will likely shape investor perception. The broader IT sector's performance, influenced by global demand and the ongoing shift towards AI-led services, will also be critical. FII and DII flows will provide further directional cues, with sustained DII support potentially offsetting FII selling pressure. Volatility is expected, and a close watch on the prevailing macroeconomic environment, especially crude oil prices, and global market sentiment will be essential.

evidence.title: Integration, Not Supply, Now Biggest Semiconductor Challenge For Industry: HCLTech Study
evidence.text:
Integration, Not Supply, Now Biggest Semiconductor Challenge For Industry: HCLTech Study

About 71% said AI is increasing the importance of semiconductor architecture as a strategic business decision.

Integration has overtaken supply chain constraints as the semiconductor industry's biggest challenge, according to a global research report by HCLTech released on Friday.

The report, titled "The Silicon Shift: When Every Industry Becomes a Chip Industry", surveyed 300 senior leaders across engineering, research and development (R&D), semiconductor and hardware, product, innovation and technology strategy functions in the United States, Europe and Asia.

According to the report, 98% of enterprises said they are more dependent on semiconductors than they were three years ago, and 99% expect this dependency to increase over the next five years.

Get the latest issue of Outlook Business

About 71% said AI is increasing the importance of semiconductor architecture as a strategic business decision.

The dependency is most acute in industrial automation, where 75% of respondents reported being much more reliant on semiconductors than three years ago, the strongest acceleration among the sectors studied, the report said.

"However, integration emerged as the industry's biggest challenge, cited by the largest share of respondents as the primary reason current solutions fall short, outpacing supply chain constraints and performance limitations. Integration was the leading concern in medical devices and industrial automation and featured in the top two across all four sectors studied," HCLTech said.

To address these challenges, enterprises said they are turning to engineering service providers that can offer greater value through hardware and software integration (67%), supply chain and lifecycle support (61%) and deeper industry expertise (59%).

The report said this suggests competitive advantage is increasingly being shaped by the quality of engineering partnerships and integration expertise, rather than silicon performance alone.

"Semiconductor dependency now shapes corporate strategy, not just engineering roadmaps. What this research reveals is that enterprises are no longer asking which chip to buy. Rather, they are asking how to build a durable capability around silicon across long product lifecycles, high regulatory stakes and complex integration environments.

"The companies that solve that problem, and the partners who help them, will define their sectors for the next decade," said Ameer Saithu, Executive Vice President & Global Head, Semiconductor Business, HCLTech.

The report found that while 79% of enterprises currently rely entirely on off-the-shelf silicon or mostly commercial silicon with limited customisation, 66% expect to move to a different model within five years.

evidence.title: Genpact’s ED NOC Rejection Quashed: Karnataka HC Remands Matter for Fresh Decision on USD 100 Million GIFT City Investment
evidence.text:
Genpact’s ED NOC Rejection Quashed: Karnataka HC Remands Matter for Fresh Decision on USD 100 Million GIFT City Investment

The Karnataka High Court has set aside the Enforcement Directorate’s rejection of Genpact application seeking a No-Objection Certificate (NOC) under Rule 10 of the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, holding that mere pendency of an investigation cannot by itself justify refusal of an NOC.

The bench of Justice Suraj Govindaraj dismissed Genpact’s separate challenge to the ED’s seizure order concerning its Gurgaon property and vacated the interim protection earlier granted against the seizure.

Buy Now: 100+ Judgements On Customs Classification

The first petition challenged the ED’s communication dated January 13, 2026, rejecting Genpact India’s application for an NOC under Rule 10 of the FEMA (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022.

Genpact had sought permission for a proposed investment of USD 100 million in its wholly owned subsidiary, Genpact Global (IFSC) Pvt. Ltd., established in Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), for setting up a global/regional corporate treasury centre.

The second petition, W.P. No. 7283 of 2026, challenged the ED’s order dated February 3, 2026, passed under Section 37A of FEMA, by which the ED had seized Genpact’s property situated at DLF City, Phase V, Sector 53, Gurgaon, Haryana.

The Court noted that the factual background of both petitions was substantially common, although the legal reliefs sought were different.

Proposed USD 100 million investment in GIFT City

Genpact India had incorporated Genpact Global (IFSC) Pvt. Ltd. in 2025 as a wholly owned subsidiary in GIFT City. The entity obtained provisional registration from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) on September 15, 2025, as a finance company for undertaking global/regional corporate treasury centre activities.

The proposed treasury activities included lending, cash pooling and investments for Genpact group entities located outside India.

Since Genpact India had earlier received summons from the ED, it applied on November 26, 2025, under Rule 10 of the FEMA Overseas Investment Rules seeking an NOC for investing USD 100 million in the GIFT City entity.

The ED rejected the application on January 13, 2026.

The dispute traces back to a series of transactions undertaken in 2015 during the restructuring of Genpact’s Indian operations.

The Court recorded that Empower Research Knowledge Services Pvt. Ltd. (“Empower India”) had been acquired by the Genpact Group and was subsequently identified as the vehicle for consolidating Genpact’s Indian operations.

In January 2015, Headstrong Singapore borrowed approximately USD 660 million from Morgan Stanley and approximately USD 77.50 million from its holding company. The funds were infused into Empower India, which used them to acquire shares of the erstwhile Genpact India. The consideration for the share acquisition was approximately USD 737.50 million.

A second phase of transactions followed in March 2015. Genpact Global Holdings Bermuda borrowed approximately USD 737.50 million from Morgan Stanley. The amount was transferred to Genpact Luxembourg, which subscribed to approximately ₹4,600 crore of non-convertible debentures (NCDs) issued by Empower India.

The Court recorded that the NCDs carried an 11% annual coupon.

The ED examined the subsequent movement of these funds and alleged that the transactions formed part of a connected arrangement involving movement of funds through various Genpact entities.

According to the ED’s case, the ₹4,600 crore received by Empower India through the NCD subscription was transferred on the same day towards acquisition of the remaining 51% shareholding in Old Genpact India. The amount was thereafter transferred through the Genpact entities and ultimately utilised towards repayment of the Morgan Stanley borrowing.

The High Court observed that the sequence, timing and relationship between the entities could be examined collectively for determining whether the transactions constituted part of a larger arrangement.

Importantly, however, the Court stated that at the stage of examining the jurisdictional foundation for action under Section 37A, it was not finally determining whether the entire arrangement constituted a FEMA contravention.

The ED subsequently passed an order dated February 3, 2026, under Section 37A of FEMA, seizing Genpact’s Gurgaon property.

Genpact challenged the action, principally contending that the underlying transactions took place in January and March 2015, whereas Section 37A of FEMA came into force only on September 9, 2015 .

Its argument was that Section 37A, being a substantive provision, could not be retrospectively applied to transactions that had already been completed before the provision came into force.

Genpact relied upon the Karnataka High Court’s earlier decision in Canara Bank v. Commissioner of Customs , where the Court had held that Section 37A was prospective in operation in relation to property mortgaged before the provision came into force.

The company argued that both the January 2015 equity transaction and March 2015 NCD transaction were completed before September 9, 2015, and therefore could not subsequently be subjected to Section 37A proceedings on the basis of retrospectivity.

ED relied on the complete movement of funds

The ED, on the other hand, maintained that the transactions could not be examined in isolation.

The material relied upon by the ED included the foreign borrowings, infusion of funds into Indian entities, acquisition of shares, issuance of NCDs, transfer of NCD proceeds and subsequent repayment of the foreign borrowing.

The Court held that the short interval between the successive transfers, the identity and relationship of the entities involved, the financial position of Empower India, the immediate onward transfer of the NCD proceeds, the purpose of the NCD structure, the subsequent amalgamation and later discharge of the NCD liability were relevant circumstances for examination.

The Court further observed that the fact that the NCDs were denominated in Indian rupees did not, by itself, conclude the issue under Sections 4 and 37A of FEMA.

Likewise, the fact that Genpact Luxembourg was a SEBI-registered FPI did not make every transaction undertaken by it immune from examination under FEMA.

The Court therefore declined to accept, at this stage, the proposition that the ED could not examine the transactions merely because the initial funds originated from a foreign lender.

Earlier Income Tax and regulatory proceedings not conclusive

Genpact relied upon various earlier proceedings before the Income Tax Department, ITAT, Delhi High Court, RBI and SEBI.

The record showed that the ITAT had set aside the CIT’s order under Section 263 in June 2022 after holding that the relevant transaction had been considered and examined. The Delhi High Court subsequently dismissed the Revenue’s challenge on December 11, 2024. The Revenue thereafter approached the Supreme Court, where notice was issued without any stay being granted, according to the judgment.

The Court, however, held that these earlier proceedings did not completely foreclose the ED’s examination under FEMA.

According to the High Court, RBI and SEBI communications demonstrated that particular aspects of the NCD transaction had been placed before and considered by the respective authorities, but they did not establish that the entire arrangement and movement of funds through the various entities had been examined and approved from the standpoint of Section 4 of FEMA .

The Court similarly held that the Income Tax proceedings concerned the liability and assessment of foreign Genpact entities and did not conclusively determine the separate question arising under FEMA in relation to the Indian company.

The more significant relief came in W.P. No. 16763 of 2026 concerning the NOC.

The Court examined whether the mere pendency of an ED investigation was sufficient to refuse an NOC under Rule 10.

The Court held that mere pendency of an investigation is not sufficient to refuse an NOC under Rule 10 . The authority must have relevant, rational and disclosed reasons demonstrating a nexus between the investigation and the proposed investment.

The Court noted that Rule 10 itself contemplates a situation where a person under investigation seeks an NOC. Therefore, the existence of an investigation cannot automatically operate as a ground for rejection.

At the same time, the Court clarified that this did not mean the proposed investment was wholly unrelated to the investigation. The proposed GIFT City entity was intended to undertake treasury activities involving financing overseas Genpact entities, while the investigation concerned alleged movement of value from India through overseas entities.

Thus, according to the Court, the ED was entitled to examine whether the proposed investment had any bearing upon the matters under investigation.

ED’s January 13 rejection lacked reasons

The crucial defect identified by the Court was in the January 13, 2026 rejection communication itself .

The communication merely stated that the request for issuance of an NOC had been rejected. It did not explain why the proposed investment was objectionable or how it was connected with the pending investigation.

The Court held that the subsequent seizure order dated February 3, 2026 could not retrospectively cure the defect in the earlier NOC rejection.

The validity of the January 13 decision had to be examined on the basis of the reasons and material available when that decision was made. A subsequent order could not supply reasons that were absent from the original decision.

The Court applied the principle associated with Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner that an administrative order must stand or fall on the reasons contained in the order itself.

No deemed NOC merely because of 60-day period

Genpact had also argued that the NOC should be deemed to have been granted because Rule 10 provides a 60-day period within which the concerned agency must either furnish the NOC or state its objection.

The High Court rejected this contention.

It noted that Genpact’s application was filed on November 26, 2025, and the ED communicated its rejection on January 13, 2026, before expiry of the 60-day period.

Accordingly, there had been a response within the prescribed period. Although the response was found inadequate because it did not disclose sufficient reasons, that did not amount to a failure to respond for purposes of the deeming provision.

In its final order, the Karnataka High Court adopted different approaches to the two writ petitions.

W.P. No. 7283 of 2026 , challenging the Section 37A seizure order, was dismissed .

The interim order staying operation of the February 3, 2026 seizure order was vacated. However, the Court clarified that seizure of the head-office premises would not prevent Genpact from continuing its lawful business operations from the premises.

Genpact was restrained from creating third-party rights in the property or transferring, alienating, encumbering or otherwise dealing with the property inconsistently with the seizure order.

In contrast, W.P. No. 16763 of 2026 was allowed in part .

The Court set aside the January 13, 2026 communication rejecting Genpact’s application for an NOC under Rule 10 and remitted the matter to the Competent Authority for fresh consideration .

Genpact was granted liberty to place all relevant facts, documents and material before the Competent Authority within 10 days from receipt of the certified copy of the judgment.

The Competent Authority has been directed to consider the material and pass a fresh, reasoned and speaking order within 10 days from receipt of the complete submission.
